R00.titleEn: In-Memory Architecture & Single-Threaded Event Loop (>100,000 ops/s)
R00.summaryEn: Analyze the 1,000x speed gap between RAM and SSD, the Single-Threaded Event Loop architecture (epoll/kqueue), the RESP3 Wire Protocol, and how to run Redis 8 safely with Docker.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> In typical web systems, traditional relational databases (**PostgreSQL / MySQL**) store data primarily on disk (**SSD/Disk**). Each query usually takes around `2ms – 10ms` for disk reads, SQL parsing, and transaction lock management. When a system experiences a traffic spike (for example **15,000 requests/second** during a Flash Sale), disk I/O and connection queues quickly become overwhelmed.
>
> **Redis** (*Remote Dictionary Server*) solves this problem by storing and processing data directly in **RAM** through 3 key technical mechanisms:
> - **In-Memory Storage:** Accessing **DRAM (`~100 nanoseconds`)** is roughly ==1,000x faster== than random reads on an SSD (`~100 microseconds`).
> - **Single-Threaded Event Loop (Lock-Free Single Thread):** Instead of using dozens of threads that modify data concurrently and require **`Mutex Lock`** synchronization along with **`Context Switch`** overhead, Redis uses **a single Main Thread** that executes commands sequentially in RAM. Because each command takes `< 1 microsecond`, this model ==completely eliminates lock contention and Deadlocks==.
> - **I/O Multiplexing (`epoll` on Linux / `kqueue` on macOS):** An operating system mechanism that allows 1 thread to monitor tens of thousands of TCP connections simultaneously without spawning a dedicated thread per connection, processing sockets only when data is ready.
>
> *Intuitive analogy:* Imagine this mechanism like a single clerk processing requests sequentially right on a desk (RAM) via an automated signal board for thousands of customers, rather than multiple clerks running down to the basement warehouse (SSD) and waiting on each other to unlock doors.

Whether you write backend services in **Python (`FastAPI` / `Django` / `asyncio`)**, **Node.js / TypeScript**, **Go**, **Java**, or are learning distributed systems for the first time, mastering these 3 pillars will help you understand why a lightweight Redis process can handle **>100,000 operations/second**:

- [>] Reading a memory cell in **DRAM (`~100 ns`)** combined with hardware-friendly data structures keeps the actual execution time of most commands under `1 microsecond`.
- [+] Because only **a single Main Thread** accesses the data store (*Keyspace*) sequentially, Redis ==eliminates 100% of Mutex Lock, Deadlock, and Context Switch overhead== across command execution threads.
- [!] From **Redis 6 → Redis 8**, Redis added **I/O Threads** on the outer network layer to read/write socket data in parallel across multiple CPU cores, while keeping the core command execution strictly sequential and completely thread-safe!

steps.headingEn: From In-Process Memory to a Shared RAM Data Store (Redis)
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Why not just use a Python `dict` or a JS/Go/Java `Map` as a Cache?
> A `cache = {}` variable in Python or `new Map()` in Node.js is very fast, but **it is isolated inside each individual process**: if you run 10 servers (or 10 Kubernetes Pods), each instance holds a different copy of the data and all data is lost whenever the process restarts. **Redis** extracts that memory into a ==Shared Networked In-Memory Data Structure Store== that every service and programming language can access consistently.

| Familiar Concept in Code | Equivalent in Redis 8 | Where Redis Excels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dict` (Python) / `Map` (JS/Java/Go) | **Global Keyspace** (`SET`, `GET`) | Shared consistently across hundreds of API containers, with built-in self-expiring timers (**`TTL`** — *Time-To-Live*) down to the millisecond |
| Nested `dict` / `set` / `collections.deque` | **Hash, Set, List, ZSet, Stream** | Data structures written in C for ultra-low RAM usage, sorting leaderboards of millions of users in `O(log N)` |
| Async event loop (`asyncio` / `libuv` / `netpoll`) | **`aeEventLoop` (`epoll` / `kqueue`)** | Each standard command completes in `< 1 µs`, enabling 1 core to reach `100k – 300k+ ops/sec` without thread race conditions |

> [!TIP] The 2026 In-Memory Ecosystem & Standard Client Libraries per Language
> In production environments or cloud system design, you will encounter sibling engines that speak the same Redis protocol:
> - **Redis 8:** The latest official release, bundling JSON, Vector Search (AI/RAG), TimeSeries, and Bloom Filter natively into the core along with major multi-threaded I/O improvements.
> - **Valkey:** A fully open-source fork (BSD license) branched from Redis 7.2 under the **Linux Foundation**, 100% command-compatible with Redis and widely supported by AWS ElastiCache and Google Cloud Memorystore.
> - **DragonflyDB:** A next-generation engine written in C++ using a *shared-nothing multi-threaded* architecture (utilizing all 32–64 CPU cores on a single machine for datasets of hundreds of GBs).
> - **Memcached:** An early minimalist multi-threaded string cache — stores only plain `key -> string` pairs, **without** ZSets/Streams/Lists or disk persistence like Redis.
> - **Recommended SDK Libraries:** Python uses **`redis-py`** (includes `redis.asyncio` for FastAPI) · Node.js/TS uses **`ioredis`** or **`node-redis`** · Go uses **`go-redis`** · Java/Spring uses **`Lettuce`** or **`Redisson`**.

steps.headingEn: RESP3 Wire Protocol: Why Does Redis Parse Commands So Much Faster Than HTTP/JSON?
steps.bodyEn:
Unlike HTTP REST APIs that attach dozens of text header lines and force the server to scan every `{...}` brace in JSON, libraries like `redis-py` or `ioredis` talk directly to Redis over TCP port `6379` using **RESP** (*Redis Serialization Protocol* — Redis's wire serialization protocol, defaulting to **RESP3** support in Redis 8).

The secret of RESP lies in **prefixing the exact byte length at the start of every element** (`$<byte-length>\r\n`): the Redis parser knows the exact number of bytes to jump to extract the entire payload (safe even for images/binary files — *binary-safe*) without spending CPU scanning character by character!

```redis
# Khi ứng dụng gửi lệnh: SET app:version "8.0"
# Khung truyền RESP thực sự chạy trên dây mạng là Mảng 3 phần tử (*3):
# *3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$11\r\napp:version\r\n$3\r\n8.0\r\n

PING
ECHO "Xin chao Redis 8"
SET app:version "8.0"
GET app:version
INFO server
INFO memory
```

Testing a connection directly from **Python (`redis-py`)** or **Node.js (`ioredis`)** takes just a few concise lines:

```python
# Python (pip install redis) — Đồng bộ hoặc bất đồng bộ với FastAPI (redis.asyncio)
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="127.0.0.1", port=6379, decode_responses=True, protocol=3)
r.set("app:version", "8.0", ex=3600)  # Ghi kèm hẹn giờ tự hủy TTL = 3600 giây
print(r.get("app:version"))           # -> "8.0"
```

> [!WARNING] The Biggest Bottleneck of the Single-Threaded Model: Head-of-Line Blocking
> Because there is only one main thread executing commands sequentially, if a single command takes a long time to run (`O(N)` complexity on a large dataset), every other connection must wait in the queue until that command finishes.
> Specifically in Redis, if you run **`KEYS *`** to scan 20 million keys (taking `800ms`), ==every other `GET`/`SET` command across the entire system is frozen for those 800ms==. A mandatory rule when operating Redis is to **always check the Big-O time complexity of a command before running it in Production**. (Think of it like a single checkout lane backing up if the person at the front takes several minutes to count items).

steps.headingEn: Three Minimum Safety Rules on Day One of Running Redis
steps.bodyEn:
Before writing your first line of application code connecting to Redis, lock down these 3 basic operational guardrails in your `redis.conf` and Docker Compose files:

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Cấu Hình Khởi Chạy Redis: Không Bảo Mật vs Chuẩn Mực An Toàn"
subtitle: "Không bao giờ mở trực tiếp cổng 6379 không mật khẩu ra ngoài mạng công cộng"
left:
  badge: "RỦI RO BỊ BOT QUÉT TỰ ĐỘNG TẤN CÔNG"
  title: "Mở 0.0.0.0 & Tắt Protected Mode"
  tone: rose
  lang: redis-conf
  code: |
    bind 0.0.0.0
    port 6379
    protected-mode no
    loglevel debug
  bullets:
    - "Bot quét cổng `6379` toàn cầu sẽ tìm thấy server trong vài phút và gọi `FLUSHALL` xóa trắng dữ liệu hoặc chiếm quyền máy chủ."
    - "`loglevel debug` ghi hàng triệu dòng nhật ký mỗi giờ làm tràn đầy ổ cứng máy chủ."
right:
  badge: "CHUẨN PHÁT TRIỂN & NỘI BỘ"
  title: "Khoá Loopback / Private IP & Giữ Khiên Bảo Vệ"
  tone: emerald
  lang: redis-conf
  code: |
    bind 127.0.0.1 -::1
    port 6379
    protected-mode yes
    loglevel notice
    tcp-keepalive 300
    slowlog-log-slower-than 10000
  bullets:
    - "Chỉ lắng nghe trên địa chỉ nội bộ được chỉ định rõ và bật khiên bảo vệ `protected-mode yes`."
    - "Ghi nhận mọi câu lệnh chạy lâu hơn `10,000 µs` (`10ms`) vào nhật ký lệnh chậm `SLOWLOG` để bắt sớm các truy vấn gây nghẽn."
```

When spinning up a local development environment with **Docker Compose v2** (`docker compose up -d`), always ==pin a specific image version like `redis:8.0-alpine`== (avoid floating `:latest` tags), bind the port exclusively to `127.0.0.1:6379:6379`, and attach a `healthcheck`:

```yaml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8.0-alpine
    container_name: shop-redis
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--loglevel", "notice"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  redis_data:
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways Before Moving to Hands-On Labs
> - **Redis is fast thanks to 3 pillars**: data lives directly in **RAM (`~100ns`)**, compact optimized data structures, and a **Single-Threaded Event Loop** combined with **I/O Multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`)** with zero `Mutex` lock overhead.
> - The **RESP2/RESP3** protocol prefixes payloads with byte lengths, allowing `redis-py`, `ioredis`, and `go-redis` to communicate at ultra-high speed over TCP port `6379`.
> - Always use **`INFO memory`**, **`INFO stats`**, and **`SLOWLOG GET`** to monitor health, and lock down `bind` + `protected-mode yes` from day one.

readings.noteEn: A careless redis.conf file once caused tens of thousands of Redis servers on the Internet to have their data wiped or crypto-mining malware installed by automated bots.
readings.taskEn: Identify the 2 most dangerous configuration lines in this file that allow anyone who knows the IP address to run FLUSHALL.
readings.answerEn: 1) `bind 0.0.0.0` listens on all public network interfaces; 2) `protected-mode no` disables the final self-defense shield while no password (`requirepass` or `ACL user`) is configured, allowing any anonymous connection from the Internet to execute full administrative commands.

readings.noteEn: A clean baseline configuration for Redis 8 when running locally or inside an isolated private network.
readings.taskEn: Comparing against the flawed config above, how have the `bind`, `protected-mode`, `tcp-keepalive`, and `loglevel` directives been configured?
readings.answerEn: The secure config locks down `bind 127.0.0.1 -::1` (accepting only local connections), enables `protected-mode yes`, sets `tcp-keepalive 300` to clean up dead/zombie connections, and keeps `loglevel notice` sufficient for diagnostics without blowing up disk space.

R00-Q1.qEn: Why does Redis choose to execute data manipulation commands on **a single Main Thread (Single-Threaded Event Loop)** and still achieve hundreds of thousands of operations per second?
choicesEn: Because the C language does not support multi-threading on the Linux operating system
Because all data resides in ultra-fast RAM, combined with I/O Multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`), completely eliminating `Mutex` lock contention and CPU context switching overhead
Because Redis automatically compiles every command into background SQL queries running on SSD
Because Redis only allows a maximum of 1 TCP connection from an application at a time
R00-Q1.explainEn: Data in RAM takes only ~100ns to access; by using I/O Multiplexing to aggregate tens of thousands of sockets and executing sequentially on 1 thread, Redis avoids Mutex Lock and Context Switching overhead while keeping every command atomic.

R00-Q2.qEn: In Redis 8, there are NO background or I/O threads whatsoever other than the single Event Loop thread.
R00-Q2.explainEn: False! Command execution is single-threaded, but Redis 6–8 uses **Threaded I/O** to read/write network socket buffers and **BIO Worker Threads** to asynchronously free memory (`UNLINK`) and flush AOF to disk (`fsync`) without blocking the main thread.

R00-Q3.qEn: What happens on an 8-core Redis host when 1 microservice accidentally runs `KEYS *` taking `300ms` over a dataset of 10 million keys?
choicesEn: The remaining 7 cores automatically share the load so other `GET`/`SET` commands still respond under `1ms`
All `GET`/`SET` commands from every other client are queued and strictly blocked for `300ms` (Head-of-Line Blocking) even though total machine CPU reports only ~12.5%
Redis automatically cancels the `KEYS *` command after `10ms` to protect other connections
Only the connection that sent `KEYS *` slows down; other connections in the Connection Pool are unaffected
R00-Q3.explainEn: Since all data access commands go through a single sequential Event Loop thread, an `O(N)` command occupying the main thread for `300ms` stalls every command queued behind it.

R00-Q4.qEn: Which exact phase of a Redis command does the execution time recorded in `SLOWLOG GET` measure?
choicesEn: The total round-trip time from when the application (Python/Node.js/Go) calls the function until it receives the response (including LAN/WAN network latency)
Only the time the Redis main thread spends executing that command in RAM (excluding network latency or socket I/O wait time)
The time the operating system takes to write an RDB snapshot to physical disk
The time spent waiting for an idle connection from the client-side Connection Pool
R00-Q4.explainEn: `SLOWLOG` only measures the pure execution time of the command inside Redis's main thread. If your app reports `200ms` latency while `SLOWLOG` is empty, the bottleneck is usually the network, DNS, Connection Pool, or a blocked Event Loop on the Node.js/Python side!

R00-Q5.qEn: Setting `bind 0.0.0.0` with `protected-mode no` in `redis.conf` on a VPS with a public IP is a safe way to make containers connect faster.
R00-Q5.explainEn: Critically false! Opening `0.0.0.0` and disabling `protected-mode` without ACLs/passwords and an internal firewall exposes full memory control to the Internet — automated bots can wipe data or compromise the host within minutes.

R00-Q6.qEn: To log any command slower than **5 milliseconds (`5ms`)** into the Slowlog, what integer value must you pass at the end of the `CONFIG SET` command below?
R00-Q6.explainEn: The `slowlog-log-slower-than` parameter uses **microseconds (`µs`)**. Since `1ms = 1000µs`, a `5ms` threshold corresponds to exactly `5000`.

R00-Q7.qEn: When you send the connection-check command without any arguments as shown below, what standard response string will the Redis server return?
R00-Q7.explainEn: When `PING` is called with no arguments, Redis immediately replies with the Simple String `PONG` over RESP (`+PONG\r\n`), confirming the Event Loop is alive and ready to process commands.

R00-FC1.frontEn: What three architectural pillars enable Redis to process over **100,000 ops/sec** at sub-millisecond (`<1ms`) latency?
R00-FC1.backEn: 1) Data stored directly in **RAM (`~100ns`)**; 2) **I/O Multiplexing (`epoll`/`kqueue`)** handling tens of thousands of TCP connections without per-connection threads; 3) **Single-Threaded Event Loop** eliminating Mutex Locks and Context Switching.

R00-FC2.frontEn: When does **Head-of-Line Blocking** occur on the Redis Event Loop?
R00-FC2.backEn: When a client runs an `O(N)` command on a large dataset (such as `KEYS *`, `HGETALL`, or `DEL` on a BigKey), monopolizing the main thread and forcing all `O(1)` commands behind it to wait in line.

R00-FC3.frontEn: What tasks do the **background/helper threads (Threaded I/O & BIO)** handle in Redis 8?
R00-FC3.backEn: Reading/writing and parsing network socket buffers (I/O Threads), asynchronously freeing large memory blocks (`UNLINK`), and background disk syncing (`appendfsync everysec`).

R00-FC4.frontEn: What unit does `slowlog-log-slower-than` use, and does it include network latency?
R00-FC4.backEn: The unit is **microseconds (`µs`)** (`10000` = `10ms`). It **only measures CPU time executing the command on the main thread** and completely excludes network transit time.

R00-FC5.frontEn: Why is the **RESP (Redis Serialization Protocol)** much faster to parse than JSON over HTTP?
R00-FC5.backEn: RESP sends a data-type prefix and exact byte length before the payload (e.g., `$5\r\nhello\r\n`), allowing the C parser to jump straight by byte count without scanning for closing braces or string escapes.

R00-FC6.frontEn: Which two minimum directives in `redis.conf` prevent accidentally exposing Redis to the public Internet?
R00-FC6.backEn: `bind 127.0.0.1 -::1` (listen only on local loopback interfaces) combined with `protected-mode yes` (reject external connections when no ACL/password authentication is configured).

R01.titleEn: Strings (SDS), TTL Mechanisms & Keyspace Naming Conventions
R01.summaryEn: Master the Simple Dynamic String (SDS) structure, atomic SET NX EX operations, INCR/DECRBY counters, Lazy + Active TTL expiration, and why SCAN must replace KEYS *.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> In **Redis**, a **`Key -> String Value`** pair is the most fundamental and widely used data type, designed with 4 key technical properties:
> - **`Key` (Identifier):** A unique name pointing to a value in RAM, typically structured hierarchically with colons like `auth:otp:user_42` for easy grouping by service.
> - **`TTL` (*Time-To-Live*):** The automatic expiration time of a key (e.g., `EX 120` for 120 seconds). Once expired, Redis automatically reclaims memory without requiring manual cleanup jobs in your app.
> - **`SDS` (*Simple Dynamic String*):** Unlike traditional C strings terminated by a null byte `\0` (which makes length checks `O(N)` and prevents storing binary data containing `0x00`), Redis implements **SDS** with explicit **`len`** and **`alloc`** fields in its header. As a result, `STRLEN` runs in `O(1)` and strings are *binary-safe* for text, JSON, images, or Protobuf/MessagePack payloads up to `512MB`.
> - **Atomicity:** Every Redis command executes in a single uninterrupted step on the main thread without interference from other commands.

In real-world production systems, the **Redis String** type serves **4 core roles** simultaneously:

- [>] **Ultra-Fast Response Cache:** Stores JSON strings or binary payloads with self-expiring timers (`EX` in seconds / `PX` in milliseconds).
- [+] **Atomic 64-bit Counters (`INCR` / `DECRBY`):** Counts video views, failed password attempts (*Rate Limiter*), or decrements promo vouchers ==without ever drifting even when thousands of users click at the exact same instant==.
- [+] **Duplicate Prevention Gate (`SET key val NX EX`):** Prevents double-click duplicate payments (*Idempotency Key*) in **a single atomic network round-trip**.
- [!] However, stuffing tens of millions of keys into a single RAM store without **naming conventions**, forgetting **`TTL`**, or accidentally running **`KEYS *`** are the leading causes of out-of-memory crashes and system outages!

steps.headingEn: The SDS Data Structure Underlying Redis Strings & 3 Memory-Saving Encodings
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Why does Redis use SDS instead of traditional C strings?
> Classic C strings do not store their length, so every length check or concatenation requires traversing the entire character array and reallocating memory. The **SDS** structure solves this by storing **`len`** (current length) and **`alloc`** (allocated capacity) directly in the header, giving `STRLEN` ==constant `O(1)` time complexity==, preventing buffer overflows, and safely storing any `bytes` (Python) or `Buffer` (Node.js) payload.

When you run `OBJECT ENCODING <key>`, Redis 8 automatically chooses **1 of 3 internal encodings** based on the stored content to minimize RAM usage:

| Internal Encoding | When Does Redis Activate It? | Practical Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`int`** | The string is a 64-bit signed integer (e.g., `"42"`, `"100050"`) | Stores the 8-byte integer directly inside the object pointer — **zero extra string allocation**, making `INCR`/`DECR` blazingly fast! |
| **`embstr`** | Short text strings **up to `44 bytes`** (UUIDs, OTP codes, order statuses) | Allocates a single contiguous memory block fitting neatly into **1 CPU Cache Line (`64B`)** |
| **`raw`** | Strings **`> 44 bytes`** (such as a product JSON blob) or after string modification via `APPEND` | Allocates a separate dynamic buffer with pre-allocated slack space to avoid frequent RAM reallocations |

```visual
    role: O(K) · Gom lô 1 vòng mạng
```

> [!WARNING] NEVER write `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE` as a second command!
> Suppose your Python, Go, or Node.js app finishes line 1 (`SETNX lock:order:99 1`) and the container crashes or loses network connectivity **before** sending line 2 (`EXPIRE lock:order:99 30`). The consequence: that key gets `TTL = -1` — becoming an ==immortal Zombie Key== stuck in RAM and deadlocking order #99 forever! Always combine them into **1 single atomic command**: `SET lock:order:99 <token> NX EX 30` (in Python `redis-py`: `r.set("lock:order:99", token, nx=True, ex=30)`).

steps.headingEn: Key Expiration (TTL) Mechanics & Keyspace Naming Conventions
steps.bodyEn:
When checking remaining lifetime with `TTL <key>` (in seconds) or `PTTL <key>` (in milliseconds), Redis always returns **1 of 3 special values** worth memorizing:
- **`>= 0`:** Remaining seconds (or milliseconds) before the key disappears automatically.
- **`-1`:** The key exists but ==has no expiration timer== (persists indefinitely until deleted or until `EXPIRE` is set).
- **`-2`:** The key **does not exist** (never created, already deleted, or already expired).

*How does Redis evict millions of expiring keys on time without freezing the system to scan all of RAM every second?* Redis coordinates **2 complementary mechanisms**:
1. **Lazy Expiration (*Passive deletion on access*):** Whenever an app runs `GET`, `TTL`, `EXISTS`, etc. on a key, Redis checks its expiration clock first — if past due, it deletes the key on the spot and returns `(nil)` / `-2`.
2. **Active Expiration (*Periodic random sampling*):** So expired keys that nobody touches again don't sit idle wasting RAM, by default **10 times per second (`hz 10`)**, Redis randomly samples 20 keys from the set of keys with a TTL. If **more than 25%** of the sample has expired, Redis immediately samples another batch to sweep away the garbage!

### Production Standards: Hierarchical Naming, `SCAN` & `UNLINK`

The industry-standard convention joins segments with colons `:` from broadest to narrowest: **`<service>:<entity>:<id>[:<attribute>]`** (e.g., `billing:invoice:882:status` or `auth:session:u4019`). When cleaning up keys in bulk or deleting huge keys:
- **Iterate keys with the `SCAN` cursor** (instead of `KEYS *`, which freezes the entire server).
- **Delete asynchronously with `UNLINK`** (instead of synchronous `DEL`): `UNLINK` takes only `O(1)` to unlink the key name from the main lookup table, then hands the heavy memory reclamation work to a **Background I/O Thread**!

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Quét Khoá Trên Production: Lệnh KEYS * (Chặn Luồng Chính) vs Con Trỏ SCAN + UNLINK"
subtitle: Cùng tìm và dọn các khoá theo mẫu `sess:expired:*` trên 20 triệu key nhưng tác động lên hệ thống khác nhau hoàn toàn
left:
  badge: CẤM TRÊN PRODUCTION
  title: KEYS sess:expired:* + DEL (Chặn cứng Server)
  tone: rose
  lang: redis
  code: |
    # Chặn đứng Event Loop suốt 450ms!
    KEYS sess:expired:*
    DEL sess:expired:1 sess:expired:2
  bullets:
    - "Quét liền một mạch toàn bộ 20 triệu mục trên bảng băm trước khi trả kết quả — **không thể dừng giữa chừng**."
    - "Làm vọt độ trễ mọi API khác, thậm chí khiến hệ thống giám sát tưởng máy chủ đã chết!"
    - "Xoá bằng `DEL` trên khoá lớn còn bắt luồng chính ngồi thu hồi RAM đồng bộ gây giật cục."
right:
  badge: CHUẨN REDIS 8 (PYTHON & NODE.JS)
  title: Con trỏ SCAN từng chặng nhỏ + UNLINK chạy nền
  tone: emerald
  lang: python
  code: |
    # Python (redis-py): Duyệt êm ái bằng scan_iter hoặc r.scan()
    cursor = 0
    while True:
        cursor, keys = r.scan(cursor=cursor, match="sess:expired:*", count=200)
        if keys:
            r.unlink(*keys)  # Nhờ luồng nền giải phóng RAM, không chặn luồng chính!
        if cursor == 0:
            break
  bullets:
    - "Mỗi nhịp `SCAN` chỉ dò qua ~`200` vị trí bảng băm (`< 0.1ms`), nhường đường cho hàng ngàn lệnh `GET`/`SET` khác chạy xen kẽ mượt mà."
    - "Bắt đầu với `cursor = 0` và chỉ kết thúc vòng lặp khi Redis trả lại **`cursor == 0`**."
    - "Lưu ý: `COUNT` là gợi ý số ô cần dò (một mẻ trả về có thể rỗng dù chưa hết dữ liệu, tức `cursor != 0`) và `SCAN` có thể lặp lại 1 khoá nếu bảng băm đang co giãn."
```

> [!TIP] Preventing Cache Avalanche When Setting Bulk TTLs
> If at 00:00 midnight you load 50,000 products into Redis and hardcode `EX 3600` for all of them, at exactly 01:00:00 all 50,000 keys will **expire simultaneously**, sending tens of thousands of queries straight to the database and overloading it! Always add ==random offset (TTL Jitter)==: e.g., `ttl = 3600 + random.randint(0, 300)` in Python (or `3600 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 300)` in JS).

> [!REMEMBER] Core Takeaways
> - **SDS Strings** store their byte length `len` for `O(1)` `STRLEN`, are binary-safe, and auto-encode as `int` (64-bit integer) or `embstr` (`<= 44B`).
> - Always use atomic **`SET key val NX EX seconds`** instead of separate `SETNX` + `EXPIRE`; use **`GETDEL`** for single-use OTP codes.
> - Three return codes of `TTL`: **`-2`** = does not exist · **`-1`** = exists permanently without expiration · **`>= 0`** = remaining seconds.
> - **Never run `KEYS *` in Production** — always iterate using the **`SCAN`** cursor and delete large keys with **`UNLINK`**.

readings.noteEn: A bash cache-cleanup script running every 5 minutes once took down a payment API at noon.
readings.taskEn: Identify the 2 critical bugs in this script when the key count in Redis exceeds 10 million.
readings.answerEn: 1) Calling `KEYS temp:export:*` has `O(N)` complexity and scans the entire hash table on the single main thread, freezing all other requests for hundreds of milliseconds to seconds; 2) Synchronously deleting keys one by one with `DEL` without batching or using asynchronous `UNLINK`.

readings.noteEn: A production-grade Python script that smoothly cleans up millions of keys without causing latency spikes.
readings.taskEn: Explain how the `SCAN` cursor loop combined with batched `UNLINK` protects the Event Loop.
readings.answerEn: The script iterates `SCAN` in small steps (`COUNT 200`), yielding the Event Loop back to other read/write commands between steps and stopping only when `cursor == 0`, while batching matched keys into `UNLINK` to offload memory reclamation to background BIO threads.

R01-Q1.qEn: Thanks to the **SDS (Simple Dynamic String)** structure storing byte length in its header, what is the time complexity of `STRLEN <key>` in Redis (even for a `100MB` string)?
choicesEn: `O(N)` — must scan every character until reaching the `\0` null terminator like traditional C strings
`O(1)` — reads the length field directly from the header without scanning the string contents
`O(log N)` — performs a binary search on a string segment tree
`O(N log N)` — decompresses the string before counting UTF-8 characters
R01-Q1.explainEn: SDS explicitly stores the length property (`len`) in the data structure header, so `STRLEN` simply reads this integer field in constant `O(1)` time.

R01-Q2.qEn: Why is writing two separate commands `SETNX lock:job 1` followed by `EXPIRE lock:job 30` a dangerous anti-pattern in distributed systems?
choicesEn: Because Redis 8 completely removed the `EXPIRE` command from the standard command set
Because if the application process crashes or loses network connectivity right between the 2 commands, `lock:job` will live forever (`TTL = -1`), causing a system-wide Deadlock
Because `SETNX` always deletes the key automatically after 1 millisecond before `EXPIRE` can run
Because `EXPIRE` only works on Hash keys, not String keys
R01-Q2.explainEn: Two separate commands do not form an atomic unit if the client fails mid-flight. Always combine them into a single atomic command: `SET lock:job <owner_token> NX EX 30`.

R01-Q3.qEn: If a key does not exist yet in Redis and you immediately run `INCR page:views`, Redis will throw an `ERR no such key` error instead of performing the addition.
R01-Q3.explainEn: False! When a key does not exist, counter commands like `INCR`, `INCRBY`, and `DECR` automatically initialize the key to `0` before performing the arithmetic (so the first `INCR page:views` returns `(integer) 1`).

R01-Q4.qEn: Which real-world problem does the `KEEPTTL` flag in `SET session:u99 "updated-payload" KEEPTTL` solve?
choicesEn: Doubles the key's current remaining lifetime on every overwrite
Updates the String value while **preserving the remaining Time-To-Live (TTL)** instead of accidentally resetting TTL to `-1` like default `SET`
Freezes the key so no `DEL` or `UNLINK` command can delete it
Moves the key from RAM to permanent disk storage
R01-Q4.explainEn: By default, `SET key new_val` without `EX`/`PX` wipes out any existing countdown TTL (reverting it to `TTL = -1`). Adding `KEEPTTL` preserves the original expiration deadline when you only need to update the value.

R01-Q5.qEn: In a `SCAN cursor MATCH user:* COUNT 100` loop, if a step returns an empty array `[]` while the returned `cursor` is non-zero (e.g., `"4096"`), it means all matching keys have been scanned and you can stop the loop immediately.
R01-Q5.explainEn: False! `COUNT 100` specifies roughly how many hash table slots Redis visits in that step before applying the `MATCH` filter — it is completely possible that none of those 100 slots contain a `user:*` key. You MUST keep iterating until the returned cursor equals `"0"`!

R01-Q6.qEn: The key `cfg:feature:darkmode` currently exists in Redis and has never been given an expiration time. When running the command below, what integer will be returned?
R01-Q6.explainEn: `TTL` returns `-1` when a key exists with no expiration limit (persistent), whereas it returns `-2` if the key does not exist or has expired.

R01-Q7.qEn: Predict the integer value returned by the final `STRLEN` command in the script below:
R01-Q7.explainEn: The initial string `"hi"` (2 bytes) concatenated with `"-redis"` (6 bytes) via `APPEND` produces `"hi-redis"`, which is exactly `8` bytes long.

R01-FC1.frontEn: What do the three result codes of `TTL <key>` (`>= 0`, `-1`, `-2`) mean?
R01-FC1.backEn: **`>= 0`**: Remaining seconds before expiration; **`-1`**: Key exists permanently (no TTL set); **`-2`**: Key does not exist (or has expired and been evicted).

R01-FC2.frontEn: What are the three internal encodings (`OBJECT ENCODING`) of a Redis String?
R01-FC2.backEn: **`int`** (64-bit signed integer), **`embstr`** (short string `<= 44 bytes` allocated contiguously in 1 CPU cache line), and **`raw`** (string `> 44 bytes` or dynamically modified).

R01-FC3.frontEn: Which two mechanisms does Redis combine to reclaim TTL-expired keys without stalling the CPU?
R01-FC3.backEn: **Lazy Expiration** (checks & deletes immediately when a client accesses an expired key) combined with **Active Expiration** (samples random keys with TTL every 100ms and continues sweeping if >25% of the sample is expired).

R01-FC4.frontEn: What happens to a key's countdown TTL if you call `SET key new_value` and forget to include `KEEPTTL` or `EX`?
R01-FC4.backEn: Default `SET` **completely wipes the old TTL** (turning the key into permanent `TTL = -1`), easily causing silent memory leaks!

R01-FC5.frontEn: When is a `SCAN` iteration loop truly finished?
R01-FC5.backEn: Only when the first returned cursor value equals **`"0"`** (even if an intermediate step returns an empty key list, you must pass the new cursor into the next call).

R01-FC6.frontEn: What is **Cache Avalanche** caused by fixed uniform TTLs, and what is the simplest prevention technique?
R01-FC6.backEn: It occurs when tens of thousands of cached keys expire at the exact same second, sending a flood of queries that overwhelm the origin DB. Prevent it by adding **TTL Jitter** (a random offset of tens to hundreds of seconds per key).

NX EX` combination to: (1) Register the key `pay:idem:ord-9001` with value `"processing"` only if it does not exist (`NX`) with a `300`-second lifetime (`EX 300`); (2) Send a second command `SET pay:idem:ord-9001 "duplicate" NX EX 300` to prove Redis rejects the overwrite with `(nil)`.

The second line attempting to write `"duplicate"` with the same `NX EX 300` flags will return `(nil)` and preserve `"processing"`.

redis-ex-r01-2.titleEn: Update Flash-Sale Counters Atomically with INCR & DECRBY

One bulk order of `3` units and one single order of `1` unit just came in (a total of `4` units sold). Use `INCRBY` and `INCR` to raise `flash:sku:airpods:sold` to `14`, while using `DECRBY` to reduce `flash:sku:airpods:stock` down to `46`.

Call `DECRBY flash:sku:airpods:stock 4` to decrement stock from 50 to 46.

redis-ex-r01-3.titleEn: Use Hierarchical Key Naming & Batch Operations with MSET / MGET
redis-ex-r01-3.promptEn: Instead of firing 6 separate commands with messy key names, follow the `<service>:<entity>:<id>` convention: use **1 `MSET` command** to initialize 3 plan configuration keys `billing:plan:free` = `"100"`, `billing:plan:pro` = `"5000"`, and `billing:plan:enterprise` = `"unlimited"`, then use **1 `MGET` command** to read all 3 keys at once.
hintsEn: The `MSET k1 v1 k2 v2 k3 v3` syntax accepts consecutive key-value pairs.
Then call `MGET billing:plan:free billing:plan:pro billing:plan:enterprise`.

redis-ex-r01-4.titleEn: Control Key Lifetimes with EXPIRE, PERSIST & Virtual Clock ADVANCE_TIME
redis-ex-r01-4.promptEn:
Currently, two keys in Redis are misconfigured in opposite ways:
1) `cache:home:hero` is a UI cache key living permanently (`TTL = -1`) — attach a `30`-second `EXPIRE` timer to it.
2) `cfg:payment:gateway` is a critical system config accidentally given a 10-second TTL — use `PERSIST` to strip the TTL and preserve the key permanently.
3) Finally, call `ADVANCE_TIME 35000` (fast-forward 35 seconds) to verify `cache:home:hero` vanishes automatically while `cfg:payment:gateway` stays safe!
hintsEn: Set a 30-second limit with `EXPIRE cache:home:hero 30` and make the expiring key permanent with `PERSIST cfg:payment:gateway`.
Call `ADVANCE_TIME 35000` on the last line to fast-forward 35 seconds (35,000 milliseconds).

redis-ex-r01-5.titleEn: Replace the Forbidden KEYS * Command with SCAN & UNLINK
redis-ex-r01-5.promptEn: The starter script below uses the dangerous `KEYS sess:stale:*` command that freezes the Event Loop and doesn't clean up stale data. **Completely remove the `KEYS` command**, replace it with `SCAN 0 MATCH sess:stale:* COUNT 10` to safely list stale sessions, and then use `UNLINK` to delete both `sess:stale:101` and `sess:stale:102` (leaving `user:active:*` keys untouched).
hintsEn: Delete the `KEYS sess:stale:*` line and replace it with `SCAN 0 MATCH sess:stale:* COUNT 10`.
Use `UNLINK sess:stale:101 sess:stale:102` to asynchronously free both expired session keys.

R02.titleEn: Hashes, listpack Memory Compression & Field-Level TTL with HEXPIRE (Redis 8)
R02.summaryEn: Model objects/entities compactly with Redis Hash, understand the listpack -> hashtable conversion thresholds, avoid the HGETALL trap, and master the latest HEXPIRE/HTTL commands.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concept & Real-World Problem
> When storing a multi-attribute object (such as a user profile with `name`, `tier`, `points`, `otp_code`, or a shopping cart) in Redis, two naive approaches both have significant drawbacks:
> 1. **Storing the entire object as a single JSON string in a `String` key:** Every time you only need to add `10` reward points, the application still has to fetch the entire `20KB` JSON string over the network, deserialize it (`json.loads` / `JSON.parse`), modify one field, and overwrite the whole key — wasting network bandwidth and risking **Lost Updates** when two requests update concurrently.
> 2. **Splitting into 10 separate `String` keys (`user:42:name`, `user:42:points`, etc.):** Each Redis key incurs per-key management metadata (hash table pointers, `robj` structures), causing auxiliary overhead to consume 3–5x more RAM than the actual data.
>
> **Redis Hash** stores a collection of **`field -> value`** pairs under a single key (analogous to `dict[str, str]` in Python, `Map<string, string>` in JS/Java, or `map[string]string` in Go), solving both problems:
> - **`listpack` (Contiguous packed encoding):** For small and medium Hashes, Redis packs field/value pairs sequentially in a single contiguous memory block without separate pointers, saving **60%–70% RAM**.
> - **`HEXPIRE` (Field-level TTL — Redis 7.4+ / Redis 8):** Lets you attach an independent expiration time to individual fields inside a Hash (for example, deleting only `otp_code` after 60 seconds) while ==keeping all other fields of `user:42` intact==.
>
> *Mental model:* Think of a Redis Hash like a folder with multiple individual entries that can be updated or expired independently, rather than re-packaging the entire folder every time a single line changes.

steps.headingEn: When to Choose JSON String vs. Redis Hash (or Redis JSON)
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Quick Selection Rule
> - Choose **JSON String** when your data has deeply nested, complex structures and your API always reads/returns the entire object at once.
> - Choose **Redis Hash** when your data is a flat collection of attributes where you frequently read or update individual fields (incrementing points with `HINCRBY`, changing item quantities in a cart, or reading just 2 small fields without transferring a `50KB` payload over the network).

steps.headingEn: Under-the-Hood RAM Optimization: listpack Replaces ziplist
steps.bodyEn:
Before Redis 7, small Hashes used the `ziplist` structure, which suffered from *cascade updates* when inserting larger elements in the middle. From **Redis 7 → Redis 8**, the default internal encoding for small Hashes is ==`listpack` — a flat, contiguous byte array in RAM==:

- **Two configuration thresholds that keep a Hash in ultra-compact `listpack` encoding** (in `redis.conf`):
  1. `hash-max-listpack-entries` (default `128` or `512` depending on the distribution): Maximum total number of fields in the Hash.
  2. `hash-max-listpack-value 64`: Both field name and field value length must be **`64 bytes` or less**.
- As soon as either threshold is exceeded (e.g., inserting a `300-byte` description or packing thousands of fields into one Hash), Redis **automatically performs a one-way upgrade** of that Hash to a **`hashtable`** to preserve `O(1)` lookup performance (and it does not automatically downgrade back to `listpack` even if you later delete fields).

steps.headingEn: Core Hash Commands & Setting Field-Level TTL with HEXPIRE (Redis 8)
steps.bodyEn:
```visual
kind: anatomy
title: Bản Đồ Lệnh Hash & Hẹn Giờ Từng Trường (Per-Field Expiration)
subtitle: Kết hợp nhuần nhuyễn nhóm lệnh O(1) với HEXPIRE/HTTL của Redis 8
items:
  - keyword: HSET & HMGET
    role: O(K) · Ghi & đọc chọn lọc
    tone: emerald
    summary: Ghi nhiều cặp `field value` cùng lúc bằng `HSET` (thay thế hoàn toàn `HMSET` cũ đã lỗi thời) và chỉ lấy đúng `K` trường cần dùng bằng `HMGET`.
    bullets:
      - "`HSET` trả về số lượng trường **được thêm mới** (trường cũ bị ghi đè vẫn cập nhật thành công nhưng không cộng vào số đếm trả về)."
    example: |
      HSET user:99 name "Linh" role "sre" quota 500
      HMGET user:99 name quota
    lang: redis
  - keyword: HINCRBY / HSETNX
    role: O(1) · Đếm & khởi tạo an toàn
    tone: sky
    summary: Cộng/trừ số nguyên ngay trên 1 trường cụ thể (`HINCRBY`) hoặc chỉ gán giá trị mặc định nếu trường đó chưa tồn tại (`HSETNX`).
    example: |
      HINCRBY cart:u:99 sku:ipad 1
      HSETNX cart:u:99 shipping "standard"
    lang: redis
  - keyword: HEXPIRE ... FIELDS
    role: Redis 7.4+ / 8.0 · Field TTL
    tone: amber
    summary: Gắn thời gian tự huỷ (giây) cho 1 hoặc nhiều trường bên trong Hash mà không ảnh hưởng tới các trường khác!
    bullets:
      - "Hỗ trợ đủ cờ điều kiện `NX` (chỉ đặt nếu trường chưa có hạn), `XX`, `GT`, `LT` đặt **trước** từ khoá `FIELDS <số-lượng-trường>`."
      - "Khi trường cuối cùng trong Hash hết hạn hoặc bị `HDEL`, toàn bộ khoá Hash rỗng cũng được Redis tự thu dọn sạch sẽ."
    example: |
      HEXPIRE cart:u:99 900 NX FIELDS 1 promo:flash20
      HTTL cart:u:99 FIELDS 1 promo:flash20
    lang: redis
  - keyword: HSCAN (thay HGETALL)
    role: Duyệt an toàn Big Hash
    tone: rose
    summary: Khi một Hash có hàng ngàn trường, bắt buộc dùng con trỏ phân trang `HSCAN` thay vì gọi `HGETALL` `O(N)` gây nghẽn Event Loop!
    example: HSCAN metrics:daily:2026-11-14 0 MATCH api:* COUNT 100
    lang: redis
```

Let's look at a real-world **Field-level TTL (`HEXPIRE`)** scenario for an e-commerce shopping cart (via CLI, Python, and Node.js):

```redis
# 1. Thêm 2 món hàng chính và 1 mã giảm giá chớp nhoáng vào giỏ hàng
HSET cart:u:777 sku:airpods "1" sku:case "2" promo:flash50 "GIAM50K"

# 2. Toàn bộ giỏ hàng sống 7 ngày (604800s), NHƯNG mã flash50 chỉ có hiệu lực 15 phút (900s)!
EXPIRE cart:u:777 604800
HEXPIRE cart:u:777 900 FIELDS 1 promo:flash50

# 3. Kiểm tra hạn sống riêng của từng trường bằng HTTL (-1 = không hạn riêng, >=0 = số giây còn lại, -2 = không tồn tại)
HTTL cart:u:777 FIELDS 2 sku:airpods promo:flash50
```

```python
# Python (redis-py >= 5.1) & Node.js (ioredis) gọi thao tác Hash chọn lọc:
r.hset("cart:u:777", mapping={"sku:airpods": "1", "promo:flash50": "GIAM50K"})
r.hincrby("cart:u:777", "sku:airpods", 1)
r.execute_command("HEXPIRE", "cart:u:777", 900, "FIELDS", 1, "promo:flash50")
items = r.hmget("cart:u:777", ["sku:airpods", "promo:flash50"])  # Chỉ đọc đúng 2 trường cần thiết!
```

> [!WARNING] Two Common Mistakes When Working with Redis Hash
> 1. **Calling `HGETALL` on an oversized Hash:** On an `8`-field profile Hash, `HGETALL` takes only a few microseconds. However, if you pack an entire 200,000-product catalog into **a single Hash key (`catalog:all`)**, every ==`HGETALL catalog:all` call blocks the main Event Loop== and transfers tens of MB over the network. Always fetch only the fields you need with **`HMGET`** or iterate incrementally with **`HSCAN`**.
> 2. **Forgetting the `<numfields>` count after the `FIELDS` keyword in `HEXPIRE` / `HTTL`:** The standard syntax strictly requires specifying the **number of fields** immediately after `FIELDS` (e.g., `HEXPIRE myhash 60 FIELDS 2 f1 f2`).

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - Use **`HSET`** (supports multiple fields — avoid the deprecated `HMSET`), **`HMGET`** (selectively read only needed fields), and **`HINCRBY`** (atomic in-place integer increments/decrements).
> - Small Hashes kept under the configured thresholds are packed contiguously with ==`listpack`, saving up to ~70% RAM== compared to splitting into separate String keys.
> - On **Redis 8** (note: `HEXPIRE` was introduced in Redis 7.4+/8 — verify your version if your cloud infrastructure runs an older branch), use **`HEXPIRE key seconds [NX|XX|GT|LT] FIELDS n f1 ...`** and **`HTTL`** to manage independent lifetimes per field.

readings.taskEn: Observe how flash promo codes (`promo:*`) are given an independent expiration timer without losing the rest of the items in the cart.
readings.answerEn: Instead of splitting out an auxiliary String key just to attach `EXPIRE`, the scenario calls `HEXPIRE cart:u:1001 900 FIELDS 1 promo:flash_voucher` directly so only the promo code field evaporates after 15 minutes, while the remaining product SKU fields in the same Hash stay alive under the cart's 7-day TTL.

readings.noteEn: How a TypeScript/Node.js app reads and writes partial object attributes via ioredis without pulling an entire blob over the network.
readings.taskEn: Why does the author use `redis.hmget(key, 'name', 'avatar', 'tier')` in the user header loader instead of storing a single `JSON.stringify` blob in a String key?
readings.answerEn: Calling `HMGET` on a Hash transfers only the 3 small fields over the network (`O(K)` with `K=3`) and allows atomic in-place balance updates via `HINCRBY`, avoiding pulling a multi-kilobyte JSON string into Node.js to `JSON.parse` -> mutate -> `JSON.stringify` overwrite and cause Race Conditions.

R02-Q1.qEn: Compared to storing a user object as a single `JSON.stringify` string in a Redis String, what key advantage does **Redis Hash** provide when the application frequently increments/decrements a `credits` field?
choicesEn: Redis Hash automatically syncs the `credits` field to PostgreSQL without any backend code
It allows atomic in-place updates on that single field using `HINCRBY` without downloading, parsing, and overwriting the whole JSON string (which risks Race Conditions)
Redis Hash supports direct `JOIN` queries between two different Hashes like SQL tables
Redis Hash never consumes RAM because it stores data entirely on disk
R02-Q1.explainEn: `HINCRBY` modifies the `credits` field directly in Redis memory in a single atomic `O(1)` operation, saving network bandwidth and eliminating Lost Update bugs under concurrent requests.

R02-Q2.qEn: In Redis 7 and Redis 8, which memory-efficient internal encoding is used by default for small Hashes (replacing the older `ziplist`)?
choicesEn: `listpack` — a contiguous byte array with no per-entry pointers that eliminates cascade updates
`skiplist` — a multi-level skip linked list
`red-black-tree` — a self-balancing binary search tree
`b-plus-tree` — a paged tree structure similar to MySQL InnoDB
R02-Q2.explainEn: Starting from Redis 7.0, `listpack` completely replaced `ziplist` for storing small Hashes, List nodes, and ZSets in a CPU-cache-friendly contiguous byte region.

R02-Q3.qEn: Once a Redis Hash exceeds `hash-max-listpack-entries` and converts to a `hashtable` encoding, if you later remove fields with `HDEL` down to just 2 fields, Redis immediately downgrades it back to `listpack`.
R02-Q3.explainEn: False! The conversion from `listpack` to `hashtable` is **one-way** to avoid the CPU overhead of repeatedly reallocating and copying memory when the entry count fluctuates around the threshold.

R02-Q4.qEn: Which of the following is the **correct Redis 8 syntax** to set a `300`-second expiration on only the 2 fields `otp` and `magic_link` inside Hash `auth:u:100`?
choicesEn: `EXPIRE auth:u:100 otp magic_link 300`
`HEXPIRE auth:u:100 300 FIELDS 2 otp magic_link`
`HSET auth:u:100 otp EX 300 magic_link EX 300`
`HEXPIRE auth:u:100 otp 300 magic_link 300`
R02-Q4.explainEn: The standard `HEXPIRE` syntax requires the `FIELDS` keyword followed by the field count `numfields` before listing the field names: `HEXPIRE key seconds [NX|XX|GT|LT] FIELDS numfields field [field ...]`.

R02-Q5.qEn: Calling `HGETALL` on a BigKey Hash containing 500,000 fields during peak traffic is completely safe because all Hash read commands have `O(1)` complexity.
R02-Q5.explainEn: False! Only `HGET` and `HMGET` are `O(1)` / `O(K)`, whereas `HGETALL` is **`O(N)`** in the total number of fields — running it on 500,000 fields stalls the Event Loop and saturates network bandwidth. Use `HMGET` or `HSCAN` instead!

R02-Q6.qEn: Predict the integer returned by the `HSET` command on the second line (note: `tier` already exists and is overwritten, while `city` is a brand-new field):
R02-Q6.explainEn: `HSET` returns the number of fields that were **newly added** to the Hash (existing fields whose values are overwritten are not counted). On line 2, `tier` is overwritten and `city` is new, so the return value is `1`.

R02-Q7.qEn: If a Hash has only 1 remaining field `temp_token`, and that field is deleted via `HDEL` (or expires via `HEXPIRE`), what integer will `EXISTS` return when checking the parent Hash key immediately afterward?
R02-Q7.explainEn: In Redis, collection types (Hash, List, Set, ZSet) cannot exist in an empty state — as soon as the last element is removed or expires, Redis automatically reclaims the parent key from the Keyspace (`EXISTS` returns `0`).

R02-FC1.frontEn: When should you store an object as a **Redis Hash** instead of a **JSON String**?
R02-FC1.backEn: When the object is flat and you frequently **read a subset of fields (`HMGET`)** or **atomically update/increment individual fields (`HSET`, `HINCRBY`)** without fetching and overwriting the entire JSON string.

R02-FC2.frontEn: Which two configuration parameters determine whether a Redis Hash stays in compact **`listpack`** encoding?
R02-FC2.backEn: `hash-max-listpack-entries` (maximum number of fields) and `hash-max-listpack-value` (maximum byte size of any field name or value).

R02-FC3.frontEn: What architectural problem previously hard to solve does `HEXPIRE` in Redis 7.4+ / Redis 8 address?
R02-FC3.backEn: It allows attaching **independent TTLs to individual fields** directly inside a Hash (such as temporary promo codes in a cart or auxiliary tokens in a session) without creating separate external String keys.

R02-FC4.frontEn: What does the integer return value of `HSET key f1 v1 f2 v2` represent?
R02-FC4.backEn: The number of fields that were **newly created** by that command (pre-existing fields whose values were updated are not included in the returned count).

R02-FC5.frontEn: How do you decrement an integer field in a Hash by `5` when Redis has no `HDECRBY` command?

R02-FC6.frontEn: What should you use instead of `HGETALL` when reading from a Hash that might contain tens of thousands of fields?
R02-FC6.backEn: Use **`HMGET`** if you know the exact field names needed, or iterate incrementally with the cursor-based **`HSCAN <key> 0 MATCH ... COUNT ...`** to avoid blocking the Event Loop.

Shopping cart `cart:u:777` has 3 fields: `sku:mouse = 1`, `sku:pad = 1`, and a flash discount code `promo:flash15 = SAVE15`. Use Redis 8's new feature:

Then run `OBJECT ENCODING product:meta:901` and `MEMORY USAGE product:meta:901` to inspect its internal encoding and RAM consumption in bytes.

Next, run `OBJECT ENCODING product:meta:901` and then `MEMORY USAGE product:meta:901`.

R03.titleEn: Lists (quicklist) & Sets (intset): Double-Ended Queues & Set Operations
R03.summaryEn: Master the hybrid quicklist structure for LTRIM-bounded Activity Feeds, safe job handoff with LMOVE, and O(1) Set operations with intset, SINTER, and SDIFF.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concept & Real-World Problem
> In regular programming, using dynamic arrays (`list` in Python or `Array` in JavaScript) at scale hits two limitations:
> 1. **FIFO queues or latest-item feeds:** Inserting an element at the head of a 100,000-item array forces the runtime to shift every subsequent memory slot (`O(N)`). **Redis List** uses **`quicklist`** (a doubly linked list of compressed `listpack` blocks) so pushing/popping at either end stays ==`O(1)`== regardless of list length.
> 2. **Unique collections & intersection/difference operations:** **Redis Set** stores an unordered collection and automatically deduplicates elements; checking membership (`SISMEMBER`) takes ==`O(1)`==. Better yet, if every member is a 64-bit integer (`<= 512` elements), Redis automatically uses a contiguous integer array **`intset`**, saving up to 80% RAM.

```visual
kind: illustration
diagram: redis:r03
alt: Cấu trúc lai quicklist hai đầu của Redis List (LPUSH + LTRIM, LMOVE) đối chiếu với biểu diễn nén intset và phép giao SINTER của Redis Set

caption: Nhấn vào sơ đồ để phóng to — quan sát cách quicklist ghép nhiều khối listpack nhỏ và cách Set tự động chọn intset khi lưu toàn số nguyên

    label: Quicklist = Doubly-Linked List của các Listpack
    desc: Kết hợp ưu điểm chèn đầu/cuối O(1) của Linked List với tính liền khối CPU cache của mảng nén listpack, không tốn 2 con trỏ prev/next cho từng phần tử lẻ!
    tone: sky
  - num: 2
    label: Cặp Đôi Kinh Điển LPUSH + LTRIM & Hàng Đợi LMOVE
    desc: LPUSH + LTRIM tạo băng chuyền cố định N tin mới nhất; LMOVE bốc nguyên tử từ queue chờ sang queue đang xử lý để không rớt job khi worker sập.
    tone: emerald
  - num: 3
    label: Set O(1) & Siêu Nén Số Nguyên intset
    desc: Khi mọi thành viên là số nguyên 64-bit và <= 512 phần tử, Redis lưu gọn trong mảng số nguyên sắp xếp intset, giảm tới 80% RAM so với bảng băm.
    tone: amber
```

steps.headingEn: Redis List (quicklist): Double-Ended Queues, LTRIM & Safe LMOVE
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Why Did Redis Design `quicklist` Instead of a Classic Linked List?
> On 64-bit architectures, each node in a classic Linked List spends `16 bytes` just to store two pointers (`prev` and `next`) — if an element is just the 2-byte string `"ok"`, pointer overhead is 8x larger than the actual data. That's why Redis uses **`quicklist`**: a doubly linked list where **each node is a `listpack` block** packing multiple elements contiguously in memory (similar to the block chunking in Python's `collections.deque`).

With this design, operations at both ends (`LPUSH`, `RPUSH`, `LPOP`, `RPOP`) are always **`O(1)`**, while accessing elements near the middle (`LINDEX` far from either end) takes **`O(N)`**. The two most important List patterns are:

```visual
kind: groups
title: Hai Mẫu Kiến Trúc Cốt Lõi Của Redis List Trên Production [!badge:sky:Patterns]
columns: 2
items:
  - num: 1
    title: Capped Activity Feed (Bảng tin giới hạn N mục)
    badge: LPUSH + LTRIM
    tone: emerald
    bullets:
      - "Luôn ghép cặp ==`LPUSH` đi kèm `LTRIM key 0 (N-1)`== (ví dụ giữ cố định 50 hoạt động gần nhất: `0 49`) để khoá không bao giờ phình to vô hạn."
      - "Đọc trang đầu siêu nhanh bằng `LRANGE key 0 19` (rất nhẹ vì lấy ngay từ đầu trái của toa đầu tiên)."
    code: |
      LPUSH feed:u:42 "order:paid:901"
      LTRIM feed:u:42 0 49
      LRANGE feed:u:42 0 9
    codeLang: redis
  - num: 2
    title: Reliable Queue Handoff (Hàng đợi an toàn LMOVE)
    badge: Thay thế RPOPLPUSH cũ
    tone: amber
    bullets:
      - "Nếu worker chỉ gọi `RPOP` (hoặc `BRPOP` chờ tin mới), ngay giây phần tử rời Redis mà tiến trình worker mất điện, tác vụ đó **bốc hơi vĩnh viễn**!"
      - "Dùng ==`LMOVE src dst RIGHT LEFT`== (hoặc bản chặn chờ `BLMOVE`): vừa rút khỏi `pending`, vừa cất ngay sang danh sách tạm `processing` trong **1 bước nguyên tử**; xử lý xong mới `LREM` khỏi `processing`."
    code: |
      LPUSH jobs:pending "invoice-881"
      LMOVE jobs:pending jobs:processing RIGHT LEFT
    codeLang: redis
```

> [!TIP] In Production: Hand-Roll `BLMOVE` or Use a Task Queue Library?
> Most well-known background job queue libraries you use daily are actually built on top of Redis List/ZSet/Streams + Lua:
> - **Python ecosystem:** **`Celery`** (long-standing industry standard), **`RQ` (*Redis Queue*)** (super lightweight and easy to learn), or **`ARQ`** (`asyncio`-native, pairs great with **FastAPI**).
> - **Node.js / TypeScript ecosystem:** **`BullMQ`** (built-in retries, delays, priorities, and rate limiting).
> - **Go ecosystem:** **`Asynq`**. When you need durable event streams with multiple independent consumer groups, you'll upgrade to **Redis Streams** in Module `R08`!

steps.headingEn: Redis Set: Automatic Deduplication, intset & In-RAM Set Operations
steps.bodyEn:
Unlike List (which preserves insertion order and allows duplicates), **Redis Set** is an **unordered, strictly unique** collection — calling `SADD` with `"redis"` 100 times still leaves only a single `"redis"` element in the Set.

Redis 8 automatically selects **1 of 3 internal encodings** for a Set based on the data you insert:
1. **`intset`:** When **100% of members are 64-bit integers** (such as numeric user IDs `1001`, `2048`, ...) and the count is `<= 512` (`set-max-intset-entries`). Zero string pointers or hash table overhead!
2. **`listpack`:** When a Set contains short strings and few elements (`<= 128`, available since Redis 7.2+, giving small tag Sets massive RAM savings).
3. **`hashtable`:** When a Set is large or contains long strings — guaranteeing `O(1)` inserts, deletes, and membership checks.

```visual
kind: anatomy
title: Bộ Lệnh Redis Set & Độ Phức Tạp Cần Thuộc Lòng
subtitle: Cẩn trọng phân biệt nhóm lệnh O(1) siêu nhanh với nhóm lệnh tập hợp O(N)
items:
  - keyword: SADD / SREM / SCARD
    role: O(1) mỗi phần tử
    tone: emerald
    summary: Thêm thành viên mới (`SADD` trả về số phần tử thực sự mới), xoá (`SREM`), và đếm tổng số phần tử tức thì (`SCARD` luôn là `O(1)`).
    example: |
      SADD post:99:likes "u:1" "u:2" "u:1"
      SCARD post:99:likes
    lang: redis
  - keyword: SISMEMBER / SMISMEMBER
    role: O(1) / O(K) · Kiểm tra nhanh
    tone: sky
    summary: Kiểm tra 1 phần tử (`SISMEMBER` -> `1` hoặc `0`) hoặc kiểm tra hàng loạt `K` phần tử trong 1 chuyến mạng (`SMISMEMBER`).
    bullets:
      - "Luôn dùng `SISMEMBER` / `SMISMEMBER` ngay trên Redis thay vì gọi `SMEMBERS` tải cả vạn phần tử về Python/Node.js/Go rồi mới kiểm tra `in` hay `.includes()`!"
    example: SMISMEMBER post:99:likes "u:1" "u:999"
    lang: redis
  - keyword: SINTER / SUNION / SDIFF
    role: O(N) · Giao / Hợp / Hiệu
    tone: cyan
    summary: Tìm phần tử chung (`SINTER` — bạn chung), gộp nhóm (`SUNION`), hoặc tìm phần tử có ở tập đầu mà chưa có ở tập sau (`SDIFF`).
    bullets:
      - "Các biến thể `SINTERSTORE`, `SUNIONSTORE`, `SDIFFSTORE` lưu thẳng kết quả vào một khoá tạm trên RAM để đọc lại nhanh."
      - "Mẹo Redis 7/8: Nếu chỉ cần **đếm số lượng bạn chung** mà không cần lấy danh sách tên, hãy dùng ==`SINTERCARD 2 setA setB LIMIT 100`== để dừng đếm sớm!"
    example: |
      SINTERSTORE mutual:a:b friends:a friends:b
      SINTERCARD 2 friends:a friends:b LIMIT 50
    lang: redis
```

> [!WARNING] Three Common Mistakes When Using Lists and Sets
> 1. **Calling `LRANGE mylist 0 -1` or `SMEMBERS myset` on large collections:** Both are `O(N)`. If a Set has 1 million users, you must paginate with cursor-based **`SSCAN key 0 COUNT 200`**.
> 2. **Adding string prefixes to an all-integer Set:** Changing `SADD uids 1001 1002` to `SADD uids "u_1001" "u_1002"` ==immediately breaks `intset` compression==, multiplying RAM consumption across millions of small Sets.
> 3. **Using deprecated `RPOPLPUSH` / `BRPOPLPUSH`:** These legacy commands are *deprecated* — standardize on **`LMOVE`** and **`BLMOVE`** with explicit direction parameters (`LEFT` / `RIGHT`).

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **List (`quicklist`):** Preserves insertion order, allows duplicates, `O(1)` at both ends. Always pair **`LPUSH` + `LTRIM`** for bounded feeds and use **`LMOVE` / `BLMOVE`** (or `Celery` / `ARQ` / `BullMQ`) for job queues.
> - **Set (`intset` / `listpack` / `hashtable`):** Unordered, automatically deduplicated. Use **`SISMEMBER` / `SMISMEMBER`** for `O(1)` membership checks, **`SCARD`** for total cardinality, and **`SINTERCARD`** when you only need the intersection count of two Sets.

readings.noteEn: The Capped Timeline pattern that keeps a fixed window of the 100 most recent notifications per user in RAM.
readings.taskEn: Why must `LPUSH` and `LTRIM key 0 99` always be paired together in the same event-writing flow?
readings.answerEn: If you only `LPUSH` without `LTRIM`, the list will grow unbounded into a BigKey and exhaust RAM; placing `LTRIM key 0 99` right after `LPUSH` turns the List into a fixed-size Ring Buffer capping at the 100 newest items at near-`O(1)` cost.

readings.noteEn: Computing mutual friends and multi-criteria product filters using in-RAM set intersections and differences.
readings.taskEn: When should you use `SISMEMBER` / `SMISMEMBER` instead of pulling the entire `SMEMBERS` output into the application layer?
readings.answerEn: `SISMEMBER` checks 1 element in `O(1)` and `SMISMEMBER` checks `K` elements in `O(K)`, whereas `SMEMBERS` is `O(N)` scanning the entire Set — if a Set holds 200,000 user IDs, calling `SMEMBERS` blocks the Event Loop and floods network bandwidth.

R03-Q1.qEn: How does Redis List's internal **`quicklist`** representation solve the memory overhead problem of a traditional Doubly-Linked List?
choicesEn: By storing millions of elements inside a single fixed-size static array that cannot grow
By doubly linking nodes where each node is a compressed **`listpack`** byte block holding multiple consecutive elements, drastically cutting `prev`/`next` pointer overhead per item
By compressing the entire list into a `.zip` file on disk and decompressing it on every `LPOP`
By turning the entire list into an alphabetically sorted binary search tree
R03-Q1.explainEn: `quicklist` combines the best of both worlds: `O(1)` head/tail insertion and removal like a Linked List, while each link is a contiguous `listpack` block that is CPU-cache-friendly and pointer-efficient.

R03-Q2.qEn: In a simple List-based queue architecture, why is **`LMOVE pending processing RIGHT LEFT`** much safer than just calling **`RPOP pending`**?
choicesEn: Because `RPOP` is `O(N)` while `LMOVE` is `O(1)`
Because if a worker crashes from power loss or OOM right after `RPOP`, that job is lost forever; `LMOVE` atomically keeps a copy of the job in the `processing` list until completion
Because `RPOP` deletes all remaining items in the `pending` list
Because `LMOVE` automatically retries sending emails if the SMTP server refuses the connection
R03-Q2.explainEn: `LMOVE` executes an atomic *pop-and-push* inside Redis: even if the worker process crashes immediately afterward, the job remains in `processing` so a monitor can recover it.

R03-Q3.qEn: Accessing an element in the middle of a 2-million-item Redis List with `LINDEX biglist 1000000` has `O(1)` complexity just like a C array.
R03-Q3.explainEn: False! Redis Lists are built on a linked list of `quicklist` blocks, so `LINDEX` is only `O(1)` near the two ends (`0` or `-1`) and takes **`O(N)`** when traversing thousands of nodes to reach the middle.

R03-Q4.qEn: When storing a set of 300 VIP user IDs in a Redis Set, which approach enables the ultra-compact **`intset`** encoding that saves ~75–80% memory?
choicesEn: `SADD vip:users "user_101" "user_102" "user_103"`
`SADD vip:users 101 102 103` (passing pure 64-bit integer strings with no alphabetic characters)
`SADD vip:users "{"id":101}" "{"id":102}"`
`LPUSH vip:users 101 102 103`
R03-Q4.explainEn: Redis maintains `intset` only when **every** member of the Set parses as a signed 64-bit integer and the total count does not exceed `set-max-intset-entries` (default 512).

R03-Q5.qEn: To check whether user `u:882` has liked `post:55:likes` (which currently has 400,000 likes), the optimal approach is to call `SMEMBERS post:55:likes`, download the whole set to your app (Python/Node.js/Go), and check in an array.
R03-Q5.explainEn: Critically wrong! `SMEMBERS` takes `O(N)` and transfers 400,000 strings over the network on every page view. You must use **`SISMEMBER post:55:likes u:882`** (or `SMISMEMBER` for multiple items), which costs **`O(1)`** and returns a `1`-byte reply!

R03-Q6.qEn: Pay attention to the push order of `LPUSH` per argument: after running the 2 commands below, which string sits at index `0` (`LINDEX q 0`) (type without quotes)?
R03-Q6.explainEn: `LPUSH q "a" "b" "c"` pushes `"a"` to the head -> `[a]`, then `"b"` to the head -> `[b, a]`, and finally `"c"` to the head -> `[c, b, a]`. So the element at index `0` is `c`.

R03-Q7.qEn: Predict the integer returned by the final `SCARD` command:
R03-Q7.explainEn: Sets automatically deduplicate `"go"`, leaving 3 elements (`go`, `rust`, `zig`) after `SADD`. After `SREM` removes `"rust"`, `SCARD` returns a cardinality of exactly `2`.

R03-FC1.frontEn: Why is **`LPUSH` + `LTRIM key 0 (N-1)`** considered a mandatory pairing for an Activity Feed?
R03-FC1.backEn: It prepends the newest event in `O(1)` while capping the list length at the latest `N` items (a Ring Buffer), preventing the List from growing unbounded into a BigKey that exhausts RAM.

R03-FC2.frontEn: Which modern command in Redis 6.2+ / Redis 8 completely replaces the legacy `RPOPLPUSH` / `BRPOPLPUSH` pair?
R03-FC2.backEn: **`LMOVE`** (and its blocking counterpart **`BLMOVE`**) — allowing you to atomically choose the pop end (`LEFT`|`RIGHT`) on the source list and push end (`LEFT`|`RIGHT`) on the destination list.

R03-FC3.frontEn: What is the time complexity of `SISMEMBER`, `SMISMEMBER`, and `SCARD` on a Redis Set?
R03-FC3.backEn:
- `SISMEMBER` and `SCARD`: **`O(1)`**
- `SMISMEMBER` (checking `K` elements): **`O(K)`**
Independent of whether the Set has 100 or 10 million members!

R03-FC4.frontEn: When does a Redis Set automatically activate **`intset`** compact encoding?
R03-FC4.backEn: When **all elements** in the Set are valid signed 64-bit integer strings and the total number of elements does not exceed `set-max-intset-entries` (default `512`).

R03-FC5.frontEn: What is the difference between `SINTER`, `SUNION`, and `SDIFF` (and their `...STORE` variants)?
R03-FC5.backEn:
- **`SINTER`**: Intersection (present in ALL Sets)
- **`SUNION`**: Union (all unique elements combined)
- **`SDIFF A B`**: Difference (in `A` but NOT in `B`)
Append `STORE` to write the result directly to a destination key in RAM.

R03-FC6.frontEn: If you only need the **count** of common elements between two Sets without transferring their values over the network, what optimized command do Redis 7/8 provide?
R03-FC6.backEn: **`SINTERCARD numkeys key1 key2 [LIMIT limit]`** — counts directly on the server and can stop early once it reaches `LIMIT`!

redis-ex-r03-1.titleEn: Build a Bounded Activity Feed with LPUSH & LTRIM
redis-ex-r03-1.promptEn:
Activity list `feed:u:101` currently has 4 events ordered newest-first: `["act-4", "act-3", "act-2", "act-1"]`. The user just generated `"act-5"` followed by `"act-6"` (newest). Do the following:
1) Use `LPUSH` to push `"act-5"` and `"act-6"` onto the left head of `feed:u:101`.
2) Use `LTRIM feed:u:101 0 2` to trim the older tail so the list **keeps only the 3 newest events** (`act-6`, `act-5`, `act-4`).
3) Run `LRANGE feed:u:101 0 -1` to inspect the trimmed list.
hintsEn: Calling `LPUSH feed:u:101 "act-5" "act-6"` pushes `act-5` then `act-6` to the left head, placing `act-6` at index `0`.
Immediately run `LTRIM feed:u:101 0 2` to lock the list size to the first 3 items.

redis-ex-r03-2.titleEn: Hand Off Queue Jobs Atomically Without Dropping Work Using LMOVE
redis-ex-r03-2.promptEn: Email queue `queue:email:pending` receives new jobs on the left (`LPUSH`), so the oldest queued job `"job-101"` is sitting at the **right tail (`RIGHT`)**. Instead of calling `RPOP`—which risks losing `"job-101"` if the worker crashes mid-flight—use **a single `LMOVE` command** to atomically move the element at the `RIGHT` of `queue:email:pending` to the `LEFT` of the tracking list `queue:email:processing`.
hintsEn: Standard Redis 6.2+ / Redis 8 syntax: `LMOVE <source> <destination> <LEFT|RIGHT> <LEFT|RIGHT>`.
Enter exactly: `LMOVE queue:email:pending queue:email:processing RIGHT LEFT`

redis-ex-r03-3.titleEn: Manage Unique Tags with SADD, SREM, SISMEMBER & SCARD
redis-ex-r03-3.promptEn:
Manage the deduplicated skill set `skills:dev:linh` using a Redis Set:
1) Use `SADD` to add 4 tags: `"typescript"`, `"redis"`, `"docker"`, and `"legacy-svn"`.
2) Use `SREM` to remove the obsolete tag `"legacy-svn"`.
3) Quickly check if `"redis"` is in the set with `SISMEMBER` (`O(1)`) and get the total tag count with `SCARD` (`O(1)`) — strictly **do not call `SMEMBERS`**.
hintsEn: `SADD skills:dev:linh "typescript" "redis" "docker" "legacy-svn"` adds multiple members in one command.
Remove with `SREM skills:dev:linh "legacy-svn"`, then call `SISMEMBER skills:dev:linh "redis"` and `SCARD skills:dev:linh`.

redis-ex-r03-4.titleEn: Find Mutual Friends & Follow Suggestions with SINTERSTORE & SDIFF
redis-ex-r03-4.promptEn:
Stored in RAM are the follow lists for An (`follow:u:an` = `u:10, u:20, u:30, u:40`) and Binh (`follow:u:binh` = `u:20, u:30, u:50`). Perform 2 set operations directly on Redis:
1) Use `SINTERSTORE` to compute the intersection (accounts **followed by both An and Binh**) and store the result directly in `mutual:an:binh`.
2) Use `SDIFF` to find accounts that **Binh follows but An does not yet follow** (watch the key order: `follow:u:binh` comes before `follow:u:an`!).
hintsEn: In `SINTERSTORE <destination> <key1> <key2>`, the first argument is the destination key `mutual:an:binh`.
Set difference `A \ B` is not commutative: put `SDIFF follow:u:binh follow:u:an` to return `"u:50"`.

redis-ex-r03-5.titleEn: Optimize RAM with Integer Set intset & Batch-Check with SMISMEMBER
redis-ex-r03-5.promptEn:
When storing user IDs for an experimental feature whitelist, omitting string prefixes allows Redis to activate ultra-lightweight **`intset`** integer array compression! Do the following:
1) Use `SADD` to create `beta:whitelist:uids` with 4 pure integers: `1001`, `1005`, `1009`, `2048`.
2) Run `OBJECT ENCODING beta:whitelist:uids` to verify Redis chose `"intset"`.
3) Use `SMISMEMBER beta:whitelist:uids 1005 9999` to check access for both IDs in a single round-trip.
hintsEn: Pass integers with no alphabetic characters: `SADD beta:whitelist:uids 1001 1005 1009 2048`.
Then run `OBJECT ENCODING beta:whitelist:uids` and `SMISMEMBER beta:whitelist:uids 1005 9999`.

R04.titleEn: Sorted Sets (ZSet) & O(log N) Skip List Structure
R04.summaryEn: Analyzing Redis ZSet's dual Hash Table + Skip List architecture for million-player leaderboards, Sliding Window Rate Limiters, and Delayed Queues.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concept & Real-World Problem
> For a leaderboard with **5 million players**, thousands of score updates per second, and tens of thousands of queries for **"Top 10"** plus **"a user's current rank"**, a SQL query like `ORDER BY score DESC` on PostgreSQL will quickly bottleneck due to disk writes and continuous B-Tree index updates.
>
> **Sorted Set (`ZSet` — score-ordered set)** solves this problem in **under `0.2 milliseconds`** by combining two data structures under a single key:
> - **Every element (`member`) is unique**, always paired with a floating-point number called a **sorting score (`score`)** (e.g., `980` points or a Unix Timestamp).
> - **Internal Hash Table:** Maps `member -> score`, enabling ==`O(1)`== lookup of any member's score (`ZSCORE`).
> - **Multi-level Skip List:** Maintains element ordering by `score` using multiple layers of forward skip pointers (upper layers take long jumps; the bottom layer links elements sequentially), allowing search, insertion, or rank calculation across **10 million elements** in ~23 comparisons (==`O(log N)`==).
>
> *Intuition:* Think of a Skip List as a transit rail network with express lines on the upper levels (skipping many stations at once) combined with a local line at the bottom level that stops at every station to reach the exact target as fast as possible.

```visual
kind: illustration
src: "/illustrations/redis/redis-skiplist-express.jpg"
diagram: "redis:r04"
alt: "Cấu trúc kép của Redis Sorted Set gồm bảng băm Hash Table O(1) và danh sách nhảy nhiều tầng Skip List O(log N)"
badge: "Cấu trúc dữ liệu · Sorted Set"
title: "Chi Tiết Cấu Trúc Kép Của ZSet — Hash Table O(1) + Skip List O(log N)"
subtitle: "Vì sao Redis chọn Skip List kèm con trỏ span thay vì cây Đỏ-Đen (Red-Black Tree) của C++ std::map?"
caption: "Nhấn vào sơ đồ để phóng to — theo dõi đường tìm kiếm từ tầng cao L3 xuống tầng cơ sở L0 và cách tính thứ hạng ZRANK"
callouts:
  - num: 1
    label: "Hash Table Nội Bộ (member -> score)"
    desc: "Giúp lệnh ZSCORE tra cứu điểm của bất kỳ người chơi nào trong đúng O(1) tức thì mà không cần dò trên cây hay danh sách."
    tone: cyan
  - num: 2
    label: "Skip List Nhiều Tầng Kèm Độ Dài Nhảy (span)"
    desc: "Tầng cao nhảy bước lớn giúp bỏ qua hàng loạt phần tử, tầng thấp dò chi tiết; nhờ lưu khoảng cách span trên mỗi liên kết, Redis tính thứ hạng ZRANK cũng trong O(log N)!"
    tone: amber
  - num: 3
    label: "Duyệt Dải Hai Chiều Mượt Mà (Range Scan)"
    desc: "Bắt được điểm đầu dải trong O(log N), sau đó chỉ việc trượt dọc liên kết tuyến tính L0 (hoặc lùi qua backward pointer cho REV) để lấy M phần tử với chi phí O(log N + M)."
    tone: emerald
```

steps.headingEn: Why Did Redis Choose Skip Lists Over Balanced Binary Trees (Red-Black Trees)?
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Fast Rank Calculation via the `span` Field in Skip Lists
> On every forward link across the Skip List levels, Redis also stores an integer **`span`** indicating how many bottom-level (`L0`) nodes that link skips over. While traversing from the top level down to the position of element `"Chi"`, Redis simply accumulates the traversed `span` values to return the exact rank (for example, **Rank #892**) in `O(log N)` without sequentially counting from the start of the list.

Compared to Red-Black Trees, Redis's **Skip List** wins decisively on 3 practical points:
1. **Natural range slicing (`ZRANGE`):** Once positioned at the starting node in `O(log N)`, fetching the next `10` players is simply walking straight along the bottom-level track (`L0`) in `O(log N + 10)`, without climbing up and down complex tree branches.
2. **Direct rank computation (`ZRANK` / `ZREVRANK`) in `O(log N)`:** Enabled by the `span` distance counter attached to each skip pointer.
3. **Automatic `listpack` compression for small ZSets:** When a ZSet has `<= 128` short elements (`<= 64 bytes`), Redis packs everything into a single flat, memory-efficient `listpack` array before switching to the `Hash Table + Skip List` pair.

*(Tie-breaking rule: When two members have the **exact same `score`**, ZSet automatically orders them lexicographically `A -> Z` by `member` name!)*

steps.headingEn: Standardizing on the Unified ZRANGE Command from Redis 6.2 → Redis 8
steps.bodyEn:
Previously, learners easily got confused by having 6–7 different ZSet read commands (`ZREVRANGE`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, ...). In **Redis 8**, you only need to master ==one central `ZRANGE` command combined with the `REV` and `BYSCORE` flags==, which is clean and consistent:

```visual
kind: anatomy
title: Bản Đồ Lệnh Sorted Set Thực Chiến Chuẩn Redis 8
subtitle: Ưu tiên cú pháp ZRANGE hợp nhất kèm cờ REV / BYSCORE / LIMIT rõ nghĩa
items:
  - keyword: ZADD [NX|XX|GT|LT|CH]
    role: O(log N) · Chèn & lọc điều kiện
    tone: emerald
    summary: Thêm hoặc cập nhật điểm — lưu ý **`score` luôn đứng TRƯỚC `member`** (`ZADD key score member`).
```

steps.bodyEn:

```visual
      - "Mỗi request lưu `score = timestamp_ms`, `member = req_uuid`."
      - "Xoá các request cũ hơn 60 giây trước bằng `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`, sau đó đếm `ZCARD` xem đã vượt hạn mức chưa!"
  - num: 3
```
