Let's see how to implement a lightweight **Sliding Window Rate Limiter** (at most 100 requests / 60 seconds) in both **Python (`redis-py`)** and **Node.js (`ioredis`)**:

```python
# Python (redis-py): Kiểm tra Sliding Window Rate Limit trong 1 chuyến Pipeline
import time, uuid

def allow_request(r, user_id: str, limit: int = 100, window_ms: int = 60_000) -> bool:
    key = f"rl:sliding:{user_id}"
    now_ms = int(time.time() * 1000)
    pipe = r.pipeline()  # Gom các lệnh chạy tuần tự trong 1 chuyến mạng
    pipe.zremrangebyscore(key, "-inf", now_ms - window_ms)
    pipe.zadd(key, {f"{now_ms}:{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}": now_ms})
    pipe.zcard(key)
    pipe.expire(key, 65)
    _, _, current_count, _ = pipe.execute()
    return current_count <= limit
```

> [!WARNING] Watch Out for `ZADD` Argument Order and 64-bit Float Precision Limits!
> - In raw Redis CLI, **`ZADD key score member`** places `score` **BEFORE** `member` (whereas Python `redis-py`'s `r.zadd(key, {member: score})` uses a `dict`, avoiding that mix-up!).
> - `score` in a ZSet is an IEEE 754 64-bit floating-point `double`: it can represent integers **with exact precision only up to ==`2^53` (`9,007,199,254,740,992` — 16 digits)==**. Never put a raw 64-bit Snowflake ID (`~10^18`, 19 digits) directly into `score`, or its least-significant digits will be rounded away!

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **Dual ZSet structure:** `Hash Table` for **`O(1)`** `ZSCORE` + `Skip List` for **`O(log N)`** `ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANK`/`ZREVRANK`, and **`O(log N + M)`** `ZRANGE`.
> - Prefer the unified **`ZRANGE key start stop REV WITHSCORES`** syntax in Redis 8 and leverage **`GT` / `LT` / `NX`** flags directly inside `ZADD`.
> - Turning `score` into a **Unix Timestamp** transforms ZSet into a canonical **Sliding Window Rate Limiter** and **Delayed Job Queue**.

readings.noteEn: Designing a real-time game leaderboard combining ZADD GT/ZINCRBY and tie-breaking.
readings.taskEn: Why does querying the Top 10 leaders among 5 million players using PostgreSQL `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10` easily bottleneck under frequent score updates, whereas ZSet handles it effortlessly?
readings.answerEn: In an RDBMS, every score increment requires updating disk pages and rebalancing a B-Tree index with row locks; by contrast, ZSet maintains ordering in RAM via a Skip List (`O(log N)` updates) paired with a Hash Table (`O(1)` individual score reads via `ZSCORE`) without any row locking.

readings.noteEn: A Delayed Job Scheduler written in TypeScript using Unix Timestamps as ZSet scores.
readings.taskEn: Observe how workers fetch jobs whose execution time has arrived (`score <= Date.now()`) without two workers running the same job twice.
readings.answerEn: Scheduled jobs are pushed via `ZADD delayed_jobs <runAtMs> <jobId>`; periodically, workers poll or run an atomic script combining `ZRANGE ... BYSCORE LIMIT` / `ZPOPMIN` to claim only elements with `score <= now` so each job is processed exactly once.

R04-Q1.qEn: Once it exceeds the small-size threshold (`listpack`), which **two internal data structures** does a Redis Sorted Set (`ZSet`) combine to achieve both ultra-fast individual score lookups and sorted order maintenance?
choicesEn: A static 1D array and a FIFO queue
A **Hash Table** (`member -> score` for `O(1)` `ZSCORE`) running alongside a **Skip List** (`O(log N)` for insertion, deletion, ranking, and range scans)
Two nested hash tables without any ordering links
An on-disk B+Tree similar to PostgreSQL
R04-Q1.explainEn: Running `dict` (Hash Table) and `zskiplist` (multi-level Skip List storing `span` distances) in tandem lets ZSet satisfy two seemingly conflicting goals: `O(1)` score lookup by member name and `O(log N)` rank/score-range queries.

R04-Q2.qEn: Because each forward link in Redis's **Skip List** stores a step-length attribute (`span`), what is the time complexity of finding the exact rank of any player with `ZREVRANK` among 10 million players?
choicesEn: `O(N)` — must count sequentially from the top player down until reaching that player
`O(log N)` — accumulates `span` values along the traversal path from upper levels down to the bottom level (~23–24 comparisons)
`O(N log N)` — must re-sort the entire list on every rank query
`O(1)` — reads directly from a global variable independent of other players' score changes
R04-Q2.explainEn: Without `span`, finding rank would take `O(N)`. By summing the `span` values of skipped links along upper levels, `ZRANK` and `ZREVRANK` compute the exact rank position in `O(log N)`.

R04-Q3.qEn: When two different members in the same Sorted Set have the **exact same `score`**, Redis orders those two members in binary lexicographical order of their `member` strings.
R04-Q3.explainEn: True! In Redis's Skip List, the sort key is the `(score, member)` tuple: when `score` values are equal, `member` strings are compared byte-by-byte in lexicographical order (`memcmp`), ensuring 100% deterministic ordering.

R04-Q4.qEn: In Redis 6.2+ and Redis 8, which modern unified command retrieves the **Top 10 highest-scoring elements** from highest to lowest along with their scores (replacing the legacy `ZREVRANGE`)?
choicesEn: `ZRANGE leaderboard 0 9 DESC SHOWSCORES`
`ZRANGE leaderboard 0 9 REV WITHSCORES`
`ZGETTOP leaderboard 10 WITHSCORES`
`ZRANGE leaderboard 1 10 BYSCORE`
R04-Q4.explainEn: The unified `ZRANGE` command uses 0-based indices `0 9` (the first 10 elements), the `REV` flag to reverse order from high to low, and `WITHSCORES` to include scores.

R04-Q5.qEn: ZSet's `score` is a 128-bit integer (`int128`), so it can store any 19-digit integer ID (such as a full 64-bit Snowflake ID) with exact precision and zero rounding.
R04-Q5.explainEn: False! `score` in a ZSet is an IEEE 754 **64-bit `double`** floating-point number, so it only represents integers with exact precision in the range `[-2^53, 2^53]` (`~9 * 10^15`, 16 digits). 64-bit integers larger than `2^53` lose precision in their least-significant digits!

R04-Q6.qEn: Predict the rank number returned by `ZREVRANK` on the last line (remember Redis ranks start at `0` for the highest-scoring member):
R04-Q6.explainEn: `car:b` has the highest score (`300`), so when ordered from highest to lowest via `ZREVRANK`, the leading position has index `0`.

R04-Q7.qEn: In the `ZCOUNT` command below, the parenthesis `(100` denotes an exclusive lower bound strictly greater than `100` (`score > 100`). Predict the number of elements counted:
R04-Q7.explainEn: Since the lower bound is `(100` (exclusive, i.e., `score > 100`) and the upper bound is `200` (`score <= 200`), only `m2` (`150`) and `m3` (`200`) qualify — so the result is `2`.

R04-FC1.frontEn: What are the time complexities of `ZSCORE`, `ZADD`/`ZINCRBY`, `ZREVRANK`, and `ZRANGE` on a Sorted Set?
R04-FC1.backEn:
- `ZSCORE`: **`O(1)`** (via Hash Table)
- `ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANK`/`ZREVRANK`: **`O(log N)`** (via Skip List + `span`)
- `ZRANGE` (fetching `M` elements): **`O(log N + M)`**

R04-FC2.frontEn: Which application-layer Race Condition do the **`GT`** and **`LT`** flags in `ZADD` eliminate?
R04-FC2.backEn: They perform conditional score updates atomically inside Redis (**`GT`**: only update if the new score is greater than the existing one; **`LT`**: only if less), removing the need for the app to `ZSCORE` read and then conditionally `ZADD` back.

R04-FC3.frontEn: How do you express exclusive (open) intervals and infinity in `ZRANGE ... BYSCORE` or `ZCOUNT`?
R04-FC3.backEn: Prepend a parenthesis `(` right before the number for an open interval (e.g., `(50 (100` means `50 < score < 100`), and use `-inf` / `+inf` for negative/positive infinity.

R04-FC4.frontEn: What are the 3 steps of the **Sliding Window Rate Limiter** pattern using a ZSet?

R04-FC5.frontEn: What is the maximum exact integer limit for `score` in a ZSet, and why?
R04-FC5.backEn: **`2^53` (`9,007,199,254,740,992`)**, because `score` is stored as an IEEE 754 64-bit `double` floating-point number (which has only 53 bits of significand/mantissa).

R04-FC6.frontEn: When two members in a ZSet have the same `score`, how can you ensure the player who achieved that score **earlier** always ranks higher on the leaderboard?
R04-FC6.backEn: Encode a fractional or time-complement component into `score`, e.g. `score = points + (MAX_TS - achievedAtSec) / 1e10` (fitting within 53-bit precision, or handled separately via Lua).

R05.titleEn: Probabilistic & Spatial Structures: Bitmap, HyperLogLog, Bloom Filter & Geo
R05.summaryEn: Trading 0.81% error for a 99.9% RAM reduction with HyperLogLog (12KB), blocking Cache Penetration with Redis 8's built-in Bloom Filter, and GEOSEARCH positioning.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concept & Real-World Problem
> At a scale of **tens of millions of users**, storing all exact elements in a `Set` or `Hash` consumes massive amounts of RAM:
> - Storing 50 million user IDs in a `Set` just to count *Unique Visitors* for one article already consumes ~3.5 GB of RAM.
> - If the system receives millions of requests with non-existent IDs (`order_id = -99182...`), continuous Cache Misses will push 100% of that load onto the Database.
>
> **Redis 8 includes 4 built-in specialized data structures** to solve these problems at minimal RAM cost:
> 1. **`Bitmap` (`0/1` bit array):** Represents each ID's binary state using exactly **1 bit** (`0` or `1`) on top of a string, storing daily check-in status for 100 million users in just `~12 MB`.
> 2. **`HyperLogLog` (`HLL`):** Estimates unique element count (*Cardinality*) in a fixed maximum of ==`12 KB` RAM== (standard error `±0.81%`), ideal for large-scale unique view counting.
> 3. **`Bloom Filter`:** Probabilistic set-membership structure: if it returns **`0`**, the element **definitely 100% does not exist** (*0% False Negative*), blocking junk queries before they reach the Database; if it returns **`1`**, the element likely exists (with a configurable false-positive rate, e.g. `1%`).
> 4. **`Geospatial`:** Encodes a longitude/latitude pair into a 52-bit integer (**`Geohash`**) stored in a `ZSet`, enabling queries for points within a `3 km` radius in just milliseconds.

steps.headingEn: Quick Decision Table: When to Choose Set, Bitmap, HyperLogLog, or Bloom Filter?
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Trade-off Between Exact Per-Element Storage and 99% RAM Savings
> - **`Set`:** Stores every original value in full; allows reading back the list, but uses linear `O(N)` memory.
> - **`Bitmap`:** Uses 1 bit per ordinal index `0..N`; suited for dense integer ID sets needing exact counts or daily bitwise operations.
> - **`HyperLogLog`:** Fixed `12 KB` RAM via probabilistic registers — knows the total unique count, but cannot retrieve original values.
> - **`Bloom Filter`:** Uses a bit array with multiple hash functions as an outer gate for fast existence checks, filtering out most junk queries before hitting the Database.

| Structure | RAM for 10M items | Retrieve member list? | Check single item existence? | Built to solve |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Set** (`SADD`) | ~`400 MB – 650 MB` | Yes (`SSCAN`) | 100% Exact (`SISMEMBER`) | Small/medium sets where original members must be read back |
| **Bitmap** (`SETBIT`) | **`1.2 MB`** (`10M bits`) | By bit offset index | 100% Exact (`GETBIT`) | `0/1` presence flags for integer IDs (`DAU`, consecutive login streaks via `BITOP AND`) |
| **HyperLogLog** (`PFADD`) | **`12 KB`** (fixed!) | **No** | **No** | Counting unique visitors (`PFCOUNT`, merging weekly/monthly via `PFMERGE`) |
| **Bloom Filter** (`BF.ADD`) | **`~11.5 MB`** (`1%` error) | **No** | ==Never False Negative!== | Blocking **Cache Penetration**, fast username availability checks, deduplication |

steps.headingEn: Detailed Commands for Bitmap, HyperLogLog & Bloom Filter in Redis 8
steps.bodyEn:
A major upgrade in **Redis 8**: previously, using `BF.ADD` required installing *Redis Stack* separately or loading the *RedisBloom* module; now **Redis 8 builds probabilistic data structures right into the default core**!

```visual
kind: anatomy
title: Bộ Lệnh Thực Chiến Cho Bitmap, HyperLogLog & Bloom Filter
subtitle: Đúng công cụ cho đúng bài toán dữ liệu lớn
items:
  - keyword: SETBIT / BITCOUNT / BITOP
    role: Bitmap trên nền String
    tone: sky
    summary: Bật/tắt bit ở vị trí `offset` (`SETBIT`), đếm tổng số bit `1` siêu nhanh bằng tập lệnh phần cứng CPU (`BITCOUNT`), và tính phép `AND`/`OR` giữa nhiều ngày (`BITOP`).
    bullets:
      - "Ví dụ kinh điển: `BITOP AND streak:3d dau:d1 dau:d2 dau:d3` lọc ra toàn bộ user online liên tiếp đủ cả 3 ngày chỉ trong vài mili-giây!"
    example: |
      SETBIT dau:2026-11-14 1042 1
      BITCOUNT dau:2026-11-14
    lang: redis
  - keyword: PFADD / PFCOUNT / PFMERGE
    role: HyperLogLog (Trần 12 KB)
    tone: cyan
    summary: Ghi nhận phần tử vào thanh ghi xác suất (`PFADD`), lấy con số ước lượng duy nhất (`PFCOUNT`), và gộp nhiều ngày thành khoá tuần/tháng (`PFMERGE`).
    example: |
      PFADD uv:home:d1 "u1" "u2" "u1"
      PFCOUNT uv:home:d1
    lang: redis
  - keyword: BF.RESERVE / BF.MADD / BF.EXISTS
    role: Bloom Filter · Redis 8
    tone: emerald
    summary: Khởi tạo bộ lọc với tỷ lệ dương tính giả & sức chứa dự kiến (`BF.RESERVE key error_rate capacity`), thêm phần tử (`BF.ADD`/`BF.MADD`) và kiểm tra (`BF.EXISTS`).
    bullets:
      - "**Định luật bất biến:** `BF.EXISTS` trả về `0` = **100% chắc chắn KHÔNG tồn tại** (chặn ngay, khỏi hỏi Database!). Trả về `1` = **Có khả năng tồn tại** (cho đi tiếp vào Cache/DB)."
      - "Lưu ý: Không thể xoá 1 phần tử lẻ khỏi Bloom Filter chuẩn (nếu nghiệp vụ bắt buộc phải xoá, Redis 8 hỗ trợ thêm biến thể **Cuckoo Filter** với nhóm lệnh `CF.*`)."
    example: |
      BF.RESERVE bf:skus 0.01 100000
      BF.MADD bf:skus "sku:1" "sku:2"
      BF.EXISTS bf:skus "sku:fake-999"
    lang: redis
```

steps.headingEn: Geospatial (GEOADD & GEOSEARCH): Find Nearby Drivers Within a Radius in Milliseconds
steps.bodyEn:
How does a ride-hailing app find every driver within a `3 km` radius around you without running expensive spherical trigonometry against all 100,000 vehicles in the city?
- When you call **`GEOADD key longitude latitude member`**, Redis interleaves the binary bits of longitude and latitude into a **52-bit Geohash** integer and stores it straight into a **Sorted Set (`ZSet`)** with `score = geohash_52bit`!
- Two coordinates that are physically close share the same Geohash prefix, so they sit adjacent on the **Skip List**. When you call ==`GEOSEARCH` (the modern standard replacing `GEORADIUS`)==, Redis only needs to scan 9 neighboring grid cells and run exact distance filtering at the very end!

```redis
# Chú ý vàng: KINH ĐỘ (Longitude: -180..180) LUÔN đứng trước VĨ ĐỘ (Latitude: -85.05..85.05)!
GEOADD drivers:hcm 106.6980 10.7725 "driver:minh" 106.6588 10.8185 "driver:tuan"

# Đo khoảng cách đường chim bay giữa 2 điểm (đơn vị: m | km | mi | ft)
GEODIST drivers:hcm "driver:minh" "driver:tuan" km

# Chuẩn Redis 6.2+ / Redis 8: Dùng GEOSEARCH (thay thế GEORADIUS cũ đã deprecated!)
GEOSEARCH drivers:hcm FROMLONLAT 106.7000 10.7750 BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 5
```

> [!WARNING] Three Common Pitfalls with Bitmap and Geospatial
> 1. **Passing huge sparse `offset` numbers to `SETBIT`:** If user IDs start at `4,000,000,000` and you pass that directly into `SETBIT key 4000000000 1`, Redis will immediately allocate a string of ==`512 MB` filled with zeros== just to flip 1 bit at the end! For large IDs, subtract a base offset (`id - BASE_ID`) or shard keys per million-ID bucket.
> 2. **Reversing Latitude and Longitude out of Google Maps habit:** In Google Maps we're used to reading `(Lat, Lon)` = `(10.7725, 106.6980)`. However, Redis `GEOADD` follows Cartesian `(X, Y)` order: **`Longitude` (`106.6980`) first, `Latitude` (`10.7725`) second** — swapping them throws an out-of-range error past `85.05°` latitude!
> 3. **Looking for a non-existent `GEODEL` command:** Since a Geo key is actually a **`zset`** under the hood, to remove a driver simply call **`ZREM <key> <member>`**!

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **Bitmap (`SETBIT`/`BITCOUNT`/`BITOP`):** Costs 1 bit per contiguous ID — optimal for Daily Active Users & Retention.
> - **HyperLogLog (`PFADD`/`PFCOUNT`/`PFMERGE`):** Capped at **`12 KB`**, **`0.81%`** standard error — optimal for large-scale Unique Visitors.
> - **Bloom Filter (`BF.RESERVE`/`BF.ADD`/`BF.EXISTS`):** Returning `0` means **100% guaranteed never seen** — outer shield against **Cache Penetration**.
> - **Geo (`GEOADD`/`GEODIST`/`GEOSEARCH`):** Parameter order is strictly ==`Longitude` first, `Latitude` second==; use `GEOSEARCH` and remove points with `ZREM`.

readings.noteEn: Three large-scale measurement tools: Bitmap for login streaks, HyperLogLog for UV counts, and Bloom Filter guarding the DB.
readings.taskEn: Why does counting 50 million unique visitors with `SADD` consume gigabytes of RAM, whereas `PFADD` stays at exactly 12 KB?
readings.answerEn: `SADD` must retain every raw IP/UUID string in a hash table so memory grows linearly `O(N)`; by contrast, HyperLogLog never stores the original elements and instead tracks the probabilistic distribution of leading `0` bits after hashing across 16,384 6-bit registers (`16384 * 6 bits = 12 KB`), trading a `0.81%` standard error for constant `O(1)` memory.

readings.noteEn: Finding drivers or stores within a user's radius in real time using 52-bit Geohash on top of ZSet.
readings.taskEn: Since Redis Geo is stored under the hood as a Sorted Set (`ZSet`), which command should you use to remove a driver who just went offline from the map?
readings.answerEn: There is no separate `GEODEL` command! Because a Geo key is actually a `ZSet` (whose `score` is the 52-bit Geohash integer interleaving longitude and latitude), call `ZREM drivers:online <driverId>` directly to remove the driver.

R05-Q1.qEn: What is the maximum memory consumed by a **HyperLogLog** key (`PFADD`) in Redis to estimate unique cardinality across hundreds of millions of items?
choicesEn: Grows linearly by about `64 bytes` for every element added
At most around **`12 KB`** with a statistical standard error of roughly **`0.81%`**
Fixed `512 MB` per key upon initialization
Equal to the exact size of a `Set` containing the same number of elements
R05-Q1.explainEn: Redis's HyperLogLog uses 16,384 6-bit registers (`16384 * 6 / 8 = 12,288 bytes = 12 KB` plus a few header bytes), storing no original element values and estimating cardinality from hash bit distributions with ~0.81% standard error.

R05-Q2.qEn: Which key probabilistic property of a **Bloom Filter** (`BF.EXISTS`) makes it an effective defense against **Cache Penetration** attacks?
choicesEn: Never has False Positives, though it occasionally has False Negatives
**Zero False Negatives**: if `BF.EXISTS` returns `0`, the element has **100% definitely never been inserted** — it can be rejected immediately without risking missed real data!
Stores the entire product JSON payload inside hashed bits to return directly to users
Automatically evicts least-recently-accessed elements using an LRU algorithm
R05-Q2.explainEn: A Bloom Filter guarantees 0% False Negatives: returning `0` means the item is definitely absent from the set (blocking junk queries in RAM); returning `1` means it is present or hit a small (~1%) hash collision probability (allowing the request to proceed to Cache/DB).

R05-Q3.qEn: After pushing visitor IP addresses into a HyperLogLog key via `PFADD uv:today ...`, you can run `SMEMBERS uv:today` to print back the full list of those IP addresses.
R05-Q3.explainEn: False! HyperLogLog is a one-way probabilistic structure that only retains statistical hash-bit state to estimate cardinality (`PFCOUNT`); it does not store original IP strings and does not support listing members.

R05-Q4.qEn: Under the hood in Redis, which underlying data structure stores a geospatial index created with `GEOADD` (and which command deletes a point)?
choicesEn: Stored as a `Hash` and deleted with `HDEL`
Stored as a **`Sorted Set (ZSet)`** with a **52-bit Geohash** integer as `score`, so use **`ZREM <key> <member>`** directly to delete a point!
Stored as a `Stream` and deleted with `XDEL`
Stored in a separate `R-Tree` and deleted with `GEODEL`
R05-Q4.explainEn: If you run `TYPE` on a key created by `GEOADD`, Redis returns `zset`! All coordinates are encoded into 52-bit Geohashes as ZSet `score`s, so the official removal command is `ZREM`.

R05-Q5.qEn: In `GEOADD key arg1 arg2 member`, Redis follows Google Maps convention by taking Latitude (`latitude`) first and Longitude (`longitude`) second.
R05-Q5.explainEn: False! Redis (`GEOADD` and `FROMLONLAT` in `GEOSEARCH`) follows the Cartesian `(X, Y)` axis order: **Longitude (`-180..180`) ALWAYS comes BEFORE Latitude (`-85.05..85.05`)**.

R05-Q6.qEn: Predict the integer returned by `BITCOUNT` on the last line after setting and clearing the bits below:
R05-Q6.explainEn: Initially 3 bit positions (`0`, `3`, `7`) were set to `1`, then position `3` was reset to `0`, leaving a total of `2` bits currently set to `1` (`BITCOUNT`).

R05-Q7.qEn: When you run `TYPE` on a geospatial key just created with `GEOADD` as shown below, which underlying data type name does Redis return?
R05-Q7.explainEn: Redis's Geospatial index is implemented directly on top of Sorted Set, so `TYPE cities` always returns `zset`.

R05-FC1.frontEn: What is the core difference between **Bitmap** and **HyperLogLog** when counting active users?
R05-FC1.backEn:
- **Bitmap (`SETBIT`/`BITCOUNT`)**: 100% exact, supports per-ID checks (`GETBIT`) and multi-day intersections (`BITOP AND`), requires contiguous integer IDs (`~12MB` for 100M users).
- **HyperLogLog (`PFADD`/`PFCOUNT`)**: Accepts arbitrary strings (IP, UUID), fixed max **`12 KB`**, ~`0.81%` error, cannot look up individual members.

R05-FC2.frontEn: Why can a **Bloom Filter** (`BF.EXISTS`) completely block **Cache Penetration**?
R05-FC2.backEn: Because a Bloom Filter guarantees **0% False Negatives**: any non-existent ID that returns `0` from `BF.EXISTS` is rejected immediately in RAM without spending a single query on the primary Database.

R05-FC3.frontEn: What trade-off do the two numeric parameters in `BF.RESERVE <key> <error_rate> <capacity>` control?
R05-FC3.backEn:
- `error_rate` (e.g., `0.01` = 1%): Desired false-positive rate — smaller values require more hash functions and more bits of RAM.
- `capacity`: Expected number of elements to insert before the filter needs to allocate an expansion sub-filter.

R05-FC4.frontEn: What memory trap occurs if you pass a large integer directly (such as `offset = 4,000,000,000`) into `SETBIT`?
R05-FC4.backEn: Redis must allocate a contiguous string large enough to reach that bit offset (`4 billion bits ≈ 500 MB` of zero bytes in RAM) in a single command! Subtract `BASE_ID` or shard keys into million-ID buckets.

R05-FC5.frontEn: What is the longitude/latitude order in `GEOADD`, and what is the standard radius search command in Redis 8?
R05-FC5.backEn: Always pass **`longitude` first, `latitude` second**; use the modern command **`GEOSEARCH ... FROMLONLAT ... BYRADIUS ...`** instead of the legacy `GEORADIUS`.

R05-FC6.frontEn: How do you remove a driver who just went offline from the Geospatial key `drivers:online`?
R05-FC6.backEn: Use **`ZREM drivers:online <driver_id>`** (because Redis's Geospatial index is actually a Sorted Set storing 52-bit Geohash codes in the `score` field).

redis-ex-r05-1.titleEn: Calculate 2-Day Consecutive Active Users with Bitmap (SETBIT, BITOP, BITCOUNT)
redis-ex-r05-1.promptEn:
The system tracks daily online status with a Bitmap (each offset is a `userId`). Yesterday `dau:2026-11-13` had active users `[101, 205, 309, 412]`; today `dau:2026-11-14` already has `[101, 309]`. Do the following:
1) Use `SETBIT` to set bit `1` at offset `412` and offset `888` for today's key `dau:2026-11-14`.
2) Use `BITOP AND retention:2d dau:2026-11-13 dau:2026-11-14` to find users active on **both consecutive days**.
3) Use `BITCOUNT retention:2d` to count total 2-day retained users (expecting `(integer) 3` corresponding to `101`, `309`, `412`).
hintsEn: Bit-setting syntax: `SETBIT dau:2026-11-14 412 1` and `SETBIT dau:2026-11-14 888 1`.
Then run `BITOP AND retention:2d dau:2026-11-13 dau:2026-11-14` followed by `BITCOUNT retention:2d`.

redis-ex-r05-2.titleEn: Count & Merge Cross-Platform Visitors with HyperLogLog (PFADD, PFMERGE, PFCOUNT)
redis-ex-r05-2.promptEn:
The Web HyperLogLog key `uv:web:d1` has recorded `[ip:1, ip:2, ip:3, ip:4]`, while Mobile `uv:mobile:d1` has `[ip:3, ip:4, ip:5]`. Do the following:
1) Use `PFADD` to record `"ip:6"` and `"ip:2"` into `uv:mobile:d1`.
2) Use `PFMERGE` to merge both `uv:web:d1` and `uv:mobile:d1` into the system-wide key `uv:all:d1` (deduplicating visitors who used both Web and App!).
3) Run `PFCOUNT uv:all:d1` to output total unique visitors (`(integer) 6`).
hintsEn: In `PFMERGE <destkey> <sourcekey1> <sourcekey2>`, the first argument is the destination key `uv:all:d1`.
Finally call `PFCOUNT uv:all:d1` to get the estimated total `(integer) 6`.

redis-ex-r05-3.titleEn: Build a Bloom Filter Shield Against Cache Penetration in Redis 8
redis-ex-r05-3.promptEn:
To block junk queries for non-existent product SKUs from hitting PostgreSQL, set up a Redis 8 Bloom Filter:
1) Initialize key `bf:catalog:skus` with `BF.RESERVE bf:catalog:skus 0.01 10000` (`0.01` = `1%` false-positive rate, `10000` capacity).
2) Bulk-insert 3 real product SKUs using `BF.MADD bf:catalog:skus "sku:101" "sku:102" "sku:103"`.
3) Batch-check both a real SKU `"sku:102"` and a fake SKU `"sku:fake-999"` with `BF.MEXISTS bf:catalog:skus "sku:102" "sku:fake-999"`.
hintsEn: Include the dot accurately in Redis 8 Bloom Filter command names: `BF.RESERVE`, `BF.MADD`, `BF.MEXISTS`.
In the `BF.MEXISTS` output, item 1 (`sku:102`) returns `(integer) 1` while item 2 (`sku:fake-999`) returns `(integer) 0` (100% non-existent).

redis-ex-r05-4.titleEn: Register Logistics Coordinates & Measure Distance with GEOADD & GEODIST
redis-ex-r05-4.promptEn:
Watch Redis's coordinate rule carefully: **Longitude ALWAYS comes before Latitude**! Do the following:
1) Use `GEOADD` to create key `vn:hubs` with 2 points in Ho Chi Minh City:
   - `"hub:ben-thanh"`: longitude `106.6980`, latitude `10.7725`
   - `"hub:tan-son-nhat"`: longitude `106.6588`, latitude `10.8185`
2) Use `GEODIST vn:hubs "hub:ben-thanh" "hub:tan-son-nhat" km` to calculate straight-line distance in kilometers (`km`).
hintsEn: `GEOADD` accepts multiple `(longitude latitude member)` triples sequentially on the same line.
Don't forget to pass the `km` unit at the end of `GEODIST` (omitting it defaults to meters `m`).

redis-ex-r05-5.titleEn: Find the 2 Nearest Drivers Within a 3km Radius with GEOSEARCH
redis-ex-r05-5.promptEn: Key `drivers:hcm:online` stores live positions of 3 drivers (`driver:minh`, `driver:tuan` in District 1 and `driver:hung` over 12km away in Thu Duc). A passenger just requested a ride at **`(longitude 106.6960, latitude 10.7720)`**. Use the modern Redis 8 **`GEOSEARCH`** command (do not use legacy `GEORADIUS`) to search `drivers:hcm:online` from center `FROMLONLAT 106.6960 10.7720`, scanning `BYRADIUS 3 km`, sorted nearest-first `ASC`, and limited to `COUNT 2` drivers.
hintsEn: Standard syntax: `GEOSEARCH <key> FROMLONLAT <lon> <lat> BYRADIUS <radius> <unit> ASC COUNT <n>`.
Exact command: `GEOSEARCH drivers:hcm:online FROMLONLAT 106.6960 10.7720 BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 2`

R06.titleEn: TCP Pipelining, MULTI/EXEC/WATCH & No-Rollback Transaction Semantics
R06.summaryEn: Multiply throughput 10x with TCP Pipelining, clearly distinguish Pipeline vs. MULTI/EXEC Transactions, apply optimistic locking with WATCH, and clean up BigKeys using UNLINK.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> When an application runs a loop calling `GET` on Redis **500 times sequentially**, the total duration can reach **`250 milliseconds`** even though Redis takes less than `0.001 milliseconds` in RAM to process each command. The bottleneck is network overhead, and Redis provides the following mechanisms to optimize throughput and control transactions:
> - **`RTT` (*Round-Trip Time*):** The time it takes for a packet to travel from the application to Redis and return with a response. If internal network RTT is `0.5ms`, sending 500 individual commands sequentially takes at least `500 × 0.5ms = 250ms` just waiting on the network.
> - **`TCP Pipelining` (Batch Sending):** Flushes all 500 commands over the TCP socket in **a single write** and reads all 500 responses back in one batch, cutting total latency from `250ms` down to ==`~1.2ms`==.
> - **`MULTI / EXEC` (Sequential Transaction):** Enqueues a group of commands (`QUEUED`) and executes them contiguously from start to finish when `EXEC` is called, ensuring no other client interleaves in between. However, unlike SQL, ==Redis does not automatically roll back== if a command inside fails with a data-type error at execution time.
> - **`WATCH` (Optimistic Locking):** Monitors one or more keys before opening `MULTI`; if any watched key is modified by another client before `EXEC` runs, the transaction automatically aborts so the application can re-read and safely retry.

```visual
kind: illustration
diagram: redis:r06
alt: Đối chiếu trực quan giữa gửi lệnh tuần tự tốn N vòng RTT, gom chuyến TCP Pipelining 1 RTT và hàng đợi nguyên tử MULTI/EXEC/WATCH của Redis
badge: Tối ưu thông lượng & Giao dịch · Level 2
title: Cơ Chế TCP Pipelining (1 RTT) vs Hàng Đợi Cô Lập MULTI / EXEC / WATCH
subtitle: Hiểu rõ khi nào chỉ cần gom gói mạng, khi nào cần cô lập tuần tự, và vì sao lỗi kiểu dữ liệu giữa chừng không được Rollback
caption: Nhấn vào sơ đồ để phóng to — quan sát đường đi của gói tin trong Pipeline so với hàng đợi QUEUED của MULTI/EXEC
callouts:

    desc: Gửi dồn K câu lệnh xuống socket không chờ phản hồi từng cái, giảm cả RTT mạng lẫn số lần chuyển ngữ cảnh đọc/ghi mạng của hệ điều hành.
    tone: emerald
  - num: 2
    label: MULTI / EXEC — Cô Lập Tuần Tự (Serialized Isolation)
    desc: Các lệnh sau MULTI trả về QUEUED; khi gặp EXEC, Redis chạy một mạch toàn bộ hàng đợi trên luồng đơn mà không cho bất kỳ client nào chen ngang.
    tone: sky
  - num: 3

    tone: rose
```

steps.headingEn: Pipelining vs. MULTI/EXEC: How Do They Differ in Python & Node.js?
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Direct Comparison: Pure Pipelining vs. `MULTI / EXEC` Transaction
> - **Pure Pipelining:** Sends multiple commands together to cut down network `RTT`s, but on the Redis server, commands from other clients can still execute interleaved between commands in your batch (**network optimization, no isolation**).
> - **`MULTI` / `EXEC`:** Redis queues all commands (`QUEUED`); when **`EXEC`** arrives, the main thread executes your entire queue contiguously before moving on to commands from any other client (**sequential isolation**).

```visual
kind: compare
title: Đối Chiếu Pure Pipelining vs Transaction MULTI / EXEC
subtitle: Lưu ý khác biệt cực kỳ quan trọng giữa Python redis-py và Node.js ioredis khi gọi .pipeline()!
left:
  badge: TỐI ƯU TỐC ĐỘ MẠNG (1 RTT)
  title: Pure Pipelining (Không bọc MULTI/EXEC)
  tone: emerald
  lang: python
  code: |
    # Python (redis-py): Truyền transaction=False để dùng Pure Pipeline!
    # (Mặc định r.pipeline() trong redis-py có bọc sẵn MULTI/EXEC)
    pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
    pipe.get("user:1:name")
    pipe.hgetall("cart:1")
    pipe.scard("notify:1")
    name, cart, unread = pipe.execute()  # Chỉ tốn 1 RTT!
  bullets:
    - "**Trên Node.js (`ioredis`):** `redis.pipeline()` mặc định là Pure Pipeline (còn `redis.multi()` mới bọc `MULTI/EXEC`)."
    - "**Nguyên tử / Cô lập?** **KHÔNG** — lệnh của kết nối khác có thể xen vào giữa các lệnh trong lô."
    - "**Kích thước lô khuyên dùng:** Chia từng mẻ **`100 – 1,000` lệnh** (tránh nhồi 500,000 lệnh vào 1 Pipeline làm phình bộ đệm RAM trên máy chủ!)."
right:
  badge: CÔ LẬP TUẦN TỰ
  title: Transaction MULTI / EXEC
  tone: sky
  lang: redis
  code: |
    MULTI
    DECRBY wallet:u:1 200
    INCRBY wallet:u:2 200
    HSET tx:99 from "1" to "2" amt "200"
    EXEC
  bullets:
    - "**Mục tiêu:** Đảm bảo không ai nhìn thấy trạng thái dở dang khi tiền đã trừ ở ví 1 mà chưa cộng vào ví 2."
    - "**Giới hạn cần nhớ:** Bên trong khối `MULTI`, mọi lệnh chỉ trả về chữ **`QUEUED`** — bạn **không thể đọc kết quả `GET` ở dòng 1 để viết `if/else` cho dòng 2**!"
```

steps.headingEn: Key Difference Between Redis Transactions and SQL: Why Doesn't Redis Support Rollback?
steps.bodyEn:
To keep the in-memory execution engine ultra-lightweight and achieve hundreds of thousands of commands per second (without writing heavy *Undo Logs* like PostgreSQL/MySQL), Redis handles two classes of errors in `MULTI / EXEC` completely differently:

1. **Syntax errors during queueing (*Queueing Error* — before calling `EXEC`):** For example, mistyping a command name like `SETX` or passing too few arguments. Redis detects this immediately instead of returning `QUEUED` and will **automatically abort the entire transaction** when `EXEC` is called (`EXECABORT`). You can also proactively discard the queue using the **`DISCARD`** command.
2. **Data-type errors at runtime (*Runtime Error* — inside `EXEC`):** For example, calling `LPUSH` on a key holding a `String`. Because the command syntax is completely valid, Redis still replies `QUEUED` during queueing! When `EXEC` runs:
   - Command 1 (`DECRBY wallet:a 100`) -> **Executes successfully and persists!**
   - Command 2 (`LPUSH wallet:a "oops"` wrong type) -> Returns error `(error) WRONGTYPE...`
   - Command 3 (`INCRBY wallet:b 100`) -> **Still continues to execute and succeeds!**
   - ==There is NO automatic rollback of Command 1 and Command 3 like in SQL!==

steps.headingEn: Optimistic Locking with WATCH (Check-And-Set) & Non-Blocking Cleanup with UNLINK
steps.bodyEn:
Because inside `MULTI` you cannot read data out to perform conditional branching (such as *"only update the auction price if nobody else has placed a higher bid"*), Redis provides a **Check-And-Set (CAS)** mechanism via **`WATCH`**:

```redis
# 1. Gắn "camera giám sát" lên khoá TRƯỚC khi mở MULTI
WATCH auction:item:88:bid

# 2. Đọc giá hiện tại ở NGOÀI MULTI để ứng dụng kiểm tra điều kiện
GET auction:item:88:bid

# 3. Nếu hợp lệ, mở MULTI xếp hàng cập nhật rồi chốt EXEC
MULTI
SET auction:item:88:bid "350"
SET auction:item:88:winner "u:linh"
EXEC
# -> Nếu giữa lúc WATCH và EXEC có người khác sửa 'auction:item:88:bid',
#    EXEC lập tức huỷ toàn bộ và trả về (nil) để ứng dụng đọc lại và thử lại!
```

Alongside batching techniques comes the discipline of **non-blocking memory cleanup off the main thread** using **`UNLINK`** and **`lazyfree`**:

```visual
kind: anatomy
title: Vệ Sinh Bộ Nhớ Không Chặn Luồng Chính (Non-Blocking Cleanup)
subtitle: Xoá 1 String nhỏ thì DEL và UNLINK tương đương; nhưng xoá 1 Hash/Set/ZSet 500,000 phần tử thì DEL sẽ chặn luồng chính gây giật độ trễ!
items:
  - keyword: UNLINK k1 [k2 ...]
    role: O(1) trên luồng chính!
    tone: emerald
    summary: Tháo ngay lập tức nhãn tên khoá khỏi bảng tra cứu chính (`O(1)`), rồi chuyển vùng nhớ khổng lồ sang **luồng dọn rác chạy nền (BIO Thread)** thu hồi êm ái.
    example: UNLINK big:zset:2025 temp:set:millions
    lang: redis
  - keyword: lazyfree-lazy-expire
    role: Cấu hình dọn nền tự động
    tone: amber
    summary: Khi một khoá lớn tự hết hạn `TTL`, mặc định cũ vẫn xoá đồng bộ gây giật! Bật `yes` cho ==`lazyfree-lazy-expire` và `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`== để mọi khâu thu hồi đều diễn ra ở luồng nền.
    example: |
      CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
      CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-expire yes
    lang: redis
```

> [!TIP] When Should You Stop Using `WATCH + MULTI/EXEC` and Switch to a Lua Script (Module `R07`)?
> If a key experiences extreme contention (for example, Flash Sale product inventory with 5,000 users clicking buy in the same second), using `WATCH` will cause **4,999 connections to abort with `(nil)` and spin in continuous retry loops** (*Retry Storm*), creating pointless network congestion! In that case, a **Lua Script (`EVAL`)** in the next module is the standard solution because checking and decrementing stock happens atomically on the server in a single call.

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **Pipelining** packs `N` commands into **1 network trip (1 RTT)** (batch `100–1,000` commands; in Python `redis-py`, use `r.pipeline(transaction=False)` when you only need pure network batching).
> - **`MULTI` / `EXEC`** executes commands contiguously without interleaving, **`DISCARD`** clears the pending queue, and Redis **DOES NOT roll back** on runtime data-type errors!
> - Use **`WATCH`** before `MULTI` for low-contention optimistic locking, and always prefer **`UNLINK`** + **`lazyfree-lazy-*`** over `DEL` for large keys.

readings.noteEn: How to properly use `redis.pipeline()` and `redis.multi()` in Node.js / TypeScript applications.
readings.taskEn: When in TypeScript code should you call `redis.pipeline()` instead of `redis.multi()`?
readings.answerEn: Use `redis.pipeline()` when you only want to send a batch of independent commands in 1 network RTT for maximum speed without making Redis spend memory queueing a transaction or blocking interleaving; only use `redis.multi()` when the entire command sequence must execute contiguously in isolation with no other client able to interleave in between.

readings.noteEn: Connection Pool patterns and `pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False)` in the Python `redis-py` ecosystem.
readings.taskEn: Watch out for a super common gotcha in `redis-py`: does calling `r.pipeline()` enable `MULTI/EXEC` by default?
readings.answerEn: Yes! In the Python `redis-py` library, `r.pipeline()` defaults to `transaction=True` (automatically wrapping commands in `MULTI` and `EXEC`). If you only want lightweight pure TCP Pipelining without transactional isolation, you must explicitly pass `r.pipeline(transaction=False)`.

R06-Q1.qEn: What is the biggest benefit of **TCP Pipelining** when sending 200 sequential Redis commands from a Node.js/Python application?
choicesEn: It lets Redis automatically run those 200 commands in parallel across 200 CPU cores
It eliminates 199 network round-trip waits (**RTT**) and reduces OS kernel `read()`/`write()` syscall context switches
It automatically rolls back all 200 commands if the 199th command hits a data-type error
It automatically encrypts all data in RAM with AES-256
R06-Q1.explainEn: Pipelining batches multiple commands into a continuous TCP write stream and reads all replies back in one pass, eliminating the biggest bottleneck: network round-trip latency (RTT) and I/O syscall overhead.

R06-Q2.qEn: Suppose the key `profile` is currently of type **Hash**. What happens when executing the `MULTI / EXEC` transaction block below containing 3 syntactically valid commands?
choicesEn: All 3 commands are rolled back, and `counter` is not created, just like in PostgreSQL

Command 1 (`SET counter 10`) and Command 3 (`INCR counter` -> `11`) **still execute successfully and persist**; only Command 2 returns a `WRONGTYPE` error because Redis **does not roll back runtime errors**!
Redis automatically deletes the old `profile` key to force `INCR profile` to succeed
The Redis process shuts down immediately to protect data integrity
R06-Q2.explainEn: This is a classic Redis interview question! Data-type errors (`WRONGTYPE`) only surface at execution time (`EXEC`); Redis reports the error solely for the 2nd element in the result array and continues executing the remaining valid commands normally WITHOUT rolling back.

R06-Q3.qEn: Using pure **TCP Pipelining** alone (without `MULTI / EXEC` or a Lua Script) is enough to guarantee that no other client's commands can interleave between the commands in your pipeline.
R06-Q3.explainEn: False! Pure pipelining is strictly a network-layer transport optimization—the Redis server can still interleave commands read from other client sockets. To run contiguously in isolation without interleaving, you must use `MULTI/EXEC` or a Lua Script.

R06-Q4.qEn: In **Optimistic Locking**, if after you call `WATCH balance` another client modifies `balance` before you call `EXEC`, how does `EXEC` respond?
choicesEn: It automatically merges the changes from both clients together
It aborts the entire queued transaction and returns **`(nil)`** (`Null reply`) to signal the conflict so the application can retry
It blocks the other client until your `EXEC` finishes before allowing its modification
It overwrites the other client's change with your value
R06-Q4.explainEn: `WATCH` implements lock-free optimistic Check-And-Set (CAS): if Redis detects that a watched key was touched by another connection before `EXEC`, it immediately aborts the transaction and returns `(nil)`.

R06-Q5.qEn: The `UNLINK big_hash` command removes the key name from the Keyspace immediately in `O(1)` on the main thread, while freeing the millions of internal memory nodes is handed off asynchronously to a BIO background thread.
R06-Q5.explainEn: True! That is exactly why in Production we always use `UNLINK` instead of `DEL` for large collections to protect the Event Loop from latency spikes.

R06-Q6.qEn: When inside a transaction block after calling `MULTI`, what uppercase status keyword does Redis reply with for each valid command you send (before calling `EXEC`)?
R06-Q6.explainEn: Between `MULTI` and `EXEC`, Redis does not execute commands immediately; instead, it pushes them onto the `txQueue` transaction queue and replies with the status string `QUEUED`.

R06-Q7.qEn: If you have already run `MULTI` and queued several commands, but notice a wrong parameter and want to **completely cancel the transaction** without executing any of them, which command should you run?
R06-Q7.explainEn: The `DISCARD` command flushes the queue of `QUEUED` commands, automatically clears any active `WATCH`, and safely exits `MULTI` mode.

R06-FC1.frontEn: What is the fundamental difference between **TCP Pipelining** and **`MULTI / EXEC`**?
R06-FC1.backEn:
- **Pipelining**: A network-side technique that sends multiple commands in one batch (**1 RTT**), with **no** atomic isolation guarantee.
- **`MULTI / EXEC`**: A server-side mechanism that queues commands (`QUEUED`) to execute contiguously without other clients interleaving.

R06-FC2.frontEn: How does Redis handle **Syntax Errors at Queue Time** vs. **Data-Type Errors at Runtime (`EXEC`)** differently in a Transaction?
R06-FC2.backEn:
- **Syntax error before `EXEC`**: Redis flags the error and rejects the entire transaction (`EXECABORT`).
- **Runtime error during `EXEC`** (such as `WRONGTYPE`): Only the failing command errors out; valid commands before and after it **still execute normally — NO Rollback**!

R06-FC3.frontEn: Why can't you write conditional logic like `if (await redis.get(k) > 0)` **inside** a `MULTI ... EXEC` block?
R06-FC3.backEn: Because inside `MULTI`, every command—including `GET`—is not executed yet and only returns **`QUEUED`**; you do not receive the actual value until after `EXEC` runs!

R06-FC4.frontEn: What is the 4-step sequence of **Optimistic Locking with `WATCH`**?
R06-FC4.backEn:
1) `WATCH key` (before `MULTI`)
2) Read with `GET`/`HGET` and check conditions in the application
3) `MULTI` + enqueue write commands
4) `EXEC` (if `(nil)` is returned, someone modified the key -> retry).

R06-FC5.frontEn: What default behavior of `r.pipeline()` in Python's **`redis-py`** differs from `redis.pipeline()` in Node.js **`ioredis`**?
R06-FC5.backEn: In `redis-py`, `r.pipeline()` enables `transaction=True` by default (automatically wrapping in `MULTI/EXEC`). To run the lightest pure Pipeline like `ioredis`, you must pass `r.pipeline(transaction=False)`.

R06-FC6.frontEn: Why should you use **`UNLINK`** along with `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` instead of relying solely on `DEL`?
R06-FC6.backEn: `DEL` frees all memory of a BigKey directly on the main Event Loop thread, stalling the server; `UNLINK` and `lazyfree` only unlink the pointer in `O(1)` and delegate the heavy memory reclamation to BIO background threads.

redis-ex-r06-1.titleEn: Batch Multi-Argument Commands to Cut Network RTTs
redis-ex-r06-1.promptEn:
The starter script below makes 5 fragmented single-key `SET` calls for configuration and leaves the service metadata incomplete. Rewrite it cleanly using just **3 multi-argument batch commands** (do not use single-key `SET` commands at all):
1) Use `MSET` to set `cfg:timeout = "5000"` and `cfg:retries = "3"`.
2) Use `HSET` on the Hash `svc:gateway` to set all 3 fields: `host = "10.0.0.5"`, `port = "8080"`, `tls = "on"`.
3) Use `SADD` on the Set `svc:gateway:tags` to add all 3 tags: `"edge"`, `"public"`, `"v2"`.
hintsEn: Remove the 2 old `SET` lines and combine them into `MSET cfg:timeout "5000" cfg:retries "3"`.
Combine all 3 fields into one `HSET svc:gateway host "10.0.0.5" port "8080" tls "on"` command and all 3 tags into one `SADD svc:gateway:tags "edge" "public" "v2"` command.

redis-ex-r06-2.titleEn: Transfer Reward Points with Sequential Isolation Using a MULTI / EXEC Block
redis-ex-r06-2.promptEn:
Wallet `wallet:u:101` currently has `500` points and wallet `wallet:u:202` has `100` points. Transfer `150` points from `101` to `202` inside **a single `MULTI` ... `EXEC` transaction block** containing 3 sequentially queued operations:
1) `DECRBY wallet:u:101 150` (leaving `350`)
2) `INCRBY wallet:u:202 150` (bringing it to `250`)
3) `HSET tx:log:9001 from "101" to "202" amount "150"`
Don't forget to commit the transaction with `EXEC` on the last line!
hintsEn: Start with `MULTI`, followed by the 3 data commands (each will respond with `QUEUED`).
End with `EXEC` to execute the entire queue with sequential isolation.

redis-ex-r06-3.titleEn: Emergency Abort of a Bad Transaction Queue with DISCARD & Re-Run Safely
redis-ex-r06-3.promptEn:
The promo budget `promo:budget` currently has `1000`. In the first 2 lines of the draft, someone opened `MULTI` and mistakenly queued `DECRBY promo:budget 9999` (running `EXEC` would push the budget deep into the negative!). **Keep the first 2 lines intact**, then append:
1) Call **`DISCARD`** to abort the entire open transaction queue.
2) Open a fresh **`MULTI`** block, queue `DECRBY promo:budget 200` along with `INCR promo:claimed_count`, and commit with **`EXEC`**.
hintsEn: Right below `DECRBY promo:budget 9999`, enter `DISCARD` — the `-9999` command will be thrown away without ever touching the data.
Then enter `MULTI`, `DECRBY promo:budget 200`, `INCR promo:claimed_count`, and `EXEC`.

redis-ex-r06-4.titleEn: Safe Bidding via Optimistic Locking with WATCH + GET + MULTI / EXEC
redis-ex-r06-4.promptEn:
Auction item `auction:item:88:bid` currently has bid `"250"` (current leader `auction:item:88:winner = "u:nam"`). To perform a textbook **Check-And-Set (CAS)** operation that automatically aborts if anyone updates the bid concurrently:
1) Place a watch using `WATCH auction:item:88:bid` **before** opening `MULTI`.
2) Read the current bid with `GET auction:item:88:bid`.
3) Open `MULTI`, update `SET auction:item:88:bid "320"` and `SET auction:item:88:winner "u:linh"`, then commit with `EXEC`.
hintsEn: `WATCH` and the `GET` read for checking conditions must always appear **BEFORE** `MULTI`.
Inside `MULTI`, queue the 2 `SET` commands, then finish with `EXEC`.

redis-ex-r06-5.titleEn: Clean Up BigKeys Without Blocking the Main Thread via UNLINK & lazyfree Flags
redis-ex-r06-5.promptEn:
The draft below uses synchronous `DEL` to remove BigKey `bigkey:report:2025` (stalling the Event Loop) and leaves `bigkey:feed:archive` untouched. Please:
1) **Completely remove the `DEL` command** and replace it with **1 `UNLINK` command** to asynchronously free both `bigkey:report:2025` and `bigkey:feed:archive` (keep `active:config:v1` intact).
2) Use `CONFIG SET` to enable both `lazyfree-lazy-eviction` to `yes` and `lazyfree-lazy-expire` to `yes` so future automatic reclamations also run on background BIO threads!
hintsEn: Replace the `DEL ...` line with `UNLINK bigkey:report:2025 bigkey:feed:archive`.
Add two config lines: `CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes` and `CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-expire yes`.

R07.titleEn: Lua Scripting & Redis Functions: Atomic Execution to Prevent Race Conditions
R07.summaryEn: Embed read-check-modify logic directly inside Redis memory with EVAL/EVALSHA, master Flash-Sale inventory deduction, safe distributed lock release, and KEYS[] vs. ARGV[] rules.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> Suppose inventory has **1 last item** left (`stock = 1`), and **2 purchase requests** arrive at 2 API servers in the exact same millisecond:
> - If checking and decrementing stock uses 2 separate commands from the app side (Step 1 calls `GET stock` and sees `1 >= 1`, Step 2 sends `DECR stock`), even a `0.5ms` network delay between the two commands is enough for **both servers to read `1` before either decrement runs**, driving inventory down to **`-1`** (overselling). This bug is a ==TOCTOU Race Condition== (*Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use*).
> - **Redis Lua Scripting (`EVAL` / `EVALSHA`)** eliminates this problem entirely using the **Lua** interpreter embedded inside the Redis process. The entire *"Read stock -> If sufficient then decrement -> Otherwise return error"* logic executes end-to-end on Redis's single main thread: **no other command can interleave**, guaranteeing ==100% atomicity== in exactly **1 network round trip (1 RTT)**.

steps.headingEn: Side-by-Side Comparison: App-Layer Race Condition vs. Atomic Lua Script
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Direct Comparison: Read-Then-Write from App vs. Server-Side Lua Execution
> - **Read-Then-Write from App:** The app sends `GET`, waits for the result over the network, evaluates `if/else` in app code, and only then sends `DECRBY`. During the network round-trip gap between those two commands, another client may have already altered the data in Redis.
> - **Lua Script (`EVAL`):** All conditional checks and updates are packaged into a script running directly on Redis's main thread as one indivisible step. (Think of it like handing your full conditional instruction to a bank teller to complete at the counter in one go, rather than calling to ask your balance and calling back later to withdraw).

```visual

title: Trừ Tồn Kho Flash-Sale — Bẫy Race Condition vs Chuẩn Nguyên Tử Lua
subtitle: Chú ý chỉ số mảng trong ngôn ngữ Lua đếm từ 1 (KEYS[1], ARGV[1]), không phải từ 0!
left:
  badge: DÍNH LỖI BÁN VƯỢT TỒN KHO (OVERSELLING)
  title: Check-Then-Act ở tầng App (Python / JS / Go)

  lang: python
  code: |
    # NGUY HIỂM: 2 worker cùng đọc thấy cur == 1!
    cur = int(r.get(sku_key) or 0)
    if cur >= qty:
        # Khoảng trống mạng 0.5ms cho request khác lọt vào!
        r.decrby(sku_key, qty)  # -> Âm kho (-1)!
        return True
    return False
  bullets:
    - "Tốn **2 chuyến mạng RTT** và hoàn toàn mất tính cô lập giữa câu lệnh đọc với câu lệnh ghi."
    - "Dưới tải 1,000 req/s, kho chỉ còn 10 chiếc nhưng có thể bán lố thành 45 đơn hàng!"

    EVAL "
      local cur = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
      local qty = tonumber(ARGV[1])
      if cur >= qty then
        return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
      else
        return -1
      end
    " 1 stock:sku:iphone16 2

```

      - "Từ Redis 7 → Redis 8 còn có **`FUNCTION LOAD` / `FCALL`** lưu bền vững thư viện hàm vào AOF và tự đồng bộ sang Replica!"

In production code, you **never need to compute SHA-1 hashes manually** — both Python `redis-py` and Node.js `ioredis` provide wrappers that automatically use `EVALSHA` (and reload the script if the Redis server just restarted):

```python
# Python (redis-py): Đăng ký hàm Lua 1 lần, gọi mượt như hàm Python bình thường!
RESERVE_STOCK_LUA = """
local cur = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local qty = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if cur >= qty then
    return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
end
return -1
"""
reserve_stock = r.register_script(RESERVE_STOCK_LUA)
remaining = reserve_stock(keys=["stock:sku:iphone16"], args=[2])  # Tự động chạy EVALSHA!
```

steps.headingEn: RESP ↔ Lua Type Conversion Rules & 3 Absolute Don'ts
steps.bodyEn:
When calling `redis.call()` inside Lua, memorize 4 Lua-specific rules to avoid subtle bugs:
- **Lua arrays are `1`-indexed (not `0`-indexed):** The first key is ==`KEYS[1]`== and the first argument is ==`ARGV[1]`== (accessing `KEYS[0]` returns `nil`!).
- **All elements in `ARGV[]` and results from `GET`/`HGET` are strings (`string`):** In Lua, comparing two strings `"9" >= "10"` evaluates to **`true`** (because character `'9'` is greater than `'1'`)! Always cast with **`tonumber(...)`** before doing math or numeric comparisons.
- **Redis `(nil)` converts to boolean `false` in Lua:** In Lua, `0` and the empty string `""` are both *truthy* (`true`), while only `false` and `nil` are *falsy* — which is why `tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')` works seamlessly!
- **`redis.call` vs. `redis.pcall`:** `redis.call` aborts immediately and raises the error back to the client; `redis.pcall` catches the error as a Lua table `{ err = "..." }` so the script can handle it gracefully.

> [!WARNING] Three Absolute DON'Ts Inside Production Lua Scripts!
> 1. **NEVER dynamically construct key names inside Lua:** Every key read or written by the script ==must be passed explicitly via the `KEYS[1..N]` array== (never write `redis.call('GET', 'user:' .. ARGV[1])`). On **Redis Cluster**, the server inspects the `KEYS` list beforehand to verify all keys belong to the same shard (*Hash Slot*)!
> 2. **NEVER run long loops or heavy computation taking more than a few milliseconds:** While Lua runs, the entire main thread is exclusively locked — a `500ms` script stalls the whole Redis instance for half a second! Keep scripts concise and under ~30 lines.
> 3. **NEVER generate non-deterministic values/timestamps inside the script:** Generate values like `now_ms` or `uuid` in your application and pass them in via **`ARGV[]`** to keep scripts deterministic.

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - Use **`EVAL` / `EVALSHA`** whenever a write step depends directly on the value just read (inventory deduction, distributed lock release, rate limiting).
> - Three mandatory Redis Lua rules: **1-based arrays (`KEYS[1]`, `ARGV[1]`)** · **Always wrap numeric comparisons in `tonumber()`** · **Every key name must go through `KEYS[]`**.
> - Leverage `r.register_script(...)` (`redis-py`) or `redis.defineCommand(...)` (`ioredis`) to automate `EVALSHA`.

readings.noteEn: Innocent-looking TypeScript code that reads stock with `await redis.get()` before calling `decrby()` — the classic culprit behind negative stock during Flash Sales.
readings.taskEn: Trace the timeline when exactly `1` iPhone remains in stock and 2 HTTP requests enter this function in the same millisecond.
readings.answerEn: At `t=0ms`, both Request 1 and Request 2 run `await redis.get('stock')` and both receive `'1'` (`>= 1`). At `t=1ms`, both pass the `if` check in Node.js and fire `decrby('stock', 1)` — resulting in stock hitting `-1`, meaning you just sold 2 orders for 1 single item (TOCTOU Race Condition)!

readings.noteEn: The iconic 4-line Lua script from the official Redis documentation for completely safe Distributed Lock release.
readings.taskEn: Why can't you split the `GET` check against `ARGV[1]` and the `DEL` command out into application code?
readings.answerEn: If the app calls `GET` and sees its own token, but in the microsecond before `DEL` arrives the lock's TTL expires and Worker B acquires a new lock, Worker A's delayed `DEL` will wipe out Worker B's valid lock! Wrapping both `GET == ARGV[1]` and `DEL` inside `EVAL` guarantees they execute as one indivisible atomic operation.

R07-Q1.qEn: What is the single greatest advantage of a **Lua Script (`EVAL` / `EVALSHA`)** over a **`MULTI / EXEC`** transaction block in Redis?
choicesEn: Lua Scripts run on a separate background thread so they can execute for 10 minutes without affecting other `GET`/`SET` commands
It allows **reading the current value, computing, and branching with `if / else` inside a single atomic execution** in just 1 network round trip (1 RTT)
It automatically connects to an external PostgreSQL database for two-way data synchronization
It automatically rolls back all prior commands if a `redis.call` errors halfway through the script
R07-Q1.explainEn: In `MULTI / EXEC`, read results are not available until `EXEC` finishes, so conditional branching is impossible; by contrast, Lua runs directly against RAM, letting you `GET`, evaluate conditions, and decide whether to `DECRBY` or reject inside the same atomic block.

R07-Q2.qEn: Why must every key accessed by a Lua script be **explicitly passed via the `KEYS[]` array** rather than hardcoding or concatenating key names inside Lua code?
choicesEn: Because the Lua language does not support string concatenation
So Redis (especially **Redis Cluster**) can inspect the touched keys upfront, verify they all map to the same Hash Slot, and route to the right node before execution
Because the `ARGV[]` array only accepts integers and rejects strings
So Redis can automatically delete all keys in `KEYS[]` once the script finishes
R07-Q2.explainEn: Redis Cluster routes commands based on the keys declared via `numkeys` (`KEYS[1..N]`). Dynamically constructing keys inside Lua that land on a different node's slot will fail with a `CROSSSLOT` error or violate sharding rules!

R07-Q3.qEn: In a Redis Lua script, if you forget `tonumber()` and write `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) >= ARGV[1]`, comparing the string `"9"` and the string `"10"` evaluates `"9" >= "10"` as **TRUE (`true`)**!
R07-Q3.explainEn: True! Both `GET` and `ARGV[1]` are `string` values; lexicographical ASCII comparison checks the first character `'9'` (`57`) against `'1'` (`49`), so `'9' > '1'` evaluates to `true`, completely breaking your stock check! Always use `tonumber(...)`.

R07-Q4.qEn: In a **Distributed Lock** workflow, what can go wrong if Worker A releases a lock using a bare `DEL lock:payment` instead of a Lua script checking `GET == my_token`?
choicesEn: `DEL` cannot delete keys created with `SET ... NX EX`
If Worker A stalls (e.g. a GC pause) past the TTL so the lock expires and Worker B acquires it, Worker A's late `DEL` will **delete Worker B's active lock**, letting Worker C enter concurrently!
Redis automatically extends the lock by 60 seconds whenever `DEL` is called
There is zero risk because only the lock creator is allowed to call `DEL`
R07-Q4.explainEn: Redis does not tie connection ownership to String keys. Each process must store a unique random `owner_token` (UUID) as the lock value and only delete it via Lua when `redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1]`.

R07-Q5.qEn: The `EVALSHA` command lets applications send a 40-character SHA1 digest instead of the full Lua source code, significantly saving network bandwidth on high-frequency calls.
R07-Q5.explainEn: True! Redis caches scripts by their SHA1 hash; applications simply send `EVALSHA <sha1> ...` and only fall back to sending full `EVAL` if they get a `NOSCRIPT` error (e.g., after a server restart).

R07-Q6.qEn: In Redis's embedded Lua environment, at what index is the first element of the `KEYS` table accessed (`KEYS[???]`)?
R07-Q6.explainEn: Unlike JavaScript, Python, or C (which are 0-indexed), Lua tables/arrays start counting at index **`1`** (`KEYS[1]`, `ARGV[1]`).

R07-Q7.qEn: Predict the integer returned by the `EVAL` command below when the key `stock:item` currently holds `"4"`:
R07-Q7.explainEn: Current stock `c = 4` is less than the requested quantity `ARGV[1] = 6`, so `c >= 6` is false and the script takes the `else` branch, returning `-1` (leaving the stock untouched at `4`).

R07-FC1.frontEn: What is a **TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use)** bug when using Redis from an app, and what is the cleanest fix?
R07-FC1.backEn: It happens when reading state via `GET`, checking a condition in app code, and then sending a write—leaving a window for another request to mutate the key in between. The cleanest fix is wrapping Read + Check + Write inside **1 atomic Lua script (`EVAL`/`EVALSHA`)**.

R07-FC2.frontEn: How is the canonical 4-line Lua script for **safe Distributed Lock release** written?
R07-FC2.backEn:
`if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`
(`KEYS[1]` is the lock key name, and `ARGV[1]` is the process's unique UUID `owner_token`).

R07-FC3.frontEn: What is the difference between **`redis.call()`** and **`redis.pcall()`** inside Lua?
R07-FC3.backEn:
- **`redis.call()`**: If the Redis command fails, the entire script aborts immediately and propagates the error to the client.
- **`redis.pcall()`** (*protected call*): Catches the error as a Lua table `{ err = '...' }` so the script can handle it and continue.

R07-FC4.frontEn: What are the three **Lua** syntax quirks that trip up JS/Python developers most often?
R07-FC4.backEn:
1) Arrays are **`1`-indexed** (`KEYS[1]`, `ARGV[1]`)
2) The not-equal operator is **`~=`** (not `!=`)
3) Both **`0`** and empty string **`""`** evaluate to **`true`** in `if` statements (only `false` and `nil` are falsy)!

R07-FC5.frontEn: How does the **`EVALSHA`** + **`NOSCRIPT`** pattern work in client libraries like `ioredis`?
R07-FC5.backEn: The library precomputes the script's SHA1 hash and always sends the lightweight `EVALSHA <sha1>` first; if Redis replies `NOSCRIPT` (not cached yet), the library automatically falls back to `EVAL` once to load it and uses `EVALSHA` for all subsequent calls.

R07-FC6.frontEn: How do **Redis Functions (`FUNCTION LOAD` / `FCALL`)** in Redis 7 & 8 improve upon traditional `EVALSHA`?
R07-FC6.backEn: They manage named functions organized as server-side libraries that are **automatically persisted to AOF/RDB and replicated to Replicas**, removing the need for applications to reload script source code on startup.

redis-ex-r07-1.titleEn: Standardize a Cluster-Compatible Lua Script Separating KEYS[1] & ARGV[1]
redis-ex-r07-1.promptEn: The starter script below has a serious bug: it passes `numkeys = 0` and hardcodes the key name directly inside the Lua body (which breaks immediately on Redis Cluster!). Rewrite the `EVAL` command properly with **`numkeys = 1`**, passing `feature:checkout:limit` via **`KEYS[1]`** and the default value `"50"` via **`ARGV[1]`**: check if `redis.call('EXISTS', KEYS[1]) == 0`, then call `redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])` and `return 1`, otherwise `return 0`.
hintsEn: Change the `0` after the script string to `1 feature:checkout:limit "50"`.
Inside the Lua body, reference the key as `KEYS[1]` and the value as `ARGV[1]` (remember Lua arrays start at index `1`).

redis-ex-r07-2.titleEn: Atomic Check-and-Decrement Inventory Without Overselling Using Lua EVAL
redis-ex-r07-2.promptEn:
Current inventory has `stock:sku:ps5 = 5` and `stock:sku:vr2 = 2`. Use an atomic Lua script that checks stock (`local cur = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')`; if `cur >= tonumber(ARGV[1])` then `DECRBY` and return the new balance, otherwise **leave stock untouched** and `return -1`) to process **2 consecutive orders**:
1) Order 1 buys `3` units of `stock:sku:ps5` (succeeds -> `2` remaining).
2) Order 2 buys `5` units of `stock:sku:vr2` (insufficient stock -> rejects with `(integer) -1`, keeping `stock:sku:vr2` safely at `2`!).
hintsEn: Always wrap both the `GET` value and `ARGV[1]` in `tonumber(...)` to avoid Lua string-comparison bugs!
Use the same `EVAL "..." 1 <key-name> <quantity>` command template for both `stock:sku:ps5 3` and `stock:sku:vr2 5`.

redis-ex-r07-3.titleEn: Safe Distributed Lock Release Using Lua
redis-ex-r07-3.promptEn:
There are currently 2 distributed locks in the system: `lock:order:77` is held by `"owner-worker-B"` (because Worker A's earlier lock expired), while `lock:order:88` is held by `"owner-worker-A"`. Worker A just finished its job and wants to release both locks using its identifier `"owner-worker-A"`.
Use Redis's canonical safe-unlock Lua script (`if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`) to run against:
1) `lock:order:77` with token `"owner-worker-A"` (must reject and return `0`, protecting Worker B's lock!).
2) `lock:order:88` with token `"owner-worker-A"` (matching owner -> deletes the lock and returns `1`!).
hintsEn: Standard Lua pattern: `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`.
Pass `1 lock:order:77 "owner-worker-A"` on line 1 and `1 lock:order:88 "owner-worker-A"` on line 2.

redis-ex-r07-4.titleEn: Build an Atomic Fixed-Window Rate Limiter (First-Hit INCR + EXPIRE) in Lua
redis-ex-r07-4.promptEn:
Write a Lua script for a `60`-second window rate limiter allowing at most `2` requests on key `rl:api:u42`:
- Accept `KEYS[1] = rl:api:u42`, `ARGV[1] = 60` (TTL in seconds), `ARGV[2] = 2` (max limit).
- Run `local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])`; if `c == 1`, set `redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])`.
- If `c > tonumber(ARGV[2])` then `return 0` (reject), otherwise `return 1` (allow).
Execute this `EVAL` command **3 times in a row** to verify that the first 2 requests return `1` and the 3rd request is blocked with `0`!
hintsEn: Inside Lua: `local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end; if c > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 else return 1 end`.
Repeat `EVAL "..." 1 rl:api:u42 60 2` across 3 consecutive lines to simulate 3 API calls.

redis-ex-r07-5.titleEn: Multi-Key Balance-Checked Transfer Using Lua & {bank} Hash Tag
redis-ex-r07-5.promptEn:
Account `acc:{bank}:alice` currently holds `300` and `acc:{bank}:bob` holds `100` (both share the Hash Tag `{bank}` so they reside on the same Hash Slot in Cluster mode!). Write **1 `EVAL` command** with **`numkeys = 2`** (`KEYS[1] = acc:{bank}:alice`, `KEYS[2] = acc:{bank}:bob`) and transfer amount `ARGV[1] = 180`:
- Check if the balance of `KEYS[1]` is `>= tonumber(ARGV[1])`; if so, `DECRBY` on `KEYS[1]`, `INCRBY` on `KEYS[2]`, and `return 1`; otherwise `return 0`.
hintsEn: Because the script operates on 2 keys, `numkeys` must be `2`: `EVAL "..." 2 acc:{bank}:alice acc:{bank}:bob 180`.
Inside the Lua body, decrement `KEYS[1]` and increment `KEYS[2]` by `ARGV[1]` (or an `amt` variable).

R08.titleEn: Pub/Sub vs Redis Streams: Real-Time Messaging & Persistent Event Log (PEL)
R08.summaryEn: Clearly distinguish fire-and-forget Pub/Sub from the Append-Only Log architecture of Redis Streams: master XADD MAXLEN ~, Consumer Groups, the PEL tracking list, XACK, and recovering crashed workers with XAUTOCLAIM.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> When a system is split into multiple microservices (for example, an **Order API** needs to emit events to a **Payment Service** and a **Background Email Service**), Redis provides **2 completely different messaging mechanisms** in terms of data durability:
> 1. **`Pub/Sub` (*Publish / Subscribe* — Ephemeral Real-Time Messaging):** Messages are pushed immediately (`< 0.3ms`) to all clients actively connected and listening at the moment of `PUBLISH`. If a service is restarting or loses connection for 2 seconds, every message emitted during that window is **lost permanently** because Redis does not store history.
> 2. **`Redis Streams` (Persistent Append-Only Event Log):** Stores the entire stream of events with monotonically increasing time-based IDs (similar to a distributed log) and supports reliable processing through 4 components:
>    - **`Consumer Group`:** Distributes messages in a stream across multiple workers within the same group for parallel processing, while allowing multiple different groups to independently consume the same stream.
>    - **`PEL` (*Pending Entries List*):** A tracking list of messages that have been delivered to individual workers but have not yet been acknowledged as completed.
>    - **`XACK` (*Acknowledge*):** An acknowledgment command sent by a worker to report that processing succeeded so Redis removes that message from the `PEL`.
>    - **`XAUTOCLAIM`:** A mechanism to automatically transfer messages stuck past a time threshold (`min-idle-time`) in the `PEL` from a crashed worker to another worker to resume processing, ==ensuring no events are missed==.
