> [!TIP] Real-World Ecosystem Picture: Choosing a Task Queue (`Celery`/`BullMQ`), `Redis Streams`, or `Apache Kafka`?
> A good engineer does not reinvent everything from scratch when a standard tool already fits the problem:
> - **Need to run background jobs (*Background Jobs*: sending emails, exporting PDFs, calling AI APIs with scheduling & automatic retries):** Use **Redis-backed Task Queue libraries** such as **`Celery`**, **`ARQ`** (async for FastAPI), **`RQ`** in Python, or **`BullMQ`** in Node.js/TypeScript!
> - **Need sub-1ms *Event Streaming* for medium-to-large Microservices (`10k – 100k events/s`) without taking on the operational cost of a new cluster:** Choose **Redis Streams** directly on your existing Redis infrastructure!
> - **When do you genuinely need Apache Kafka (or RabbitMQ)?** Choose **Kafka** when you need to retain **Terabytes** of event history on cheap disk for weeks or months for replay (*Event Sourcing / Data Lake*) or throughput of millions of messages/sec; choose **RabbitMQ** when you need complex branching routing (*Topic/Header Exchange*).

steps.headingEn: Analyzing the Message Lifecycle Inside Consumer Groups & PEL
steps.bodyEn:
The most important aspect of working with Redis Streams is understanding the **3 special ID symbols** (`$`, `0`, `>`) and the closed-loop 4-step workflow:

```visual
kind: flow
title: Hành Trình Khép Kín Của Một Sự Kiện Từ XADD Đến XACK / XAUTOCLAIM [!badge:sky:At-Least-Once]
direction: LR
steps:
  - label: "1. XADD MAXLEN ~"
    detail: "Sinh ID <ms>-<seq> nối đuôi Listpack"
    tone: sky
  - label: "2. XREADGROUP ... >"
    detail: "Giao tin mới chưa ai nhận & ghi vào PEL"
    tone: violet
  - label: "3A. XACK (Thành công)"
    detail: "Xoá ID khỏi PEL -> Giải phóng theo dõi"
    tone: emerald
  - label: "3B. XAUTOCLAIM (Sập pod)"
    detail: "Thu hồi tin treo quá min-idle-time rồi XACK"
    tone: amber
```

1. **When creating a group with `XGROUP CREATE <key> <group> <id> MKSTREAM`**:
   - Pass **`$`**: Only receive messages **newly produced from the moment the group is created onward**.
   - Pass **`0`**: Replay **the entire history starting from the very first message** currently in the Stream.
   - Always append the **`MKSTREAM`** keyword at the end to automatically create an empty Stream if the Worker service boots before the Producer.
2. **When reading messages with `XREADGROUP GROUP <group> <consumer> COUNT n BLOCK ms STREAMS <key> <id>`**:
   - Pass **`>`** at the end: *"Deliver new messages to me that have never been delivered to anyone in this group"* (while immediately recording them in the **PEL**).
   - Pass **`0`** at the end: *"Return the list of old messages still sitting unfinished in my own PEL after a restart"*.
3. **When rescuing stuck messages with `XPENDING` & `XAUTOCLAIM`**:
   - `XPENDING` inspects which messages are stuck, how many milliseconds they have been idle (`idle time`), and how many times they have been retried (`deliveryCount`).
   - ==`XAUTOCLAIM orders:stream payment-cg worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10`== automatically transfers ownership of messages stuck for more than `60,000ms` (1 minute) to `worker-2` and returns the message payloads immediately for processing!

> [!WARNING] Two Common Causes of RAM Exhaustion and Infinite Loops in Redis Streams
> 1. **Forgetting to trim with `MAXLEN ~` when calling `XADD`:** The `XACK` command **only removes the tracking entry from the `PEL` and does NOT delete the original message from the Stream** (because other groups may still need to read it!). Without ==`MAXLEN ~ 50000`== (using the tilde `~` to trim whole `listpack` nodes quickly in `O(1)`), the Stream will grow unbounded and consume all RAM!
> 2. **Leaving a "Poison Message" looping forever:** If an order has malformed data that causes Worker code to throw an exception repeatedly, `XAUTOCLAIM` will pass it back and forth endlessly. Check if `deliveryCount > 5` and route it to a separate error stream (`orders:dlq` — *Dead-Letter Queue*), then call `XACK` to release it from the `PEL`!

steps.headingEn: Production-Grade Worker Pattern (Python redis-py & Node.js ioredis)
steps.bodyEn:
Because Redis Streams guarantees **At-Least-Once** delivery, an order can be processed again if a previous Worker crashed right after charging payment before sending `XACK`. Therefore, the `process_order` handler must always be designed to be **Idempotent**:

```python
# Python (redis-py) — Chu trình Worker chuẩn: XAUTOCLAIM giải cứu tin treo + XREADGROUP + XACK
from redis.exceptions import ResponseError

def init_stream_group(r, stream="orders:stream", group="payment-cg"):
    try:
        r.xgroup_create(stream, group, id="$", mkstream=True)
    except ResponseError as exc:
        if "BUSYGROUP" not in str(exc):
            raise  # Nhóm đã tồn tại -> bỏ qua an toàn

def poll_orders_once(r, consumer_name: str):
    # 1. Thu hồi các đơn hàng bị treo quá 60,000ms từ các worker đã sập:
    _, claimed, *_ = r.xautoclaim("orders:stream", "payment-cg", consumer_name, min_idle_time=60_000, start_id="0-0", count=10)
    for entry_id, fields in claimed:
        process_order_idempotently(entry_id, fields)
        r.xack("orders:stream", "payment-cg", entry_id)

    # 2. Nhận mẻ đơn hàng mới ('>') kèm chờ tối đa 2 giây nếu vắng việc:
    batches = r.xreadgroup("payment-cg", consumer_name, {"orders:stream": ">"}, count=10, block=2000)
    for _, entries in batches:
        for entry_id, fields in entries:
            process_order_idempotently(entry_id, fields)
            r.xack("orders:stream", "payment-cg", entry_id)  # Xoá khỏi sổ chờ PEL!
```

```ts
// Node.js / TypeScript (ioredis) — Phát sự kiện kèm cắt ngọn xấp xỉ MAXLEN ~ 10000
await redis.xadd(
  "orders:stream",
  "MAXLEN", "~", 10_000,
  "*",
  "orderId", "ord-101",
  "amount", "490000"
);
```

> [!REMEMBER] Rules of Thumb When Designing a Messaging System
> - Need to broadcast real-time signals to every listening server (live chat, cursor coordinates, L1 cache invalidation) and can tolerate message loss on disconnect -> Choose **Pub/Sub** (or **`SSUBSCRIBE`** on Cluster).
> - Need simple background jobs in Python/Node.js code -> Use **`ARQ` / `Celery` / `RQ`** or **`BullMQ`**.
> - Need a durable event log stream read independently by multiple services with minimal operational overhead -> Choose **Redis Streams (`XADD MAXLEN ~` + `XREADGROUP` + `XACK` + `XAUTOCLAIM`)**.

readings.noteEn: An order-processing worker written in TypeScript makes 2 serious mistakes simultaneously: firing `XADD` without a `MAXLEN ~` cap and consuming via `XREADGROUP` while forgetting to call `XACK`.
readings.taskEn: What will happen to Redis RAM usage and the `PEL` list after 1 week of continuous operation at 500 orders/sec?
readings.answerEn: Without `MAXLEN ~`, the underlying stream entries grow indefinitely until hitting `maxmemory` and causing `OOM` errors. Equally severe, every message read via `XREADGROUP ... >` without `XACK` remains permanently in the Consumer Group's `PEL` (Pending Entries List) — creating a hidden memory leak even if you later trim the Stream!

readings.noteEn: A production-grade Node.js worker pattern combining an `XREADGROUP BLOCK` loop, `XACK` confirmation after a successful DB write, and periodic `XAUTOCLAIM` sweeps to reclaim orphaned messages.
readings.taskEn: Why must the processing function inside the Worker be **Idempotent** (running twice produces no duplicate side effects) even when `XACK` is used?
readings.answerEn: Redis Streams provides **At-Least-Once Delivery** semantics: if Worker A finishes charging/saving to the DB but crashes 1ms before sending `XACK` back to Redis, after `min-idle-time` expires Worker B will use `XAUTOCLAIM` to receive that exact same message a second time. Thus, the business layer must always check a deduplication key (`orderId`) before executing!

R08-Q1.qEn: What happens when you publish a message using **`PUBLISH orders:paid "ord-101"`** at the exact moment all Subscriber services are restarting (disconnected for 3 seconds)?
choicesEn: Redis automatically queues the message to a temporary disk file and redelivers it as soon as Subscribers reconnect
That message **vanishes permanently** because Pub/Sub operates as *Fire-and-Forget* (pushing only to sockets actively listening at publish time, with no RAM storage)
The `PUBLISH` command blocks until at least 1 Subscriber comes back online
Redis automatically converts the Pub/Sub channel into a Stream data type
R08-Q1.explainEn: Pub/Sub has no history buffer or acknowledgment tracking list. If you need guaranteed zero event loss during Worker restarts or network drops, you must use **Redis Streams**.

R08-Q2.qEn: In the command **`XREADGROUP GROUP payment-cg worker-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS orders:stream >`**, what does the special **`>`** symbol at the end mean?
choicesEn: Tells Redis to sort messages in descending order from newest to oldest
Delivers only **brand-new messages never before delivered to any consumer** in group `payment-cg` (while recording them in the PEL)
Deletes all older messages after reading finishes
Re-reads only messages currently stuck in `worker-1`'s own PEL
R08-Q2.explainEn: The `>` symbol requests new messages past the Consumer Group's `last-delivered-id`; conversely, passing ID `0` to `XREADGROUP` makes Redis return unacknowledged messages still sitting in that consumer's own PEL.

R08-Q3.qEn: When a Worker calls **`XACK orders:stream payment-cg 1700000000100-0`**, Redis removes that entry from the **PEL** tracking list of group `payment-cg`, while **the original message still remains in `orders:stream`** until trimmed by `MAXLEN` / `MINID` or `XDEL`.
R08-Q3.explainEn: Correct! A single Stream can serve multiple independent Consumer Groups (e.g., `payment-cg`, `email-cg`, `analytics-cg`), so `XACK` only clears the pending entry in the calling group's PEL. To cap RAM for the underlying Stream, you must pair `XADD` with `MAXLEN ~ <count>`.

R08-Q4.qEn: Why is it always recommended in production to write **`XADD events MAXLEN ~ 50000 * ...`** (with the tilde `~`) instead of exact trimming `MAXLEN = 50000`?
choicesEn: Because the `=` sign was completely removed from Redis 8 syntax
The `~` lets Redis trim only when it can free an **entire `listpack` macro-node** at the head of the Radix Tree in ultra-fast **O(1)** time, avoiding CPU overhead from shifting individual entries
The `~` automatically compresses JSON text with Gzip
The `~` automatically calls `XACK` on behalf of all Consumer Groups
R08-Q4.explainEn: Redis Streams packs multiple consecutive entries into `listpack` nodes. Approximate trimming (`~`) lets Redis wait until the entire leading node exceeds the threshold and drop the whole node in O(1), keeping write throughput at hundreds of thousands of ops/sec.

R08-Q5.qEn: When `worker-1` suddenly crashes (`SIGKILL`) while mid-way through processing 3 orders, which command on Redis 6.2+ / Redis 8 lets `worker-2` **automatically scan and reclaim** messages idle for over 60 seconds in a single network round-trip?
choicesEn: `XAUTOCLAIM orders:stream payment-cg worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10`
`XRANGE orders:stream - + COUNT 10`
`BLPOP orders:stream 60`
`SPUBLISH orders:stream "reclaim"`
R08-Q5.explainEn: `XAUTOCLAIM` combines finding entries past `min-idle-time` (`60000ms`) in the PEL with transferring ownership to `worker-2` and returning the message payloads immediately.

R08-Q6.qEn: On a **Redis Cluster**, **Sharded Pub/Sub (`SSUBSCRIBE` / `SPUBLISH`)** scales better than classic `SUBSCRIBE` / `PUBLISH` because channel traffic is routed only within the nodes owning that channel's Hash Slot instead of being broadcast to every node in the cluster.
R08-Q6.explainEn: True! In classic Pub/Sub on a Cluster, every `PUBLISH` is replicated and sent to all nodes, creating internal bandwidth storms as the cluster grows; Sharded Pub/Sub (introduced in Redis 7.0+) eliminates this bottleneck.

R08-Q7.qEn: Fill in the missing **keyword option** at the end of the `XGROUP CREATE` command below so Redis automatically creates an empty Stream if the key `orders:stream` does not yet exist:
R08-Q7.explainEn: The `MKSTREAM` option safely initializes both an empty Stream and the Consumer Group at once when the Worker service starts before the Producer.

R08-FC1.frontEn: What is the most fundamental difference between **Redis Pub/Sub** and **Redis Streams** regarding data durability?
R08-FC1.backEn:
- **Pub/Sub**: *Fire-and-Forget* (At-most-once) — pushes instantaneously to connected clients, stored nowhere in RAM, messages lost on disconnect.
- **Redis Streams**: Persistent *Append-Only Log* (At-least-once) — stored in RAM + AOF/RDB, supports historical replay, load-balancing via Consumer Groups, and tracking in the **PEL** until **`XACK`**.

R08-FC2.frontEn: What is the **PEL (Pending Entries List)** in Redis Streams and what causes RAM leaks in the PEL?
R08-FC2.backEn: The **PEL** is an in-memory table inside each Consumer Group tracking every message delivered via `XREADGROUP ... >` that has **not yet received `XACK`**. If a Worker forgets to call `XACK` (or hits a poison message that crashes repeatedly without routing to a DLQ + `XACK`), the PEL grows unbounded!

R08-FC3.frontEn: What is the difference between the **`$`** and **`0`** IDs when running `XGROUP CREATE <key> <group> <id> MKSTREAM`?
R08-FC3.backEn:
- **`$`**: Consumes only events **newly produced from the moment the group is created onward**.
- **`0`** (or `0-0`): Replays (**replay**) all historical messages currently in the Stream from the beginning.

R08-FC4.frontEn: What is the difference between **`>`** and **`0`** at the end of `XREADGROUP GROUP <g> <c> STREAMS <key> <id>`?
R08-FC4.backEn:
- **`>`**: Requests **new messages never yet delivered** to anyone in the group.
- **`0`**: Re-reads messages **currently pending in consumer `<c>`'s own PEL** (useful when a pod restarts keeping the same consumer name).

R08-FC5.frontEn: How does the workflow for recovering orphaned messages from a crashed Worker using **`XAUTOCLAIM`** work?
R08-FC5.backEn: A live Worker periodically calls `XAUTOCLAIM <stream> <group> <my_name> <min_idle_ms> 0-0 COUNT <n>` to claim ownership of messages idle longer than `min_idle_ms`, executes **Idempotent** business logic, and must then call **`XACK`** to remove them from the PEL.

R08-FC6.frontEn: Why must business logic downstream of Redis Streams always be designed to be **Idempotent**?
R08-FC6.backEn: Because Streams provides **At-Least-Once** semantics: if Worker A finishes writing to the DB/charging a payment but crashes right before executing `XACK`, Worker B will `XAUTOCLAIM` and reprocess that exact message a second time!

redis-ex-r08-1.titleEn: Log Bounded Events with XADD MAXLEN ~ and Query with XRANGE
redis-ex-r08-1.promptEn: The starter script calls `XADD` with **no capacity limit**, which will grow RAM indefinitely over time! Append **4 consecutive events** (`evt-1`, `evt-2`, `evt-3`, `evt-4`) to the Stream `events:checkout` using the approximate trimming flag **`MAXLEN ~ 3`** and auto-generated ID **`*`** (with field pairs `event <id>` and `step "paid"`). Then run **`XLEN events:checkout`** (expecting exactly `3` latest entries retained) and **`XRANGE events:checkout - +`** to list all remaining entries.
hintsEn: Standard syntax: `XADD events:checkout MAXLEN ~ 3 * event "evt-1" step "paid"` (repeat for `evt-1` through `evt-4`).
At the end of the script, call `XLEN events:checkout` then `XRANGE events:checkout - +` to verify `evt-1` was trimmed and 3 entries remain.

redis-ex-r08-2.titleEn: Safely Create a Consumer Group with MKSTREAM and Publish New Orders
redis-ex-r08-2.promptEn:
In a microservice deployment, Worker pods often boot **before** the first order arrives, so the key `orders:stream` does not exist yet — causing the starter's `XGROUP CREATE` command to fail immediately! Complete the following:
1) Fix the command creating group **`payment-cg`** on key **`orders:stream`** starting from **`$`** with the **`MKSTREAM`** option to auto-create an empty Stream if missing.
2) Append **2 new orders** (`ord-101` and `ord-102`) to `orders:stream` using `XADD orders:stream MAXLEN ~ 1000 * orderId <id> amount <amount>`.
hintsEn: Add the `MKSTREAM` keyword at the end of the command: `XGROUP CREATE orders:stream payment-cg $ MKSTREAM`.
Next, run 2 commands: `XADD orders:stream MAXLEN ~ 1000 * orderId "ord-101" amount "350000"` and similarly for `"ord-102"`.

redis-ex-r08-3.titleEn: Consume Orders with XREADGROUP and Acknowledge with XACK to Prevent PEL Leaks
redis-ex-r08-3.promptEn: There are already 2 pending orders (`1700000000100-0` and `1700000000200-0`) waiting in `orders:stream` for group `orders-cg`. The starter code pulls these 2 messages for `worker-1` using `XREADGROUP ... >`, but **forgets to call `XACK`**, leaving both trapped permanently in the **PEL** (`Pending Entries List`)! Add an **`XACK`** command acknowledging both IDs for group `orders-cg`, then call `XPENDING orders:stream orders-cg` to verify the pending count drops to `0`.
hintsEn: `XACK` accepts multiple IDs on a single line: `XACK orders:stream orders-cg 1700000000100-0 1700000000200-0`.
Keep the `XREADGROUP` command at the top so `worker-1` receives the 2 orders `ord-501`, `ord-502` before calling `XACK`.

redis-ex-r08-4.titleEn: Rescue Stuck Orders from a Crashed Worker Using XPENDING, XAUTOCLAIM, and XACK
redis-ex-r08-4.promptEn:
Production incident: the `worker-crashed` process was just `OOMKilled` while holding order `1700000000100-0` (`ord-999`) in the PEL of group `orders-cg` on `orders:stream` for over **120 seconds** (`120000ms`)! Write the standard recovery workflow on the new process **`worker-rescue`**:
1) Keep `XPENDING orders:stream orders-cg - + 10` to inspect details of the stuck message.
2) Use **`XAUTOCLAIM`** on `orders:stream` for group `orders-cg` to transfer ownership of messages idle for at least **`60000`** ms (scanning from **`0-0`**, `COUNT 10`) to **`worker-rescue`**.
3) After reclaiming and processing, call **`XACK`** for ID `1700000000100-0` to bring `orders-cg`'s PEL down to `0`!
hintsEn: Auto-claim syntax: `XAUTOCLAIM orders:stream orders-cg worker-rescue 60000 0-0 COUNT 10`.
Note: `XAUTOCLAIM` only transfers ownership in the PEL from `worker-crashed` to `worker-rescue`; you must still call `XACK orders:stream orders-cg 1700000000100-0` to clear it from the PEL!

redis-ex-r08-5.titleEn: Combine Real-Time PUBLISH with Full Historical Stream Replay (from ID 0)
redis-ex-r08-5.promptEn:
The key `audit:stream` already holds 2 historical security events (`1700000000010-0` and `1700000000020-0`). The Audit team just deployed a new service **`compliance-cg`** that needs to read **the entire history from the start**, but the starter mistakenly set the starting ID to **`$`** (causing `XREADGROUP` to return `(nil)` and miss all existing data!). Complete the following:
1) Broadcast a real-time Pub/Sub notification to channel **`ws:alerts`** with payload `"audit-replay-start"` using **`PUBLISH`**.
2) Fix the `XGROUP CREATE` command for **`compliance-cg`** on `audit:stream` to start from **`0`** (instead of `$`).
3) Pull both historical entries with `XREADGROUP GROUP compliance-cg auditor-1 COUNT 2 STREAMS audit:stream >` and call **`XACK`** for both IDs (`1700000000010-0` and `1700000000020-0`).
hintsEn: Send the live alert with `PUBLISH ws:alerts "audit-replay-start"`.
Change `$` to `0` in `XGROUP CREATE audit:stream compliance-cg 0` to replay history from the start, then call `XACK audit:stream compliance-cg 1700000000010-0 1700000000020-0`.

R09.titleEn: Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, Read/Write-Through, Write-Behind & Invalidation
R09.summaryEn: Master the 4 read/write topologies between Application, Redis, and Relational Database: choose properly among Cache-Aside, Read/Write-Through, and Write-Behind, eliminate cache-invalidation Race Conditions (`UNLINK` after DB commit), and apply Versioned Keys and Negative Caching.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> If a product detail page receives 50,000 views per minute while its price only changes once or twice a day, forcing PostgreSQL to re-execute a complex `SELECT` query 50,000 times/minute is extremely wasteful. Placing **Redis as a Cache** in front reduces read latency from `25ms` down to under **`0.4ms`**:
> - **`Cache Hit`:** The data already exists in Redis -> the application reads and returns it to the client immediately.
> - **`Cache Miss`:** The key is missing in Redis (or its `TTL` expired) -> the application queries the Database, then writes a copy to Redis with a `TTL` for subsequent requests to reuse.
> - **`Cache Invalidation`:** The process of deleting or refreshing a stale cached copy when the source-of-truth data in the Database changes, ==preventing users from reading outdated data (*Stale Data*)==.

> [!NOTE] Direct Comparison of the 3 Read/Write Caching Strategies
> - **Cache-Aside (*Lazy Loading*):** The application checks Redis first; only on a `Cache Miss` does it read from the Database and populate Redis.
> - **Write-Through:** Every write synchronously updates both the Database and Redis before returning success.
> - **Write-Behind (*Write-Back*):** The application writes immediately to Redis (`< 1ms`) and returns success, while a background worker batches updates to the Database asynchronously later.

steps.headingEn: The Big Picture of 4 Caching Topologies
steps.bodyEn:
No single pattern fits every workload. Systems engineers choose based on the **Read/Write ratio**, staleness tolerance, and data criticality:

```visual
kind: illustration
diagram: "redis:r09"
badge: "Caching Topologies · R09"
title: "Kiến Trúc 4 Luồng Đọc/Ghi Giữa Application, Redis và Database"
subtitle: "So sánh đường đi dữ liệu của Cache-Aside, Write-Through và nguy cơ Race Condition khi đồng bộ kép"
caption: "90% microservice Web/API hiện đại chọn Cache-Aside kết hợp UNLINK sau khi commit Database."
callouts:
  - num: 1
    label: "Cache-Aside (Lazy Populate)"
    desc: "App tự kiểm tra Redis trước; nếu Miss mới đọc DB rồi nạp ngược lên Redis kèm TTL bắt buộc."
    tone: sky
  - num: 2
    label: "Invalidate thay vì Update đè"
    desc: "Khi sửa dữ liệu gốc ở DB, xoá khoá bằng UNLINK an toàn và nhẹ hơn nhiều so với tính toán lại rồi SET đè."
    tone: emerald
  - num: 3
    label: "Write-Through & Write-Behind"
    desc: "Write-Through giữ cache luôn tươi mới cho luồng đọc nóng; Write-Behind gom batch tăng tốc ghi nhưng chấp nhận rủi ro mất mát nếu sập nguồn."
    tone: amber
```

- [>] **1. Cache-Aside (*Lazy Loading*)** [!badge:emerald:Most common - 90% of systems]: The application actively coordinates both sides. Its biggest strength is that Redis **only spends RAM on data actually requested**, and if Redis suffers a brief outage, the app can automatically fall back to reading the Database directly instead of going completely down.
- [>] **2. Read-Through / Write-Through** [!badge:sky:Always fresh cache]: Every write synchronously writes to both the Database and Redis before returning. Eliminates *Cold Misses* right after creating or updating records (such as topping up a wallet or upgrading VIP status), at the cost of higher write latency.
- [>] **3. Write-Behind (*Write-Back*)** [!badge:amber:Maximum write throughput]: The app writes directly to Redis (`HINCRBY`, `ZINCRBY`, `XADD`) and returns immediately in under `1ms`, while a background Worker batches writes (*Batch UPSERT*) into PostgreSQL/ClickHouse. Ideal for **video view counts, livestream hearts, and vehicle GPS coordinates**, but never use for bank balances without careful durability safeguards!
- [>] **4. Stale-While-Revalidate (*SWR* — Serve stale while silently refreshing)** [!badge:violet:Smooth tail latency]: Embeds a soft expiration timestamp inside the cached payload; right after soft expiry, clients still receive an instant `0.4ms` response while a single background task quietly refreshes the new value from the Database.

steps.headingEn: Data Sync Strategy: Update in Place or Delete Cache When Database Changes?
steps.bodyEn:
This is a classic System Design interview question! Suppose product `id=108` just dropped in price from `5,000,000 VND` to `4,290,000 VND`. Why is ==the industry standard always: Commit Database first -> Delete (`UNLINK`) Cache second==?

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Bẫy Bất Nhất Dữ Liệu (Dual-Write Race) vs Chuẩn Mực Xoá Sau Commit"
subtitle: "Tại sao tự SET đè hoặc xoá Cache TRƯỚC khi ghi Database đều dễ sinh ra dữ liệu cũ nằm lì suốt hàng giờ?"
left:
  badge: "SAI LẦM PHỔ BIẾN"
  title: "Cập nhật đè Cache hoặc Xoá Cache TRƯỚC DB"
  tone: rose
  code: |
    # Bẫy: Xoá Cache TRƯỚC khi commit DB -> Luồng đọc chen ngang!
    await redis.delete(f"cache:product:{id}")
    # [!] Ngay mili-giây này Request B nhảy vào thấy Miss,
    # đọc giá CŨ từ DB và SET ngược lại vào Redis suốt 1 giờ!
    await db.execute("UPDATE products SET price = $1...", price)
  lang: python
  bullets:
    - "**Race Condition khi 2 luồng cùng SET đè:** Request A cập nhật DB trước, Request B cập nhật DB sau, nhưng vì trễ mạng nên B `SET` Redis trước rồi A `SET` đè giá cũ lên sau!"
    - "**Lãng phí tài nguyên:** Nếu mặt hàng đổi giá 50 lần/phút nhưng cả tiếng mới có 1 người xem, tính toán lại JSON 50 lần là vô ích."
right:
  badge: "CHUẨN PRODUCTION"
  title: "1. Commit DB -> 2. UNLINK Cache bất đồng bộ"
  tone: emerald
  code: |
    # 1. Ghi nguồn sự thật (PostgreSQL) thành công trước
    await db.execute("UPDATE products SET price = $1 WHERE id = $2", price, id)

    # 2. Gỡ khoá cũ dưới nền O(1) bằng UNLINK (thay vì DEL)
    await redis.unlink(f"cache:product:{id}")
  lang: python
  bullets:
    - "**Xác suất lệch cực thấp:** Dữ liệu chỉ được nạp lại vào Redis khi thực sự có người đọc tiếp theo sau khi DB đã lưu xong bản mới."
    - "**`UNLINK` thay vì `DEL`:** Tháo con trỏ khóa trong `O(1)`, nhường việc giải phóng RAM cho luồng nền mà không làm khựng Event Loop."
```

> [!WARNING] How to Handle `db.execute()` Succeeding While the Immediate `redis.unlink()` Fails Due to a Network Blip?
> 1. **Safety Net #1 — Always attach a finite `TTL` (`300s–900s`):** Ensures that even if `unlink` drops over the network, stale data expires naturally within minutes rather than diverging forever!
> 2. **Safety Net #2 (Large-scale systems):** Retry the `unlink` command up to 2 times, or use a **CDC (*Change Data Capture* — such as Debezium tailing PostgreSQL's WAL)** stream to automatically emit cache invalidation events until succeeded.

steps.headingEn: Three Cache Key Design Techniques & Real-World Library Ecosystem
steps.bodyEn:
```visual
kind: anatomy
title: "Ba Kỹ Thuật Thiết Kế Khóa Cache An Toàn"
subtitle: "Chống lỗi lệch cấu trúc khi cập nhật code mới, chống cạn kiệt RAM và chặn truy vấn rác"
items:
  - keyword: "Versioned Key"
    role: "Triển khai Zero-Downtime"
    tone: cyan
    summary: "Nhúng hậu tố phiên bản cấu trúc (`v1`, `v2`) vào tên khoá khi thay đổi định dạng dữ liệu."
    bullets:
      - "Khi bản code mới thêm trường `discount_pct` vào JSON, đổi tên khoá sang ==`cache:product:v2:108`== giúp container code cũ và code mới chạy song song êm ái lúc triển khai (Rolling Update)!"
    example: |
      SET cache:product:v2:108 '{"price":4290000,"discount_pct":15}' EX 600
    lang: redis
  - keyword: "Mandatory Atomic TTL"
    role: "Kỷ luật Quản trị Bộ nhớ"
    tone: emerald
    summary: "Mọi khoá Cache ĐỀU PHẢI gắn hạn sống (`EX` / `PX`) ngay trong cùng 1 câu lệnh `SET`."
    bullets:
      - "Không bao giờ viết rời `SET` rồi mới `EXPIRE` kẻo sinh ra **Zombie Key** tồn tại vĩnh viễn ăn mòn RAM."
    example: |
      SET cache:product:v2:108 '{"price":4290000}' EX 600
    lang: redis
  - keyword: "Negative Cache"
    role: "Ngăn truy vấn ID không tồn tại"
    tone: amber
    summary: "Lưu chuỗi đánh dấu rỗng (`\"__NULL__\"`) với TTL ngắn (`30s–60s`) khi Database trả về 0 dòng."
    bullets:
      - "Ngăn chặn việc khách hỏi đi hỏi lại một mã giảm giá không tồn tại làm chọc thẳng xuống Database ở mọi request."
    example: |
      SET cache:coupon:GHOST2026 "__NULL__" EX 45
    lang: redis
```

> [!TIP] Multi-Tier Caching Libraries (L1 RAM + L2 Redis) & Redis 8's `CLIENT TRACKING`
> In production, instead of repeating `if cached: ...` boilerplate across hundreds of APIs, engineers rely on battle-tested libraries supporting **2-tier Caching** (ultra-fast `~50ns` local app RAM L1 + shared Redis L2) or **Server-Assisted Client-Side Caching (`CLIENT TRACKING`)** built into `redis-py` and `ioredis` (when a key changes on Redis, Redis proactively sends an invalidation message telling the app to evict its local L1 copy immediately!):
> - **Python / FastAPI:** **`cashews`** (built-in Cache-Aside, SWR, Singleflight, Client-side tracking), **`fastapi-cache2`**, or `cachetools` + `redis.asyncio`.
> - **Node.js / TypeScript:** **`bentocache`** (powerful multi-tier L1+L2 + SWR) or `cache-manager`.
> - **Java / Spring Boot:** **`Caffeine` (L1) + `Redisson` / `Spring Cache` (L2)**.

steps.headingEn: Production Cache-Aside Reference Implementation (Python Async & TypeScript)
steps.bodyEn:
```python
# Python (FastAPI + redis.asyncio): Cache-Aside + Negative Cache ngắn hạn + UNLINK sau khi ghi DB
import json

SENTINEL_NULL = "__NULL__"

async def get_product_by_id(r, db, product_id: int) -> dict | None:
    key = f"cache:product:v2:{product_id}"
    cached = await r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return None if cached == SENTINEL_NULL else json.loads(cached)

    row = await db.fetch_one("SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE id = $1", product_id)
    if row is None:
        await r.set(key, SENTINEL_NULL, ex=45)  # Negative Cache 45 giây
        return None

    payload = dict(row)
    await r.set(key, json.dumps(payload), ex=600)  # Gộp nguyên tử SET + EX
    return payload

async def update_product_price(r, db, product_id: int, new_price: int) -> None:
    await db.execute("UPDATE products SET price = $1 WHERE id = $2", new_price, product_id)
    await r.unlink(f"cache:product:v2:{product_id}")  # Xoá bất đồng bộ sau khi DB commit!
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways from R09
> 1. **Cache-Aside + Delete After DB Write (`Commit DB -> UNLINK Cache`)** is the safest and most widely used default recipe for 90% of Web/API systems.
> 2. Always combine atomically with **`SET key val EX <ttl>`**; never dump giant multi-megabyte ORM objects into a single Cache key.
> 3. Pair ==Versioned Keys (`v1`, `v2`)== for JSON schema upgrades with ==Negative Caching (`"__NULL__"` TTL `30–60s`)== for non-existent records.

readings.noteEn: Production Cache-Aside implementation in TypeScript using asynchronous `UNLINK` invalidation after the SQL transaction has successfully committed.
readings.taskEn: When updating a user profile, why does the write function choose to call `redis.unlink(cacheKey)` AFTER `db.commit()` instead of calling `redis.set(cacheKey, newJson)` directly?
readings.answerEn: If 2 concurrent updates both call `SET` on Redis, the thread that finished SQL earlier but had its network packet arrive at Redis later will overwrite newer data with stale data until the TTL expires. Asynchronous deletion with `UNLINK` after `db.commit()` forces the next read to fetch the latest authoritative copy from the DB.

readings.noteEn: The Stale-While-Revalidate (SWR) strategy serves data in under 1ms while silently refreshing in the background without making users wait.
readings.taskEn: What is the difference between Redis's physical TTL and a logical expiration field (`logical_exp`) stored inside the JSON payload?
readings.answerEn: A physical TTL removes the key completely from RAM when it hits 0; `logical_exp` allows the app to keep reading and returning the slightly stale record in milliseconds while a single background worker queries the DB to refresh it.

R09-Q1.qEn: In a Cache-Aside pattern paired with PostgreSQL, which update sequence minimizes the risk of data inconsistency (Race Conditions holding stale values for a long time)?
choicesEn: Delete the Redis key first, then run the UPDATE statement on PostgreSQL
Execute UPDATE and COMMIT successfully on PostgreSQL first, then call UNLINK to delete the key on Redis
Write the new value straight to Redis with SET first, then enqueue a cronjob to update PostgreSQL 1 hour later
Run both in parallel `Promise.all([db.update(), redis.set()])` regardless of order
R09-Q1.explainEn: Deleting the cache before DB commit allows a concurrent read to fetch old DB data and populate Redis for the entire TTL. Having two concurrent writers both `SET` Redis can let the older DB write arrive at Redis later and overwrite newer data. Thus, Commit DB -> `UNLINK` cache is the safest standard.

R09-Q2.qEn: In production operations, splitting `SET cache:item:1 data` and `EXPIRE cache:item:1 600` into two separate network commands is completely as safe as the combined command `SET cache:item:1 data EX 600`.
R09-Q2.explainEn: False! If the application Pod is OOMKilled, crashes, or loses its network connection right after `SET` and before sending `EXPIRE`, that key gets `TTL = -1` (becoming a Zombie Key living in RAM forever).

R09-Q3.qEn: Instead of using `DEL` which frees memory synchronously on the main thread and can stall the Event Loop on large payloads, which Redis command unlinks the key in `O(1)` and reclaims memory asynchronously in a background thread?
R09-Q3.explainEn: `UNLINK` only removes the key pointer from the keyspace hash table in `O(1)` on the main thread, then hands off heavy memory deallocation to the `bio_lazy_free` background thread.

R09-Q4.qEn: Which Caching pattern allows the application to write directly to Redis and return immediately, while a background Worker periodically batches writes down to the Database — great for video view counters, but risky for bank account balances?
choicesEn: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
Read-Through
Write-Through
Write-Behind (Write-Back)
R09-Q4.explainEn: Write-Behind (Write-Back) absorbs write spikes directly in RAM and flushes batches to the DB asynchronously, trading off the risk of losing unflushed writes if the Redis node suffers a severe crash.

R09-Q5.qEn: When implementing Negative Caching (storing a sentinel value `"__NULL__"` for an ID that does not exist in the Database), why should you set a short TTL of around `30–60 seconds` instead of `24 hours`?
choicesEn: Because Redis does not allow empty or short strings to have a TTL greater than 60 seconds
To block immediate repeated query storms while ensuring that if the record is genuinely created soon after, users aren't stuck seeing an empty result all day
Because after 60 seconds Redis automatically converts String keys into Stream keys
To force PostgreSQL to restart connections once every minute
R09-Q5.explainEn: A short TTL (30–60s) strikes the ideal balance between shielding the DB from 99% of futile repeated queries and keeping natural recovery time short if new data is inserted.

R09-Q6.qEn: In the Stale-While-Revalidate (SWR / Logical Expiration) pattern, embedding a logical expiration timestamp inside the payload lets the read path keep returning stale data in `< 1ms` while triggering a single background task to refresh smoothly.
R09-Q6.explainEn: True! Because the key is not physically evicted immediately, users never suffer P99 Database query latency spikes right when a key turns stale.

R09-Q7.qEn: When releasing API v2 with a changed JSON schema stored in Redis (while both v1 and v2 Pods run concurrently during a Rolling Update), which key naming strategy completely prevents cross-version parsing errors?
choicesEn: Run FLUSHALL to wipe all of Redis every second throughout the deployment
Embed a schema version suffix in the key name (Versioned Key, e.g., changing from `cache:product:v1:108` to `cache:product:v2:108`)
Disable TTL completely on all v1 keys
Change Redis's default port from 6379 to 8080
R09-Q7.explainEn: Versioned Keys completely isolate keyspaces between v1 Pods and v2 Pods during a Rolling Update; old `v1` keys expire naturally via their TTL without scanning or deleting.

R09-FC1.frontEn: What is the standard read and write workflow for the Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) pattern?
R09-FC1.backEn:
**On read:** Check Redis first -> on Hit return immediately; on Miss read DB then `SET key val EX ttl`.
**On write:** Update and Commit DB first -> call `UNLINK key` to delete the stale copy from Redis.

R09-FC2.frontEn: Why should you `UNLINK` a cache key after updating the DB rather than computing and overwriting it with `SET`?
R09-FC2.backEn:
1) Prevents **Dual-Write Race Conditions** (2 concurrent writes arriving at DB and Redis out of order, leaving stale data cached).
2) **Lazy Evaluation**: Avoids wasting CPU serializing JSON and RAM caching an updated record that nobody reads.

R09-FC3.frontEn: What is the core difference between Write-Through and Write-Behind (Write-Back)?
R09-FC3.backEn:
**Write-Through:** Writes synchronously to both Cache and DB before reporting success (safe, higher write latency).
**Write-Behind:** Writes only to Redis and returns immediately, while a background Worker batches writes to the DB later (ultra-fast, but risks losing unflushed data).

R09-FC4.frontEn: What is a Zombie Key in Caching and how do you prevent it completely?
R09-FC4.backEn: A cache key with `TTL = -1` (living forever and leaking RAM) caused by splitting `SET` and `EXPIRE` when the app crashes in between. Prevent it by always using the atomic command `SET key val EX <seconds>`.

R09-FC5.frontEn: What problem does Negative Caching solve and what is the rule for setting its TTL?
R09-FC5.backEn: Stores a special sentinel value (like `"__NULL__"`) when the DB returns nothing to block repeated queries for non-existent IDs. Always use a **short TTL (`30–60s`)** so newly created records take effect promptly.

R09-FC6.frontEn: What 2 major operational benefits does a Versioned Cache Key (`cache:catalog:v2:...`) provide?
R09-FC6.backEn:
1) Lets old code Pods and new code Pods run side by side during a **Rolling Update** without JSON schema conflicts.
2) Invalidates an entire namespace of data instantaneously in `O(1)` cost by bumping the version pointer.

redis-ex-r09-1.titleEn: Populate Cache-Aside Atomically with TTL to Prevent Zombie Keys
redis-ex-r09-1.promptEn:
The read path for product `id=108` just hit a **Cache Miss** in Redis and fetched the record from PostgreSQL: `'{"id":108,"name":"Keychron Q1","price":4290000}'`.

The starter script below makes the classic mistake: calling `SET` without an expiration, turning the key into a **Zombie Key** that lives forever!

- **Tasks:**
  1. Fix the `SET` command for key `cache:product:108` to store the exact JSON string `'{"id":108,"name":"Keychron Q1","price":4290000}'` and atomically attach the expiration flag **`EX 600`** (`10 minutes`).
  2. Call `GET cache:product:108` and `TTL cache:product:108` to verify both the data and its remaining lifetime.
hintsEn: Append the `EX 600` flag right at the end of `SET cache:product:108 '...' EX 600`.
Never split this into two separate commands in production, as a mid-flight process crash would drop the TTL step.

redis-ex-r09-2.titleEn: Invalidate Cache Asynchronously with UNLINK After DB Write
redis-ex-r09-2.promptEn:
User `501` just updated their default shipping address and PostgreSQL has successfully `COMMIT`ted. Redis still holds stale profile snapshots in two keys: `cache:user:501:profile` and `cache:user:501:addresses`.

- **Operational rule:** Strictly **DO NOT use `DEL`** (since synchronous memory freeing on the main thread stalls the Event Loop for large payloads).
- **Task:** Use **`UNLINK`** to asynchronously remove both `cache:user:501:profile` and `cache:user:501:addresses`, then call `EXISTS cache:user:501:profile cache:user:501:addresses` to verify.
hintsEn: `UNLINK` accepts multiple keys at once just like `DEL`: `UNLINK cache:user:501:profile cache:user:501:addresses`.
Make sure no line in your script starts with `DEL`.

redis-ex-r09-3.titleEn: Rotate Versioned Cache Keys When Releasing Schema v4
redis-ex-r09-3.promptEn:
The Backend team just deployed a new release that changes the format of the homepage featured products list. Currently the version pointer `meta:catalog:ver` is at **`3`** and the old key is `cache:catalog:v3:featured`.

- **Tasks:**
  1. Atomically increment the version counter `meta:catalog:ver` to **`4`** using `INCR`.
  2. Populate the new versioned key `cache:catalog:v4:featured` with the value `'["sku-101","sku-205","sku-309"]'` and TTL **`EX 900`**.
  3. Clean up the old version key `cache:catalog:v3:featured` with `UNLINK`.
hintsEn: Use `INCR meta:catalog:ver` to bump the pointer from `3` to `4`.
Write the new key with `SET cache:catalog:v4:featured '["sku-101","sku-205","sku-309"]' EX 900`, then call `UNLINK cache:catalog:v3:featured`.

redis-ex-r09-4.titleEn: Simulate Atomic Write-Through with MULTI / EXEC on a Hash
redis-ex-r09-4.promptEn:
The member Wallet service applies the **Write-Through** pattern for the account overview page (which sees very high read traffic right after a top-up). After the DB top-up transaction commits, the Write-Through layer must synchronously update the Hash `wallet:summary:u900` and reset its TTL inside **the same `MULTI` / `EXEC` atomic block**.

- **Task:** Open a `MULTI` .. `EXEC` transaction executing sequentially:
  1. `HSET wallet:summary:u900 balance 1500000 tier gold updated_at 1700000500`
  2. `EXPIRE wallet:summary:u900 1800` (`30 minutes`).
hintsEn: Unlike `SET`, `HSET` has no direct `EX` flag for the whole Hash, so wrapping `HSET` + `EXPIRE` in `MULTI` ... `EXEC` is standard practice to avoid leaking a Zombie Hash.
Don't forget to close the block with `EXEC` on the last line!

redis-ex-r09-5.titleEn: Short-Term Negative Caching to Block Queries for Non-Existent Promo Codes
redis-ex-r09-5.promptEn:
The system detected thousands of requests per minute trying to apply the promo code `GHOST2026` (which does not exist in PostgreSQL's `coupons` table). Because the DB query returns `null`, naive code caches nothing in Redis, causing every subsequent request to hammer PostgreSQL!

The draft below mistakenly sets the Negative Cache TTL to `86400` seconds (`24 hours`) — if Marketing actually creates `GHOST2026` this afternoon, customers would be falsely rejected all day!

- **Task:** Store the empty sentinel value `"__NULL__"` in key `cache:coupon:GHOST2026` with a short TTL between **`30` and `60` seconds** (for example `EX 45`).
hintsEn: Lower `EX 86400` down to `EX 45` (comfortably within the safe 30–60 second window).
The string value must match `"__NULL__"` exactly so the application layer can distinguish it from a Cache Miss (`nil`).

R10.titleEn: Handling 3 Classic Caching Failures: Cache Stampede, Penetration & Avalanche
R10.summaryEn: Identify and build production-grade shields against 3 classic database-crashing scenarios at million-request scale: Cache Stampede, Cache Penetration, and Cache Avalanche.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> A system handling `20,000 requests/second` with Redis serving `99.5%` of actual reads is typically placed in front of a **Database that can only handle around `200 SQL queries/second`**. If the Cache layer loses its ability to absorb load for even a few seconds, the flood of queries hitting the database directly will quickly exhaust the Database Connection Pool.
>
> Database overload incidents bypassing the Cache layer typically fall into **3 main scenarios**:
> 1. **`Cache Stampede` (*Hot Key Breakdown*):** A heavily accessed key reaches its `TTL` expiration; during the few dozen milliseconds before it is repopulated, thousands of concurrent requests hit a `Cache Miss` and send the exact same query to the Database simultaneously. The fix is using **`Singleflight`** or a **`Mutex Lock`** so only 1 thread/worker queries the Database and rebuilds the Cache.
> 2. **`Cache Penetration`:** The system receives a massive volume of queries for IDs that **exist in neither Redis nor the Database** (e.g., `product_id = -1` or fake UUIDs), driving `Cache Miss` to 100% and sending every request straight to the Database. The fix is placing a **`Bloom Filter`** check at the Redis layer combined with **`Negative Cache`**.
> 3. **`Cache Avalanche`:** Tens of thousands of Cache keys expire at the exact same moment (often caused by setting the same constant TTL during bulk data loading), or a Redis node loses connectivity, causing a massive traffic spike to the Database. The fix is adding randomized **`TTL Jitter`** and deploying Redis HA.

steps.headingEn: Scenario #1: Stopping Cache Stampede (*Hot Key Breakdown*)
steps.bodyEn:
**Symptom:** A single **key with extremely high read traffic** (such as the homepage `cache:home:hero` or a midnight flash-sale item `cache:flashsale:iphone`) just hits `TTL = 0`. Within the mere `40ms` while the first query is busy running SQL against the Database and hasn't `SET` the value back into Redis yet, `5,000` other requests arrive simultaneously, all see `(nil)`, and open `5,000` identical SQL queries!

- [>] **Mitigation 1 — In-Process Request Coalescing (`Singleflight`) + Distributed Lock (`SET ... NX PX`):**
  1. Inside each application process (Go's `singleflight.Group`, a per-key `asyncio.Lock` in Python, or a `Map<string, Promise>` in Node.js), coalesce 500 duplicate-key requests so they share the result of **a single call**.
  2. Across 20 application servers, compete for cache-rebuild ownership with ==`SET lock:rebuild:home <uuid> NX PX 3000`==: only **the 1 server that wins the lock** is allowed to query PostgreSQL; the other 19 wait `30–50ms` and read the fresh value from Redis!
- [>] **Mitigation 2 — Logical Expiration (Never Delete a Hot Key Outright):**
  For ultra-hot keys on event nights, set a long physical TTL (e.g., `3600s`) but embed a soft expiration timestamp `logical_exp` (`now + 300s`) inside the payload. Once logically expired, all clients still immediately receive the current data in `0.3ms`, while a single background worker quietly refreshes it!

steps.headingEn: Scenario #2: Stopping Cache Penetration (*Fake ID Bypass*)
steps.bodyEn:
**Symptom:** Scraper bots or attackers fire tens of thousands of queries with `product_id = -1` or random UUIDs that **exist in neither Redis nor PostgreSQL**, driving the cache miss rate up to `100%`!

> [!WARNING] Why Negative Caching (`"__NULL__"`) alone is NOT ENOUGH against a random-ID scan attack?
> If an attacker generates **10 million completely distinct random UUIDs** in 5 minutes and your app dutifully stores `"__NULL__"` for all 10 million of them: the first pass still pierces through to the Database, and worse, **10 million junk keys will completely fill up Redis RAM**, evicting legitimate customer data!

The standard solution is placing a **`Bloom Filter` gatekeeper** (covered in `R05`) right in front:

```python
# Python (redis-py): Chặn đứng 100% ID không tồn tại ngay từ cổng bằng Validate + Bloom Filter
import re

SKU_RE = re.compile(r"^sku-\d{3,10}$")

async def get_sku_safely(r, db, sku_id: str):
    # Bước 0: Kiểm tra định dạng cơ bản ngay trên CPU ứng dụng (0ms)
    if not SKU_RE.match(sku_id):
        return None

    # Bước 1: Hỏi Bloom Filter trên Redis 8 (trả về 0 => Chắc chắn 100% không có trong DB!)
    might_exist = await r.execute_command("BF.EXISTS", "bf:valid_skus", sku_id)
    if not might_exist:
        return None

    # Bước 2: Đi tiếp vào luồng Cache-Aside có kèm Negative Cache 45s (cho ~1% dương tính giả)
    return await read_with_singleflight(r, db, sku_id)
```

steps.headingEn: Scenario #3: Neutralizing Cache Avalanche (*Simultaneous Expiration Spike*)
steps.bodyEn:
**Symptom:** Tens of thousands of different keys **vanish at the exact same second** (usually caused by a nightly job loading `50,000` promotional items with the exact same constant `EX 3600`), OR an entire Redis server suddenly drops off the network.

```visual
kind: troubleshoot
title: "Bảng Chẩn Đoán & Khắc Phục Nhanh 3 Sự cố Điển hình Caching [!badge:rose:SRE Playbook]"
subtitle: "Nhìn biểu đồ Metrics trên Grafana để phân biệt trúng bệnh trong 30 giây đầu tiên"
items:
  - symptom: "DB QPS dựng đứng theo nhịp từng nấc cố định (vd đúng mỗi 5 phút 1 gai nhọn)"
    badge: "Cache Stampede / Avalanche"
    tone: rose
    cause: "Một Hot Key khổng lồ vừa hết hạn (Stampede) hoặc Cronjob nạp hàng loạt khoá dùng chung một hằng số `EX 300` không có độ lệch ngẫu nhiên (Avalanche)."
    fix: "Thêm biến thiên ngẫu nhiên **TTL Jitter** (`base_ttl + random(5..60)`) cho mọi tác vụ nạp lô và bọc khoá nóng bằng Mutex `SET lock:rebuild:... NX PX 3000`."
    cmd: "SET cache:banner:top '{\"v\":1}' EX 317"
  - symptom: "Redis Hit Rate lao dốc nhưng số lượng bản ghi DB trả về hầu hết bằng 0 rows"
    badge: "Cache Penetration"
    tone: amber
    cause: "Bot hoặc luồng crawler quét tuần tự hàng triệu ID sản phẩm/coupon không tồn tại xuyên thẳng qua Redis xuống PostgreSQL."
    fix: "Khởi tạo `BF.RESERVE bf:valid_skus 0.01 1000000`, nạp tập ID hợp lệ vào Bloom Filter và chặn ngay mọi truy vấn có `BF.EXISTS == 0`."
    cmd: "BF.RESERVE bf:valid_skus 0.01 100000 && BF.EXISTS bf:valid_skus sku-999999"
  - symptom: "Toàn cụm Redis phản hồi Connection Refused kéo theo DB chết ngạt ngay lập tức"
    badge: "Node Failure Avalanche"
    tone: cyan
    cause: "Chạy Redis đơn lẻ (Single Point of Failure) không có Sentinel/Cluster và ứng dụng không có Circuit Breaker giới hạn tải đổ về DB."
    fix: "Triển khai Redis Sentinel/Cluster HA, bật bộ đệm nội bộ L1 ngắn hạn (in-memory LRU vài giây) và cài Rate Limiter/Circuit Breaker bảo vệ DB."
    cmd: "redis-cli INFO replication && redis-cli INFO memory"
```

- [+] **`TTL Jitter` Rule:** Never hardcode `ttl = 300`. Always add ==`10% – 20%` random offset== (`ttl = base_sec + random.randint(10, int(base_sec * 0.2))`) to spread expiration times smoothly over time!

steps.headingEn: Combining Cache Protection Techniques in Production Apps (TypeScript / Node.js & Python)

readings.noteEn: A seemingly harmless Cache-Aside snippet in dev that will burn through PostgreSQL's entire Connection Pool the exact second the Hot Key expires.
readings.taskEn: What happens at millisecond `T = 300.001s` when the homepage key expires and 5,000 concurrent requests hit `getHomepageFeed()` in this file?
readings.answerEn: All 5,000 requests execute `redis.get()` and all receive `null` before any thread can repopulate the cache, causing 5,000 heavy SQL `JOIN` queries to slam straight into PostgreSQL, exhausting the Connection Pool and taking down the entire API cluster.

readings.noteEn: A Bloom Filter shield stops 99% of nonexistent random-ID scan queries right at the Redis edge before they ever reach the Database layer.
readings.taskEn: Between `BF.EXISTS` returning `0` versus returning `1`, which assertion is 100% certain and which carries a false-positive probability?
readings.answerEn: When `BF.EXISTS` returns `0`, it is 100% certain the element does NOT exist (Zero False Negatives), so a `404` can be returned immediately. When it returns `1`, there is a small false-positive probability (e.g., `1%`), in which case the request proceeds to check the Cache and Database (paired with a short-lived Negative Cache).

R10-Q1.qEn: What is the exact name of the phenomenon where thousands of concurrent threads slam into the Database at the exact moment ONE ultra-hot key (Hot Key) reaches its TTL expiration?
choicesEn: Cache Penetration
Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd (Hot Key Breakdown)
Memory Fragmentation
Split-Brain
R10-Q1.explainEn: Cache Stampede occurs around a single heavily accessed key that just expired, causing tens of thousands of concurrent readers to receive `nil` simultaneously and race to rebuild the data from the DB.

R10-Q2.qEn: When `BF.EXISTS bf:valid_skus sku-999` returns `(integer) 0`, there is still roughly a 1% chance that `sku-999` actually exists in the Database.
R10-Q2.explainEn: False! A Bloom Filter mathematically guarantees **Zero False Negatives**: if it returns `0`, it is 100% certain the element was never added. The 1% error rate only applies in the opposite direction (False Positives when returning `1`).

R10-Q3.qEn: When running `TTL <key>` on Redis to diagnose an incident, which integer code is returned if the key does NOT exist at all (already expired or deleted)?
R10-Q3.explainEn: In Redis, `TTL` returns `-2` if the key does not exist, and `-1` if the key exists but has no associated expiration.

R10-Q4.qEn: Which solution most directly and effectively resolves **Cache Avalanche** caused by a Cronjob loading 100,000 products at midnight with the exact same `EX 3600` parameter?
choicesEn: Drop all indexes in PostgreSQL to speed up reads
Apply TTL Jitter: add a randomized offset (e.g., `3600 + random(60, 600)`) to each key during batch loading
Convert all 100,000 String keys into a single List key
Run KEYS * once every minute to keep memory warm
R10-Q4.explainEn: TTL Jitter breaks synchronized expiration, turning a sharp spike of 100,000 SQL queries at second 3600 into a smooth, evenly distributed refresh stream spread over 10 minutes.

R10-Q5.qEn: When an attacker scans 20 million random nonexistent UUIDs (Cache Penetration), why can relying solely on Negative Caching (`SET uuid "__NULL__" EX 60`) backfire and harm Redis?
choicesEn: Because Redis throws a syntax error when storing the string `__NULL__`
Because 20 million single-use junk keys will overflow Redis `maxmemory` and force eviction of legitimate users' real data keys
Because SET EX 60 increases PostgreSQL disk bandwidth by 100x
Because UUIDs cannot be used as key names in Redis
R10-Q5.explainEn: Negative Caching only works well when an attacker repeatedly queries *the same small set of fake IDs*. When an attacker rotates through millions of unique random fake IDs, placing a Bloom Filter in front is the memory-efficient way (~1.2 bytes/element) to stop junk from ever being written to Redis.

R10-Q6.qEn: In-process Singleflight in each Node.js/Go Pod's RAM can coalesce 500 concurrent requests on that same Pod into 1 call to Redis/DB, but with 40 Pods running in parallel, up to 40 queries can still reach the DB unless combined with a Redis Mutex lock.
R10-Q6.explainEn: True! In-process Singleflight only coordinates within a single OS process. Combining In-process Singleflight (reducing network load to Redis) + Redis Mutex `SET NX PX` (narrowing down to just 1 Pod hitting the DB) is the optimal two-tier architecture.

R10-Q7.qEn: What is the Redis command used to pre-allocate capacity and target error rate for a new Bloom filter?
R10-Q7.explainEn: `BF.RESERVE <key> <error_rate> <capacity>` initializes the bit array structure and optimal number of hash functions matching the desired error rate and expected capacity.

R10-FC1.frontEn: Quickly distinguish the 3 major failures: Cache Stampede, Cache Penetration, and Cache Avalanche?
R10-FC1.backEn:
- **Stampede:** 1 Hot Key expires -> thousands of threads slam the DB simultaneously.
- **Penetration:** Queries for IDs missing in both Redis and DB -> 100% bypass to DB.
- **Avalanche:** Tens of thousands of keys expire in the same second (or an entire Redis node goes down).

R10-FC2.frontEn: What are the two most effective ways to completely eliminate Cache Stampede on a Hot Key?
R10-FC2.backEn:
1) **Singleflight + Distributed Mutex** (`SET lock:rebuild:<key> <id> NX PX 3000`) allowing only 1 thread to query the DB.
2) **Logical Expiration (SWR)**: keep a long physical TTL and embed a logical expiration inside the payload to serve stale data immediately while 1 background worker refreshes it.

R10-FC3.frontEn: How does a Bloom Filter's error profile (`BF.EXISTS`) prevent Cache Penetration?
R10-FC3.backEn:
- Returns `0`: **100% guaranteed NOT to exist** (Zero False Negatives) -> block immediately at the edge!
- Returns `1`: May exist (small False Positive rate, e.g. `1%`) -> allow through to Cache + Negative Cache.

R10-FC4.frontEn: What is the TTL Jitter formula to prevent Cache Avalanche during bulk cache warming?
R10-FC4.backEn: Instead of hardcoding `EX 3600`, always add a randomized offset `baseTTL + random(5%..20% baseTTL)` to spread out the batch's expiration times smoothly.

R10-FC5.frontEn: What do the two special negative return values `-1` and `-2` of `TTL <key>` mean?
R10-FC5.backEn:
- **`-1`**: The key exists but has **no expiration** (persistent).
- **`-2`**: The key **does not exist** in the keyspace.

R10-FC6.frontEn: Why do ultra-high-load architectures place an in-process L1 Cache in application RAM (1–2s TTL) in front of L2 Redis?
R10-FC6.backEn: To absorb network bandwidth for extreme Hot Keys (preventing single-core saturation on a single Redis shard) and act as a temporary lifeline against Avalanche if the network to the Redis cluster blips.

redis-ex-r10-1.titleEn: Stop Cache Stampede with an Atomic SET NX PX Mutex Lock
redis-ex-r10-1.promptEn:
The ultra-hot key `cache:flashsale:99` just expired during peak traffic. To prevent 50 API Pods from simultaneously opening 50 PostgreSQL queries, Pod `worker-01` must acquire the rebuild Mutex lock before reading from the DB.

- **Tasks:**
  1. Acquire the rebuild lock using the atomic command `SET lock:rebuild:flashsale:99 "worker-01" NX PX 3000` (create only if not already held `NX`, auto-release after `3000ms` if the Pod crashes).
  2. Simulate a late-arriving second Pod `worker-02` attempting to acquire the same lock `SET lock:rebuild:flashsale:99 "worker-02" NX PX 3000` (Redis will return `(nil)` and preserve `worker-01` as owner).
  3. Repopulate `cache:flashsale:99` with `'{"id":99,"stock":500}'` and **`EX 300`**.
hintsEn: Standard syntax: `SET lock:rebuild:flashsale:99 "worker-01" NX PX 3000`.
When `worker-02` runs the same command with `NX`, it returns `(nil)`, proving mutual exclusion works properly.

redis-ex-r10-2.titleEn: Build a Bloom Filter Shield Against Cache Penetration
redis-ex-r10-2.promptEn:
A botnet is scanning fake product IDs like `sku-hacker-999` straight through the Cache into PostgreSQL. Initialize a **Bloom Filter** in Redis to block nonexistent SKUs right at the edge!

- **Tasks:**
  1. Allocate the filter `bf:valid_skus` with a false-positive rate of **`0.01`** (`1%`) and capacity of **`10000`** elements using `BF.RESERVE`.
  2. Load the 3 valid SKUs `sku-101`, `sku-102`, `sku-103` into `bf:valid_skus` (using `BF.MADD` or `BF.ADD`).
  3. Verify with `BF.EXISTS bf:valid_skus sku-101` (returns `1`) and `BF.EXISTS bf:valid_skus sku-hacker-999` (returns `0` — block immediately!).
hintsEn: The parameter order for `BF.RESERVE` is: `BF.RESERVE <key> <error_rate> <capacity>`, i.e., `BF.RESERVE bf:valid_skus 0.01 10000`.
Use `BF.MADD bf:valid_skus sku-101 sku-102 sku-103` to insert all 3 SKUs cleanly in one command.

redis-ex-r10-3.titleEn: Spread Randomized TTL Jitter to Prevent Cache Avalanche on Batch Load
redis-ex-r10-3.promptEn:
A midnight *Cache Warming* job loads 3 homepage UI blocks: `cache:banner:top`, `cache:banner:mid`, and `cache:banner:bot`. The current script hardcodes `EX 300` on all 3 keys, causing them to **expire at the exact same instant**!

- **Task:** Apply **TTL Jitter** (adding staggered offsets to the `300s` baseline) so the 3 keys expire out of phase across 3 separate windows:
  1. `cache:banner:top` has a TTL between **`305` – `320` seconds** (e.g., `EX 312`).
  2. `cache:banner:mid` has a TTL between **`321` – `340` seconds** (e.g., `EX 331`).
  3. `cache:banner:bot` has a TTL between **`341` – `360` seconds** (e.g., `EX 354`).
hintsEn: Simply update the values after `EX` on the 3 `SET` lines to e.g. `312`, `331`, and `354`.
In production application code, you generate this offset dynamically via `300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60)`.

redis-ex-r10-4.titleEn: Design Logical Expiration (SWR) on a Hash for the Homepage Hot Key
redis-ex-r10-4.promptEn:
To guarantee the homepage config `hot:hero:home` **is never empty** during the midnight Mega Sale, the architecture team adopts the **Logical Expiration (Stale-While-Revalidate)** pattern.

- **Tasks:**
  1. Use `HSET` to store two fields in `hot:hero:home`: `payload` with value `'{"campaign":"MegaSale11.11"}'` and `logical_exp` with Unix timestamp **`1700000300`** (`5 minutes` ahead).
  2. Set a backup physical TTL 12x longer via `EXPIRE hot:hero:home 3600` (`1 hour`) so that even past `logical_exp`, reader threads still have data ready to serve immediately while waiting for a background refresh.
hintsEn: Run `HSET hot:hero:home payload '{"campaign":"MegaSale11.11"}' logical_exp 1700000300`.
Next, run `EXPIRE hot:hero:home 3600` to establish the memory safety net.

redis-ex-r10-5.titleEn: On-Call #1 — Diagnose and Extinguish an iPhone 16 Cache Stampede
redis-ex-r10-5.promptEn:
PagerDuty alerts are firing: PostgreSQL CPU just spiked to `98%` because the ultra-hot key `cache:flash:iphone16` suddenly vanished from Redis!

Perform these exact **2 SRE incident response steps**:
- **Step 1 (Required in the Diagnostic Terminal):** Run `redis-cli TTL cache:flash:iphone16` in the **Diagnostic Terminal** pane to verify the key's state (it will return `-2`, meaning the key is completely gone).
- **Step 2 (Hotfix Script Below):**
  1. Acquire the protection lock `SET lock:rebuild:flash:iphone16 "sre-oncall" NX PX 3000`.
  2. Repopulate `cache:flash:iphone16` with `'{"sku":"ip16pro","price":28990000}'` and a **TTL Jitter** between **`315` and `360` seconds** (do NOT use the round number `300`!).
hintsEn: Run `redis-cli TTL cache:flash:iphone16` in the Diagnostic Terminal above first so the system records the diagnostic check (returns `(integer) -2`).
In the editor below, enter `SET lock:rebuild:flash:iphone16 "sre-oncall" NX PX 3000` and `SET cache:flash:iphone16 '{"sku":"ip16pro","price":28990000}' EX 337`.

R11.titleEn: Distributed Coordination: Lua Distributed Locks, Fencing Tokens & Rate Limiters
R11.summaryEn: Build safe distributed locks that never accidentally delete another owner's lock, understand the Redlock vs Fencing Token debate, and master Fixed Window, Sliding Window ZSet, and Lua Token Bucket rate limiters.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> When an application runs in a single process, in-process locks (`threading.Lock` in Python or `sync.Mutex` in Go) suffice to keep two threads from mutating the same resource concurrently. But once a service scales out to **10 containers across multiple hosts**, two payment requests arriving milliseconds apart can land on 2 independent servers. At that point, the system needs **Redis as a centralized coordinator**:
> - **`Distributed Lock`:** A mechanism to claim exclusive ownership of a resource via the atomic command `SET key <uuid> NX PX <ms>`. The `uuid` uniquely identifies the lock holder, while `PX` ensures the lock auto-expires if the holding container crashes (preventing deadlocks). When releasing the lock, you MUST use a **Lua script** to verify your own `uuid` before deleting, avoiding accidentally deleting the next process's lock.
> - **`GC Pause` & `Fencing Token`:** If the lock-holding process freezes (e.g., a *Garbage Collection Pause*) longer than the `PX` lease duration, the lock expires and moves to another process. To prevent the stalled process from waking up and overwriting newer data, each lock grant should include a **monotonically increasing sequence number (`Fencing Token`: `33`, `34`, `35`...)** so the target Database rejects writes carrying a token older than the latest seen.
> - **`Rate Limiter`:** Caps the maximum number of requests from an account or IP within a time window (mitigating login brute-force attacks and API overload).

steps.headingEn: SRE-Grade Distributed Lock Anatomy (Avoiding 3 Common Pitfalls)
steps.bodyEn:
```visual
kind: compare
title: "Khóa Phân Tán Không An Toàn vs Khóa Phân Tán Chuẩn Production"
subtitle: "Thiếu kiểm tra UUID khi giải phóng khóa có thể dẫn đến xóa nhầm khóa của worker khác đang giữ tài nguyên"
left:
  badge: "KHÔNG AN TOÀN"
  title: "SETNX rời rạc & Nhả khoá bằng DEL trần"
  tone: rose
  code: |
    # 1. Nếu sập giữa 2 dòng -> Khoá chết vĩnh viễn!
    if r.setnx("lock:order:88", "1"):
        r.expire("lock:order:88", 5)

    # ... Worker A bị khựng 6 giây (khoá đã hết hạn & sang tay Worker B) ...
    # 2. Xoá mù quáng -> Xoá luôn khoá đang hợp lệ của Worker B!
    r.delete("lock:order:88")
  lang: python
  bullets:
    - "**Lỗi 1 (Deadlock):** `SETNX` và `EXPIRE` tách rời; mất điện ở giữa làm khoá sống vĩnh viễn (`TTL = -1`)."
    - "**Lỗi 2 (Giá trị tĩnh `'1'`):** Không biết ai mới là chủ sở hữu thực sự của khoá."
    - "**Lỗi 3 (Xoá nhầm khoá người khác):** Gọi `DEL` thẳng thừng phá vỡ hoàn toàn tính loại trừ lẫn nhau."
right:
  badge: "CHUẨN CÔNG NGHIỆP"
  title: "SET uuid NX PX + Lua Compare-And-Delete"
  tone: emerald
  code: |
    -- Bước 1: Chiếm khoá nguyên tử kèm UUID riêng cho từng lượt thuê
    SET lock:order:88 "f47ac10b-worker-03" NX PX 5000

    -- Bước 2: Giải phóng khoá nguyên tử bằng EVAL Lua
    EVAL 'if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
      return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
    else
      return 0
    end' 1 lock:order:88 "f47ac10b-worker-03"
  lang: redis
  bullets:
    - "**Nguyên tử lúc chiếm:** ==`SET key uuid NX PX ms`== thực thi trọn gói trong 1 nhịp."
    - "**Định danh duy nhất mỗi lượt gọi:** Sinh `uuid4()` mới cho từng lần mượn khoá."
    - "**Nguyên tử lúc nhả:** Kịch bản Lua đối chiếu khớp đúng `uuid` mới xoá."
```

> [!TIP] The Redlock vs Fencing Token Debate & Standard Libraries (Don't Roll Your Own)
> - **When using a lock to avoid duplicate work** (preventing Cache Stampede, ensuring 2 servers don't run the same report Cronjob): **a single Redis node + `SET NX PX` + Lua Unlock** is the leanest, most effective choice! In **Python `redis-py`**, the built-in **`with r.lock("lock:order:88", timeout=10):`** automatically generates a `UUID` and unlocks cleanly via Lua! In **Java**, **`Redisson` (`RLock`)** even includes a built-in *Watchdog* that auto-renews the lock if work runs longer than expected; **Go** has **`redsync`**; **Node.js** has **`redlock`**.
> - **When using a lock to protect strict financial correctness** (guarding against lock loss if a Master fails over before replicating to a Replica or during a GC Pause): pair it with a ==Fencing Token (`INCR fencing:order:88`)== and check `WHERE last_token < :token` directly inside PostgreSQL's `UPDATE` statement!

    bullets:
      - "Chỉ tốn đúng **1 khoá String số nguyên** cho mỗi user/IP."
      - "Nhược điểm **Vọt gấp đôi ở mép phút**: Khách gửi 100 req lúc `00:59` và 100 req lúc `01:01` -> lọt **200 req chỉ trong 2 giây**!"

      EVAL 'local s=tonumber(redis.call("GET",KEYS[1]) or "0")
