steps.headingEn: Production Implementation: Lua Scripts & Library Ecosystem
steps.bodyEn:
When integrating a Rate Limiter into a real project, you can use the lightweight Lua script below or leverage battle-tested libraries:
- **Python (`FastAPI` / `Flask` / `Django`):** **`slowapi`** / **`limits`** (backed by `redis://`, supporting both Fixed Window and Moving Window), or **`fastapi-limiter`**.
- **Node.js / TypeScript:** **`rate-limiter-flexible`** or **`@upstash/ratelimit`**.
- **Go:** **`go-redis/redis_rate`** (ships with a rock-solid Lua implementation of GCRA / Token Bucket).

```lua
-- Kịch bản Lua chuẩn cho Token Bucket / Atomic Quota (lưu tại lua/token-bucket-ratelimiter.lua)
-- KEYS[1] = khoá xô thẻ bài | ARGV[1] = sức chứa tối đa | ARGV[2] = số thẻ cần rút
local current = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or ARGV[1])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[2])

if current < requested then
  return -1
end

local remaining = current - requested
redis.call("SET", KEYS[1], tostring(remaining), "EX", 60)
return remaining
```

> [!WARNING] Mandatory Rule for Calling Lua on Redis Cluster
> All key names must be passed through **`KEYS[1]`** (never dynamically concatenate key names inside Lua) and keep script execution under `< 1ms` so it never blocks other connections!

> [!REMEMBER] Core Takeaways from R11
> 1. **Acquiring a distributed lock:** Always combine atomically ==`SET <lockKey> <uniqueUuid> NX PX <leaseMs>`==.
> 2. **Releasing a distributed lock:** Always use ==Lua Compare-And-Delete== (`GET == myUuid` then `DEL`, or use `redis-py`'s `r.lock()` / `Redisson`), plus a **Fencing Token** when strict Database-level protection is required.
> 3. **Choosing a Rate Limiter:** Simple password brute-force blocking -> **Fixed Window**; exact millisecond precision -> **Sliding Window ZSet**; API Gateway-style short-term burst allowance -> **Lua Token Bucket**.

readings.noteEn: A classic 5-line Lua Compare-And-Delete script that completely prevents Pod A from waking up after a GC Pause and deleting Pod B's lock.
readings.taskEn: Why CAN'T we write `if (await redis.get(k) === myToken) await redis.del(k)` in Node.js/Go application code instead of pushing it into `EVAL` Lua?
readings.answerEn: Because splitting it into two network commands (`GET` then `DEL`) leaves a gap: in the millisecond between `GET` (matching the token) and `DEL`, the lock's `PX` lease can expire and be acquired by Pod B — the delayed `DEL` still arrives and wipes out Pod B's lock! Only `EVAL` Lua executes single-threaded and atomically on Redis, guaranteeing nothing interleaves between `GET` and `DEL`.

readings.noteEn: A millisecond-accurate Sliding Window Rate Limiter built with a Sorted Set, packed cleanly into a single network round-trip.
readings.taskEn: Why must each element added via `ZADD` in a Sliding Window Rate Limiter have a unique `member` (`requestId` or `timestamp:random`) rather than reusing the username?
readings.answerEn: In a Sorted Set, `member` values are unique. If you reuse a fixed string as the `member`, each subsequent `ZADD` simply updates the existing element's `score` instead of increasing the element count (`ZCARD`), leaving the counter stuck at `1`!

R11-Q1.qEn: When using a Redis Distributed Lock, why must the stored value be a unique random identifier per acquisition (such as a UUID) rather than a constant like `"1"`?
choicesEn: Because Redis rejects values shorter than 8 characters when the NX flag is set
So that when releasing the lock via Lua, the process can verify the lock still belongs to itself and hasn't expired and been acquired by another process
To encrypt the TCP connection between the application and Redis
To speed up CRC16 hashing by 4x
R11-Q1.explainEn: If Pod A freezes in a GC Pause longer than the `PX` lease, the lock expires and Pod B legitimately acquires it. When Pod A wakes up, comparing UUIDs in the Lua script detects the mismatch against Pod B's UUID, preventing Pod A from deleting Pod B's active lock.

R11-Q2.qEn: The application snippet `if (await redis.get(lockKey) === myUuid) { await redis.del(lockKey); }` is 100% as safe as running a Lua Compare-And-Delete script.
R11-Q2.explainEn: False! Between the two network calls `redis.get()` and `redis.del()`, network/CPU latency exists: right after `get` returns `true`, the lock could hit `PX` expiration and be acquired by another Pod, causing `del` to delete the new owner's lock! It must be bundled into `EVAL` Lua for atomic execution.

R11-Q3.qEn: In a Fixed Window rate limiter on Redis 7+/8, which flag appended to `EXPIRE rl:login:ip 60 ____` ensures the TTL is set only on initial creation and is NOT reset on subsequent requests?
R11-Q3.explainEn: `EXPIRE key seconds NX` sets the expiration only when the key does not currently have a TTL (`TTL == -1`), keeping the initial window boundary fixed.

R11-Q4.qEn: What is the biggest weakness of the **Fixed Window Counter** algorithm that pushes many API systems toward **Sliding Window** or **Token Bucket**?
choicesEn: It cannot run on Linux
The Boundary Burst effect: a user can send up to N requests at second 59 of the previous minute and N requests at second 01 of the next minute, producing 2N requests within 2 seconds
It consumes 1,000x more RAM than a Sorted Set
It wipes all RDB data whenever a window ends
R11-Q4.explainEn: At the boundary between two fixed windows, the quota resets from zero, so actual traffic across a short interval straddling the boundary can spike to double the configured limit.

R11-Q5.qEn: According to Martin Kleppmann's well-known analysis of distributed locks, when absolute correctness is needed at the target storage layer (such as preventing file/balance overwrites after a long GC Pause), what mechanism should be paired with a distributed lock?
choicesEn: Fencing Token (a monotonically increasing sequence number issued per lock acquisition so the Database/Storage rejects operations carrying older tokens)
Reducing the lock TTL to 1 millisecond
Running FLUSHDB after every lock release
Disabling TCP Keepalive
R11-Q5.explainEn: Fencing Tokens push the final validation check down to the target storage resource itself: if Pod A holding token `33` stalls and tries to write late after Pod B holding token `34` has already written, Storage sees `33 < 34` and immediately rejects the stale write.

R11-Q6.qEn: When writing Lua scripts for Redis (`EVAL` / `EVALSHA`), every key name the script touches should be passed explicitly via the `KEYS[...]` array instead of being dynamically concatenated inside Lua code so the script stays compatible with Redis Cluster.
R11-Q6.explainEn: True! Redis Cluster inspects the `KEYS` array prior to executing the script to determine target Hash Slots and ensure all keys reside on the same shard.

R11-Q7.qEn: Which Rate Limiting algorithm models a bucket holding up to `B` tokens refilled steadily at `R` tokens per second — allowing legitimate short-term traffic bursts while keeping the long-term average rate steady?
choicesEn: Fixed Window Counter
Token Bucket
HyperLogLog
GeoHash
R11-Q7.explainEn: Token Bucket is the standard algorithm across modern API Gateways (Kong, Envoy, AWS API Gateway) thanks to cleanly separating instantaneous burst capacity (`capacity B`) from sustained refill rate (`refill rate R`).

R11-FC1.frontEn: What is the industry-standard syntax to acquire and release a Distributed Lock in Redis?
R11-FC1.backEn:
- **Acquire:** `SET lock:<res> <unique_uuid> NX PX <lease_ms>`
- **Release:** Run `EVAL` Lua checking `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`.

R11-FC2.frontEn: What failure scenario happens if you release a distributed lock with a bare `DEL` without checking ownership?
R11-FC2.backEn: Pod A hits a GC Pause or I/O stall longer than `PX` -> lock auto-expires -> Pod B legitimately acquires lock -> Pod A wakes up and calls `DEL`, deleting Pod B's lock -> Pod C jumps in and runs concurrently with Pod B!

R11-FC3.frontEn: What is a Fencing Token and what Distributed Lock flaw does it solve?
R11-FC3.backEn: A monotonically increasing integer (`33, 34, 35...`) issued alongside each lock lease. If a Pod holding token `33` stalls and writes late after a Pod holding token `34`, the Database compares `33 < 34` and rejects the overwrite.

R11-FC4.frontEn: What are the 4 core commands that make up a Sorted Set Sliding Window Rate Limiter?
R11-FC4.backEn:
1) `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` removes timestamps older than the window.
2) `ZADD` records the current timestamp with a unique `requestId`.
3) `ZCARD` counts total requests in the window.
4) `PEXPIRE` auto-cleans the key when the user stops calling.

R11-FC5.frontEn: When should you choose Token Bucket over Sliding Window Log?
R11-FC5.backEn: When you need maximum RAM efficiency (only 2 numeric fields instead of storing every request in a ZSet) and want to allow legitimate short-term **bursts** as long as the average rate stays within limits.

R11-FC6.frontEn: What are the two golden rules for writing Lua scripts for production Redis clusters?
R11-FC6.backEn:
1) Always pass all key names via `KEYS[...]` (never construct key names dynamically inside Lua to avoid `CROSSSLOT` errors on Cluster).
2) Keep scripts ultra-fast (`< 1ms`) with no large loops because Lua blocks the single-threaded Event Loop.

redis-ex-r11-1.titleEn: Acquire an Atomic SET NX PX Distributed Lock to Prevent Deadlocks
redis-ex-r11-1.promptEn:
A bank payout service must guarantee transaction `txn-772` is never processed twice by two Pods. The draft below uses the outdated separate `SETNX` + `EXPIRE` pair and stores a meaningless value `"1"`!

- **Tasks:** Replace it completely with **a single atomic `SET` command** on key `lock:payout:txn-772`:
  1. Store the unique owner identifier `"uuid-pod-a91"`.
  2. Attach the **`NX`** flag (acquire only if unheld) and auto-expiring lease **`PX 5000`** (`5000 milliseconds`).
  3. Do **NOT use `SETNX`**.
hintsEn: Remove the `SETNX` line and write: `SET lock:payout:txn-772 "uuid-pod-a91" NX PX 5000`.
You can also run `PTTL lock:payout:txn-772` to inspect the remaining lease time in milliseconds.

redis-ex-r11-2.titleEn: Safe Lock Release via Lua Compare-And-Delete (Prevent Wrong-Owner Deletion)
redis-ex-r11-2.promptEn:
Redis currently holds 2 movie-seat reservation locks:
- `lock:seat:A1` now belongs to `"owner-bob"` (because Alice's session expired during a GC Pause).
- `lock:seat:B2` currently belongs legitimately to `"owner-alice"`.

If Alice calls bare `DEL` on both keys, she will **accidentally delete Bob's lock on seat `A1`**!

- **Tasks:** Write a Lua script inside **`EVAL`** that checks `redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1]` before calling `redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])` (returning `0` on owner mismatch), and run it as `"owner-alice"` on both keys:
  1. Run `EVAL` to release `lock:seat:A1` with `ARGV[1] = "owner-alice"` → Must return `(integer) 0` and leave Bob's lock intact!
  2. Run `EVAL` to release `lock:seat:B2` with `ARGV[1] = "owner-alice"` → Must return `(integer) 1` and delete `lock:seat:B2`!
hintsEn: Standard command template: `EVAL 'if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1]) else return 0 end' 1 lock:seat:A1 "owner-alice"`.
Duplicate a second line changing `lock:seat:A1` to `lock:seat:B2`.

redis-ex-r11-3.titleEn: Brute-Force-Proof Fixed Window Rate Limiter with EXPIRE ... NX
redis-ex-r11-3.promptEn:
The login gateway limits each IP address to `5` password attempts per `60-second` window. A classic beginner bug is calling `EXPIRE key 60` **without the `NX` flag** on every request — unintentionally resetting the 60-second timer every time the attacker tries again!

- **Tasks:** Implement the proper Redis 7+/8 counting flow for IP `203.0.113.9` on key `rl:login:203.0.113.9`:
  1. Increment the counter with `INCR rl:login:203.0.113.9`.
  2. Set the 60-second TTL **only if the key has no TTL yet** using `EXPIRE rl:login:203.0.113.9 60 NX`.
  3. Simulate 20 seconds elapsing with `ADVANCE_TIME 20000`, then run the `INCR` + `EXPIRE ... 60 NX` pair again (the counter must rise to `2` and the remaining TTL must be `40s`, not reset back to `60s`!).
hintsEn: Simply append the `NX` flag to the end of both `EXPIRE rl:login:203.0.113.9 60 NX` lines.
Thanks to `NX`, the second `EXPIRE` call returns `(integer) 0` and preserves the remaining 40 seconds of the initial window.

redis-ex-r11-4.titleEn: Millisecond-Accurate Sliding Window Rate Limiter with Sorted Sets
redis-ex-r11-4.promptEn:
The system clock is currently at **`1700000000000`** ms. We are enforcing a **`60,000 ms` (`60-second`) Sliding Window** for user `u42` on Sorted Set `rl:api:u42` (meaning any old request with a timestamp `<= 1699999940000` has slid out of the window and must be purged).

`rl:api:u42` currently contains 2 expired old requests and 2 active requests.

- **Tasks:** Execute all 4 Sliding Window steps for the new request `"req-now-5"`:
  1. Purge old out-of-window requests with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:api:u42 -inf 1699999940000`.
  2. Record the current request with `ZADD rl:api:u42 1700000000000 "req-now-5"`.
  3. Count total valid requests in the window with `ZCARD rl:api:u42` (must equal `3`).
  4. Set an auto-cleanup TTL on the entire ZSet with `PEXPIRE rl:api:u42 60000`.
hintsEn: `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rl:api:u42 -inf 1699999940000` will remove the exact 2 elements `req-old-1` and `req-old-2`.
Then add `ZADD rl:api:u42 1700000000000 "req-now-5"`, `ZCARD rl:api:u42`, and `PEXPIRE rl:api:u42 60000`.

redis-ex-r11-5.titleEn: Lua Atomic Inventory / Token Guard Against Overselling
redis-ex-r11-5.promptEn:
The Flash Sale inventory has exactly **`5`** consoles left at key `stock:ps5:limited`. Calling an unconditional `DECRBY` would push inventory negative!

- **Tasks:** Write a Lua `EVAL` command taking `KEYS[1]` as the stock key and `ARGV[1]` as the requested quantity:
  - If `tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or "0") >= tonumber(ARGV[1])`, call `redis.call("DECRBY", KEYS[1], ARGV[1])` and return the remaining stock.
  - Otherwise, do not decrement and return `-1`.
- Test **2 consecutive orders** using that exact `EVAL` script:
  1. Order 1 requests **`3`** units (`ARGV[1] = 3`) → Succeeds, remaining stock is **`2`**.
  2. Order 2 requests **`4`** units (`ARGV[1] = 4`) → Rejected with **`(integer) -1`**, preserving stock at **`2`** (never going negative!).
hintsEn: In Lua, `redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])` returns a string, so wrap it in `tonumber(...)` before comparing `>= tonumber(ARGV[1])`.
Invoke line 1 with trailing arguments `1 stock:ps5:limited 3`, and line 2 with trailing arguments `1 stock:ps5:limited 4`.

R12.titleEn: jemalloc Memory Allocation, Eviction Policies (LRU vs LFU) & RAM Quotas on K8s
R12.summaryEn: Master the 24-bit redisObject layout, LFU's probabilistic Morris Counter, the bio_lazy_free background reclamation mechanism, and how to size RAM limits to prevent OOMKilled (Exit Code 137).

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> Because **Redis stores all data in RAM**, when memory reaches its limit (`maxmemory`) without proper configuration, Redis will either **reject all new write commands (`OOM command not allowed`)** or have its process terminated by the Linux kernel with **`OOMKilled (Exit Code 137)`**. To operate reliably, you must master 4 core mechanisms:
> - **`jemalloc` (Memory Allocator):** Redis's default memory allocator, which partitions RAM into fixed-size bins (`8B`, `16B`, `32B`...) to optimize allocation speed and minimize **Memory Fragmentation**.
> - **`Eviction` (Key Reclamation When Memory Is Full):** When `used_memory` reaches `maxmemory`, the `maxmemory-policy` setting determines whether Redis rejects new writes (`noeviction`) or automatically deletes existing keys to make room.
> - **`LRU` (*Least Recently Used*) vs `LFU` (*Least Frequently Used*):**
>   - **`LRU`** prioritizes evicting keys that have been **unaccessed for the longest time** — the drawback is that a single one-off batch scan can push genuinely hot keys out of the cache.
>   - **`LFU`** prioritizes evicting keys with the **lowest access frequency** (with time-based decay) — ==protecting genuinely hot keys with high read frequency==.
> - **`Headroom` (30%–35% Memory Buffer):** On Docker/Kubernetes, if a container has a `4 GB` RAM limit, `maxmemory` should only be set to around **`2.6 GB` (`65%`)**; the remaining space is reserved for network connection buffers, the `Replication Buffer`, and `Copy-on-Write` overhead during `BGSAVE`.

```visual
kind: illustration
diagram: "redis:r12"
badge: "Memory & Eviction Internals · R12"
title: "Cấu trúc Không gian RAM jemalloc, 24-bit redisObject & Luồng Giải phóng (Eviction)"
subtitle: "Sự chênh lệch giữa used_memory và used_memory_rss cùng thuật toán lấy mẫu xấp xỉ Approximated LFU"
caption: "Redis không dùng danh sách liên kết đôi tốn 16-24 bytes/khoá cho LRU mà nhúng khéo léo dấu thời gian/tần suất vào đúng 24 bit sẵn có của header redisObject!"
callouts:
  - num: 1
    label: "used_memory vs used_memory_rss"
    desc: "used_memory là byte logic do jemalloc cấp; used_memory_rss là trang RAM vật lý Linux thực giữ (tính cả phân mảnh và trang Copy-on-Write)."
    tone: cyan
  - num: 2
    label: "Approximated LFU (Morris Counter)"
    desc: "Lấy mẫu ngẫu nhiên maxmemory-samples=10 khoá, dùng 8 bit đếm xác suất logarit (đo tới ~1 triệu lượt truy cập) và 16 bit giảm dần theo phút."
    tone: emerald
  - num: 3
    label: "65% K8s Pod Headroom"
    desc: "Luôn đặt maxmemory khoảng 65%-70% giới hạn RAM của Container để chừa 30%-35% khoảng thở cho BGSAVE fork COW, Output Buffer và jemalloc."
    tone: amber
```

steps.headingEn: Checking Memory Usage with INFO memory and RAM Fragmentation Ratio
steps.bodyEn:
Storing `2GB` of string data does not mean the `redis-server` process consumes only `2GB` of physical RAM! The ratio **`mem_fragmentation_ratio = used_memory_rss / used_memory`** in `INFO memory` is the RAM health thermometer every engineer must know how to read:

- [>] **`1.0` – `1.4` (Ideal & Healthy):** `jemalloc` packs memory blocks tightly with low natural overhead.
- [>] **`> 1.5` (High Memory Fragmentation):** Often occurs after deleting tens of thousands of small keys interspersed with large keys, leaving memory pages riddled with holes like Swiss cheese that cannot yet be returned to the OS. **Smooth remediation:** Enable online automatic defragmentation with **`activedefrag yes`**!
- [!] **`< 1.0` (RED ALERT — Swapping to Disk!):** When actual physical RAM held (`rss`) is smaller than the logical data Redis is managing, the server has run out of physical RAM and the OS is pushing Redis's memory pages to disk **Swap**! Latency will spike from `0.2ms` to `500ms` — disable Swap (`vm.swappiness=0`) and add RAM immediately!

steps.headingEn: Comparing the 8 Eviction Policies (maxmemory-policy): Choosing the Right One per Role
steps.bodyEn:
When `used_memory` hits `maxmemory`, Redis relies on `maxmemory-policy` to decide how to handle incoming writes:

```visual
kind: groups
title: "Phân Nhóm 8 Chính Sách maxmemory-policy Trong Redis 8"
subtitle: "Chọn sai chính sách có thể làm mất dữ liệu trong hàng đợi hoặc khiến API bị từ chối lệnh ghi!"
columns: 2
items:
  - num: 1
    title: "Nhóm allkeys-* (Đào thải trên toàn bộ khoá)"
    badge: "Chuẩn Pure Cache"
    tone: emerald
    desc: "Cho phép Redis thu hồi bất kỳ khoá nào ít giá trị nhất (kể cả khoá lỡ quên đặt EXPIRE)."
    bullets:
      - "==`allkeys-lfu` (Khuyên dùng số 1 cho Cache)==: Giữ lại các khoá có tần suất truy cập thực tế cao nhất, chống ô nhiễm cache khi có tác vụ quét hàng loạt."
      - "**`allkeys-lru`:** Đào thải khoá lâu chưa được chạm vào nhất trong tập lấy mẫu."
      - "**`allkeys-random`:** Xoá ngẫu nhiên khi mọi khoá có tần suất đọc ngang nhau."
    code: |
      maxmemory 2gb
      maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu
      maxmemory-samples 10
    codeLang: redis-conf
  - num: 2
    title: "Nhóm noeviction (Cấm xoá tuyệt đối)"
    badge: "Chuẩn Queue / Stream / Lock"
    tone: rose
    desc: "Mặc định gốc của Redis: bảo toàn 100% dữ liệu, trả lỗi OOM cho lệnh ghi mới khi đầy RAM."
    bullets:
      - "**Bắt buộc dùng** khi Redis đóng vai trò Hàng đợi (`Streams` / `BullMQ` / `Celery`), Khoá phân tán (`Lock`), hoặc trạng thái phiên thanh toán."
      - "Các lệnh đọc (`GET`, `XREADGROUP`) và lệnh xoá (`DEL`, `UNLINK`) vẫn chạy bình thường để bạn giải phóng chỗ."
    code: |
      maxmemory 4gb
      maxmemory-policy noeviction
    codeLang: redis-conf
  - num: 3
    title: "Nhóm volatile-* (Chỉ xoá khoá có gắn TTL)"
    badge: "Dùng chung hỗn hợp"
    tone: amber
    desc: "Chỉ thu hồi các khoá có đặt thời hạn sống (EXPIRE), giữ nguyên các khoá vĩnh viễn (TTL = -1)."
    bullets:
      - "Gồm **`volatile-lfu`**, **`volatile-lru`**, **`volatile-ttl`** (ưu tiên xoá khoá sắp hết hạn nhất) và **`volatile-random`**."
      - "**Lưu ý:** Nếu trong RAM không còn khoá nào có gắn TTL để xoá, nhóm `volatile-*` sẽ báo lỗi OOM y hệt `noeviction`! Tốt nhất nên tách riêng máy chủ Cache và máy chủ Queue."
    code: |
      maxmemory-policy volatile-lfu
    codeLang: redis-conf
  - num: 4
    title: "Bộ 3 Cờ Giải phóng Nền (Lazyfree)"
    badge: "Chống giật độ trễ P99"
    tone: cyan
    desc: "Chuyển việc thu hồi vùng nhớ nặng nhọc từ luồng chính sang luồng nền bio_lazy_free."
    bullets:
      - "`lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes`: Không chặn luồng chính khi đào thải khoá lúc đầy RAM."
      - "`lazyfree-lazy-expire yes`: Không chặn luồng chính khi khoá lớn hết hạn TTL."
      - "`lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes`: Không chặn luồng chính khi lệnh `SET` ghi đè lên một khoá cũ khổng lồ!"
    code: |
      lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes
      lazyfree-lazy-expire yes
      lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes
    codeLang: redis-conf
```

> [!TIP] Under the Hood: How Redis Counts LFU Frequency in Just 8 Bits
> Instead of spending dozens of extra bytes per key, Redis cleverly reuses **24 available bits** in each key's object header: the **first 16 bits** store a minute-level timestamp to gradually decay "hotness" when a key stops being read (`lfu-decay-time`), while the **last 8 bits** (`0..255`) run a **logarithmic probabilistic counter (Morris Counter)**! Newly created keys start at `5` so they aren't unfairly evicted right after creation. You can inspect a key's hotness yourself with `OBJECT FREQ <key>` (when LFU is enabled) or its idle time with `OBJECT IDLETIME <key>` (when LRU is enabled)!

steps.headingEn: Configuring Safe maxmemory Limits When Running Redis on Docker and Kubernetes
steps.bodyEn:
A very common mistake in container deployments is giving a Kubernetes Pod `limits.memory: 4Gi` and then setting `maxmemory 4gb` in `redis.conf` — causing the Pod to be abruptly killed every night during background snapshots with ==`OOMKilled (Exit Code 137)`==!

```yaml
# Cấu hình chuẩn Production cho Pod Redis trên Kubernetes (Chừa 35% khoảng thở Headroom)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: redis-cache
spec:
  serviceName: redis-cache-headless
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis-cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis-cache
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:8.0-alpine
          args:
            - "--maxmemory"
            - "2688mb"              # ~65% của 4096Mi -> Chừa ~1.4GiB đệm an toàn!
            - "--maxmemory-policy"
            - "allkeys-lfu"
            - "--lazyfree-lazy-eviction"
            - "yes"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: 4Gi           # Đặt requests == limits để đạt mức ưu tiên Guaranteed QoS!
            limits:
              memory: 4Gi
```

**Three mandatory reasons to reserve 30%–35% RAM headroom above `maxmemory`:**
1. **Temporary duplicated memory (*Copy-on-Write*) during disk snapshots (`BGSAVE`):** Covered in detail in lesson `R13` next.
2. **Client & Replica Output Buffers (*Output & Replication Buffers*):** Hold queued data waiting to be sent over the network to thousands of connections.
3. **`jemalloc` management overhead and natural fragmentation** (`10%–20%`).

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways from R12
> 1. **Clear Role Separation:** **Pure Cache** clusters should use **`allkeys-lfu`** + `maxmemory-samples 10`; **Queue / Stream / Lock** clusters must keep **`noeviction`**.
> 2. Always enable all 3 directives: ==`lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, `lazyfree-lazy-server-del`== to avoid latency spikes when reclaiming large keys.
> 3. **The 65%–70% Headroom Rule:** For a container limited to `4Gi`, set `maxmemory` to around `2.6GB–2.8GB` and set `requests.memory == limits.memory`.

readings.noteEn: Production-standard configuration for a dedicated Pure Cache Redis node: explicit RAM ceiling, prioritizing hot keys with allkeys-lfu, and asynchronous memory reclamation.
readings.taskEn: Why are all three directives `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, and `lazyfree-lazy-server-del` set to `yes` in this file?
readings.answerEn: By default, Redis frees the memory of evicted, expired, or overwritten keys synchronously on the main thread! If it hits a Hash/Set with hundreds of thousands of elements, the main thread stalls for tens of milliseconds. Enabling all 3 `lazyfree` flags offloads all heavy `free()` work to the `bio_lazy_free` background thread.

readings.noteEn: Default configuration trap that causes peak-hour outages at night: forgetting to set a `maxmemory` cap while leaving `noeviction` enabled on a Cache cluster.
readings.taskEn: What two different consequences occur when `maxmemory 0` (unlimited) is set on a Linux/K8s host compared to setting `maxmemory 2gb` with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`?
readings.answerEn: With `maxmemory 0` on K8s, Redis overflows past the Pod's `resources.limits.memory` and gets killed instantly by the Linux Kernel OOMKiller (Exit Code `137`, wiping all in-memory data). With `maxmemory 2gb` and `noeviction`, the process stays alive but rejects all new write commands with `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'`!

R12-Q1.qEn: When running `INFO memory` on a Redis node and seeing `mem_fragmentation_ratio: 0.72` (less than `1.0`), what dangerous condition is actually happening on the server?
choicesEn: Redis automatically compressed the data to save 28% memory using an AI algorithm
The server has exhausted physical RAM, so the Linux Kernel is pushing some of Redis's memory pages to disk Swap, causing latency to spike hundreds of times
All keys in Redis are 64-bit integers
TLS mode is operating normally
R12-Q1.explainEn: `mem_fragmentation_ratio = used_memory_rss / used_memory`. When `used_memory_rss` (actual physical RAM pages held) is less than the logical bytes allocated by Redis, the OS has paged part of Redis's memory out to disk Swap — a severe performance bottleneck for an in-memory database!

R12-Q2.qEn: To implement LRU/LFU, Redis attaches two doubly-linked list pointers (`prev` and `next`, costing an extra 16 bytes on 64-bit machines) to every single key to maintain a globally exact ordering.
R12-Q2.explainEn: False! To save every byte of RAM when holding hundreds of millions of keys, Redis does NOT use a doubly-linked list; instead, it reuses the 24 bits already present in `redisObject` combined with an **approximated random sampling** algorithm (`maxmemory-samples`, default 5, recommended 10).

R12-Q3.qEn: Which `maxmemory-policy` is the top recommendation for modern **Pure Cache** clusters to prioritize keeping the most frequently accessed keys (preventing cache pollution during one-off batch scans)?
R12-Q3.explainEn: `allkeys-lfu` (Least Frequently Used across the entire keyspace) uses a logarithmic Morris Counter plus a decay time to retain genuinely hot keys, outperforming `allkeys-lru` against Cache Pollution.

R12-Q4.qEn: Why, on Kubernetes, if you allocate `resources.limits.memory: 4Gi` to a Redis Pod, should you set Redis's `maxmemory` to only around `2.6GB – 2.8GB` (65%–70%) instead of the full `4GB` ceiling?
choicesEn: Because Kubernetes charges a 30% licensing fee on every Pod's RAM capacity

To leave safe headroom for Copy-on-Write pages during `fork()` for BGSAVE/AOF Rewrite, Client/Replication output buffers, and jemalloc fragmentation overhead — preventing the Linux OOMKiller from killing the Pod with Exit Code 137
Because Redis 8 cannot address more than 3GB of RAM on 64-bit architectures
To reserve 1.3GB of RAM for installing Chrome inside the same Redis container
R12-Q4.explainEn: `maxmemory` only caps the keyspace (`dataset`), excluding dynamic connection buffers, `jemalloc` fragmentation, and especially duplicated memory pages during `fork()` when persisting to disk.

R12-Q5.qEn: If a Redis cluster dedicated to **payment Streams** queues and **Distributed Locks** hits `maxmemory`, which `maxmemory-policy` keeps data safest?
choicesEn: allkeys-random
allkeys-lru
noeviction
volatile-ttl
R12-Q5.explainEn: For unprocessed message queues and distributed coordination locks, silently evicting keys causes lost orders or breaks Mutual Exclusion. `noeviction` explicitly rejects writes (triggering monitoring alerts immediately) while preserving 100% of existing data.

R12-Q6.qEn: When `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru` is set, if NONE of the keys in Redis have a TTL (`TTL = -1`), Redis will reject new writes and return an OOM error just like `noeviction`.
R12-Q6.explainEn: True! The `volatile-*` policies can only select eviction candidates from keys with an expiration (`expires`) set. If that set is empty, Redis evicts nothing and returns an OOM error.

R12-Q7.qEn: Which subcommand after `OBJECT` lets you read the LFU access frequency counter (`0..255`) of a specific key?
R12-Q7.explainEn: `OBJECT FREQ <key>` returns the key's current logarithmic Morris Counter value (whereas `OBJECT IDLETIME <key>` returns idle seconds used for LRU).

R12-FC1.frontEn: What is the difference between `used_memory` and `used_memory_rss` in `INFO memory`?
R12-FC1.backEn:
- **`used_memory`**: Total logical bytes managed internally by Redis's `jemalloc` allocator.
- **`used_memory_rss`**: Total physical RAM pages actually allocated to the process by the Linux kernel (including fragmentation and overhead).

R12-FC2.frontEn: What are the three diagnostic thresholds for `mem_fragmentation_ratio`?
R12-FC2.backEn:
- **`1.0 – 1.4`**: Normal and healthy.
- **`> 1.5`**: High memory fragmentation -> enable `activedefrag yes`.
- **`< 1.0`**: Critical! The process is being pushed to disk **Swap**, collapsing performance.

R12-FC3.frontEn: Why is `allkeys-lfu` superior to `allkeys-lru` for most caching systems?
R12-FC3.backEn: LRU only looks at the most recent access, making it vulnerable to a one-off batch scan (*Cache Scan Pollution*) evicting hot keys that were idle for just a few seconds. LFU uses the Morris Counter frequency tracker to reliably protect genuinely popular keys.

R12-FC4.frontEn: What is the 65%–70% Headroom rule when deploying Redis on Docker / Kubernetes?
R12-FC4.backEn: Set `maxmemory` to only **65%–70%** of the Pod's `resources.limits.memory` (e.g., `2688mb` on a `4Gi` Pod) to leave room for `fork()` Copy-on-Write during RDB/AOF persistence, Client/Replication Output Buffers, and `jemalloc` — avoiding cgroup `OOMKilled (137)`.

R12-FC5.frontEn: What is the purpose of the 3 directives `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, and `lazyfree-lazy-server-del`?
R12-FC5.backEn: They offload memory deallocation (`free()`) during eviction at full RAM, TTL expiration, and overwriting existing keys to the `bio_lazy_free` background thread, keeping the main thread from stalling on Bigkeys.

R12-FC6.frontEn: How are the 24 bits of the `lru` field in `redisObject` partitioned in LFU mode?
R12-FC6.backEn: The **upper 16 bits** store a minute-precision timestamp for decaying hotness (`lfu-decay-time`), while the **lower 8 bits** (`0..255`) run the logarithmic probabilistic **Morris Counter** (`lfu-log-factor`).

redis-ex-r12-1.titleEn: Configure Production Pure Cache redis.conf with allkeys-lfu and High-Accuracy Sampling
redis-ex-r12-1.promptEn:
You are configuring `redis.conf` for a product cache cluster running on a 3GB RAM VM. The default config file below currently has `maxmemory 0` (unlimited) and `noeviction`!

- **Task:** Edit `redis.conf` to satisfy all 3 Pure Cache standards:
  1. Cap dataset memory with **`maxmemory 2gb`** (`2 GiB`).
  2. Set the eviction policy to **`maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`** to retain the most frequently read keys.
  3. Increase the approximation sample size to **`maxmemory-samples 10`** (instead of the default `5`) for near-exact LFU accuracy.
hintsEn: Change `maxmemory 0` to `maxmemory 2gb`.
Change `maxmemory-policy noeviction` to `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu` and set `maxmemory-samples 10`.

redis-ex-r12-2.titleEn: Protect a Redis Message Broker / Lock Cluster with the noeviction Policy
redis-ex-r12-2.promptEn:
Unlike a Cache cluster, this Redis cluster stores **payment event Redis Streams** and **Distributed Locks (`lock:*`)**. A teammate accidentally copied `allkeys-lru` from the Cache cluster — if RAM fills up, Redis will **silently delete unprocessed payment events**!

- **Task:** Fix `redis.conf` for this Broker cluster running on a 6GB RAM host:
  1. Declare an explicit memory ceiling **`maxmemory 4gb`** (to avoid being killed abruptly by the OS OOMKiller).
  2. Set **`maxmemory-policy noeviction`** so critical data keys are never silently evicted (returning an explicit error to trigger RAM scaling alerts).
hintsEn: Set `maxmemory 4gb` and change `maxmemory-policy` back to `noeviction`.
In practice, always separate Pure Cache (`allkeys-lfu`) and Broker/State (`noeviction`) into two independent instances.

redis-ex-r12-3.titleEn: Enable the Lazyfree Trio & Active Defrag to Eliminate P99 Latency Spikes
redis-ex-r12-3.promptEn:
Your Redis cluster's P99 latency graph occasionally spikes to `85ms` whenever large Set/Hash keys expire via TTL or get overwritten, while `mem_fragmentation_ratio` stays stuck at `1.78`.

- **Task:** Complete `redis.conf` by setting all 4 background memory optimization mechanisms to **`yes`**:
  1. `lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes`
  2. `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes`
  3. `lazyfree-lazy-server-del yes`
  4. `activedefrag yes`
hintsEn: Change the value from `no` to `yes` for all 4 lines: `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, `lazyfree-lazy-server-del`, and `activedefrag`.

redis-ex-r12-4.titleEn: Inspect Morris Counter (OBJECT FREQ) and Hot-Patch Eviction Without Restarting
redis-ex-r12-4.promptEn:
A live Redis Cache node cannot be restarted right away, yet it is misconfigured with `maxmemory-policy` set to `noeviction` and `lazyfree-lazy-eviction` disabled.

- **Task:**
  1. Inspect the LFU access frequency of a hot key with `OBJECT FREQ cache:item:hot` and the idle time of a cold key with `OBJECT IDLETIME cache:item:cold`.
  2. Hot-patch the eviction policy immediately using `CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`.
  3. Enable asynchronous eviction reclamation with `CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes`.
  4. Run `INFO memory` to verify the new configuration is active.
hintsEn: `CONFIG SET` updates most memory parameters live in RAM without dropping existing client connections (on a real host, you can also run `CONFIG REWRITE` afterward to persist to disk).
Run `CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu` and `CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes`.

redis-ex-r12-5.titleEn: Apply the 65% Memory Headroom Rule to a Redis StatefulSet on Kubernetes
redis-ex-r12-5.promptEn:
Pod `redis-cache-0` on Kubernetes keeps crashing with **`OOMKilled (Exit Code 137)`** every night during `BGSAVE` because a previous engineer set `limits.memory: 2Gi` while passing `--maxmemory 2048mb` (0% headroom for Copy-on-Write and Output Buffers)!

- **Task:** Upgrade the `StatefulSet` manifest below to follow the **65%–70% Headroom Rule** and **Guaranteed Memory QoS**:
  1. Increase both `resources.requests.memory` and `resources.limits.memory` on the `redis` container to **`4Gi`** (`4096Mi`).
  2. Change the argument right after `--maxmemory` in the `args` array to **`"2688mb"`** (~65.6% of `4096Mi`, leaving over `1.3GiB` of safety buffer).
  3. Change the value after `--maxmemory-policy` from `noeviction` to **`"allkeys-lfu"`**.
hintsEn: Change `args[1]` from `"2048mb"` to `"2688mb"` and `args[3]` from `"noeviction"` to `"allkeys-lfu"`.
Don't forget to update both `requests.memory: 4Gi` and `limits.memory: 4Gi` near the bottom of the YAML file.

R13.titleEn: Persistence: RDB Snapshots, Copy-on-Write, Multi-Part AOF & Hybrid Persistence
R13.summaryEn: Analyze BGSAVE's fork() Copy-on-Write mechanism, RPO/Latency trade-offs across the 3 appendfsync modes, Multi-Part AOF architecture in Redis 8, and Linux kernel tuning to prevent crashes during snapshots.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> Although Redis processes data directly in RAM, it supports **Persistence to disk** to recover data after restarts or power outages through the following mechanisms:
> - **`RDB` (*Redis Database Snapshot*):** Periodically takes a point-in-time binary snapshot of the entire dataset (e.g., every 15 minutes) into `dump.rdb`. The file is compact, easy to back up to Object Storage (S3/GCS), and restores tens of GBs in seconds; however, changes made since the last snapshot are lost.
> - **`AOF` (*Append-Only File*):** Appends every write command (`SET`, `INCR`, `HSET`...) to a log file and syncs it to disk on a configured schedule (default **`appendfsync everysec`** — once per second), reducing potential data loss on power failure to ==at most `<= 1 second`==.
> - **`Hybrid RDB + AOF` (Default in Redis 7/8):** When compacting the AOF file (`BGREWRITEAOF`), the baseline dataset is written in compact binary **RDB** format followed by trailing **AOF** commands — ==combining second-level durability with fast restarts==.
> - **`fork()` & `Copy-on-Write` (`CoW`):** When running `BGSAVE`, the main process calls Linux `fork()` to spawn a child process sharing the same memory **Page Table** in milliseconds. The main process continues serving clients normally; the OS only duplicates a `4KB` memory page when the main process modifies that specific page.

```visual
kind: illustration
src: "/illustrations/redis/redis-rdb-aof-persistence.jpg"
diagram: "redis:r13"
alt: "Cơ chế lưu trữ bền vững RDB Copy-on-Write kết hợp nhật ký AOF Hybrid trong Redis 8"
badge: "Persistence Internals · R13"
title: "Cơ chế Luồng BGSAVE Copy-on-Write & Cấu trúc Multi-Part Hybrid AOF"
subtitle: "Cách tiến trình con dùng chung bảng trang bộ nhớ ảo (Page Table) với tiến trình cha và cấu trúc RDB Preamble + AOF Tail"
caption: "Trên Redis 7.0+ và Redis 8, tệp AOF được tách thành thư mục appendonlydir gồm tệp gốc (base RDB), tệp tăng trưởng (incr AOF) và tệp manifest quản lý nguyên tử."
callouts:
  - num: 1
    label: "BGSAVE & OS fork() Copy-on-Write"
    desc: "Tiến trình cha chỉ nhân bản bảng Page Table (vài mili-giây); trang RAM 4KB chỉ bị copy thực sự khi có lệnh ghi mới sửa đúng trang đó."
    tone: cyan
  - num: 2
    label: "AOF appendfsync everysec"
    desc: "Ghi nối đuôi vào Page Cache của OS và gọi fsync() xuống đĩa mỗi 1 giây ở luồng nền bio_aof_fsync — cân bằng vàng giữa tốc độ và RPO <= 1s."
    tone: amber
  - num: 3
    label: "Hybrid RDB Preamble (Multi-Part AOF)"
    desc: "Khi chạy BGREWRITEAOF, phần nền được nén thành định dạng nhị phân RDB gọn nhẹ, theo sau là luồng lệnh AOF mới nhất — khởi động nhanh gấp 5-10 lần!"
    tone: emerald
```

steps.headingEn: RDB Snapshot Mechanics: Difference Between BGSAVE (Background) and SAVE (Main-Thread Blocking)
steps.bodyEn:
- [+] **`BGSAVE` (*Background Save* — Always use in Production):** Calls `fork()` to spawn a background child process that writes data to a temporary file and atomically renames it to `dump.rdb`, while the main thread continues serving client commands normally.
- [!] **`SAVE` (*Synchronous Save* — Never use in Production):** Writes the entire dataset to disk directly on the single main thread, freezing all client connections for tens of seconds. In Production, administrators typically disable `SAVE` via ACL permissions.

steps.headingEn: Comparing the 3 AOF Disk-Sync Modes (appendfsync)
steps.bodyEn:
When you execute a write command with `appendonly yes`, Redis writes the command into the OS page cache (*OS Page Cache* — still in RAM) and relies on **`appendfsync`** to decide when to physically flush it to SSD (`fsync()`):

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Cạm Bẫy Đốt Cháy Ổ Đĩa (appendfsync always) vs Điểm Cân Bằng Vàng (everysec)"
subtitle: "Hiểu rõ ranh giới giữa lệnh write() vào bộ đệm hệ điều hành và lệnh fsync() ép ghi vật lý xuống SSD"
left:
  badge: "GIẢM MẠNH THÔNG LƯỢNG"
  title: "appendfsync always (Ép đĩa ở mọi lệnh)"
  tone: rose
  code: |
    appendonly yes
    # Mỗi lệnh ghi đều phải chờ ổ đĩa vật lý
    # xác nhận ghi xong mới trả OK cho ứng dụng!
    appendfsync always
  lang: redis-conf
  bullets:
    - "**Thông lượng sụt giảm 50–100 lần:** Kéo tốc độ Redis từ `100,000 ops/s` tụt xuống ngang tốc độ ghi vật lý của ổ đĩa mạng (chỉ còn vài nghìn lệnh/giây)."
    - "**Làm mòn ổ SSD rất nhanh** do ép ghi liên tục."
    - "Nếu nghiệp vụ bắt buộc không được mất dù chỉ 1 giao dịch khi rút phích điện (như sổ cái ngân hàng), hãy ghi giao dịch gốc vào PostgreSQL!"
right:
  badge: "CHUẨN PRODUCTION"
  title: "appendfsync everysec + Hybrid RDB Preamble"
  tone: emerald
  code: |
    appendonly yes
    appendfsync everysec
    aof-use-rdb-preamble yes
    auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
    auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb
  lang: redis-conf
  bullets:
    - "**Tốc độ gần như RAM thuần:** Luồng chính không phải chờ đĩa; luồng phụ `bio_aof_fsync` gom trọn 1 giây gọi `fsync()` đúng 1 lần!"
    - "==Tối đa chỉ mất <= 1 giây dữ liệu== nếu cả máy chủ mất nguồn điện đột ngột (còn nếu chỉ tiến trình Redis văng lỗi mà HĐH Linux vẫn sống thì **mất 0 giây**!)."
    - "**Multi-Part AOF (Redis 7/8):** Tự động nén gọn nhật ký khi kích thước tăng gấp đôi (`100%`) mà không làm phình bộ nhớ tạm."
```

*(The third mode is `appendfsync no`: letting the OS flush buffers on its own roughly every ~30 seconds — fastest, but risks losing up to 30 seconds of data on power loss.)*

steps.headingEn: Three Critical Infrastructure Settings to Keep BGSAVE from Failing at Midnight
steps.bodyEn:
```visual
kind: anatomy
title: "Ba Thiết Lập Hạ Tầng Quan Trọng Cho Redis Persistence"
subtitle: "Từ tắt ghi đĩa cho Pure Cache đến hai tham số nhân Linux giúp fork() mượt mà"
items:
  - keyword: 'save ""'
    role: "Tắt sạch RDB cho cụm Pure Cache"
    tone: sky
    summary: "Mặc định Redis TỰ BẬT sẵn RDB ngay cả khi bạn không viết dòng save nào trong redis.conf!"
    bullets:
      - "Nếu cụm Redis chỉ thuần làm bộ đệm tạm (dữ liệu gốc nằm hết ở PostgreSQL), tắt ghi đĩa giúp tiết kiệm 100% I/O đĩa và tránh tốn RAM Copy-on-Write."
      - "Để tắt hoàn toàn, phải khai báo rõ cả hai dòng: ==`save \"\"` và `appendonly no`==."
    example: |
      save ""
      appendonly no
    lang: redis-conf
  - keyword: "vm.overcommit_memory=1"
    role: "Tham số Linux chống lỗi fork() thiếu RAM"
    tone: amber
    summary: "Cho phép Linux cấp phát bộ nhớ lạc quan để `BGSAVE` không bị từ chối khi Redis dùng trên 50% RAM máy chủ."
    bullets:
      - "Nếu để mặc định `0`, một tiến trình Redis `20GB` trên máy `32GB` gọi `fork()` sẽ bị Linux từ chối vì tưởng nhầm tiến trình con cần thêm hẳn `20GB` mới, dù thực tế Copy-on-Write chỉ tốn vài trăm MB!"
    example: |
      sysctl -w vm.overcommit_memory=1
    lang: shell
  - keyword: "THP = never"
    role: "Tắt Transparent Huge Pages trên máy chủ"
    tone: rose
    summary: "Giữ kích thước trang bộ nhớ nhỏ gọn `4KB` thay vì gộp thành khối khổng lồ `2MB`."
    bullets:
      - "Nếu bật THP (`2MB`/trang), trong lúc đang `BGSAVE`, ứng dụng chỉ sửa đúng **1 byte** cũng bắt Linux nhân bản nguyên cả tảng `2MB` (gấp 512 lần!), gây giật độ trễ nặng."
    example: |
      echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
    lang: shell
```

steps.headingEn: Deploying a Persistent Redis Container with Docker Compose v2
steps.bodyEn:
When running Redis with persistence enabled on Docker or Kubernetes, all RDB files and the `appendonlydir` directory live inside **`/data`**. Never forget to mount a **persistent Volume** at `/data` — otherwise every container recreation will wipe all data!

```yaml
services:
  redis-durable:
    image: redis:8.0-alpine
    container_name: redis-durable
    command:
      - "redis-server"
      - "--appendonly"
      - "yes"
      - "--appendfsync"
      - "everysec"
      - "--aof-use-rdb-preamble"
      - "yes"
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  redis-data:
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways from R13
> 1. **Pure Cache Clusters:** Disable disk writes completely with **`save ""`** + **`appendonly no`** to optimize RAM and I/O.
> 2. **Durable State / Streams / Session Clusters:** Enable ==`appendonly yes` + `appendfsync everysec` + `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`== alongside periodic RDB snapshots backed up to Object Storage (S3/GCS).
> 3. Only run background **`BGSAVE` / `BGREWRITEAOF`** (never synchronous `SAVE`), and on Linux hosts always configure `vm.overcommit_memory=1` + disable `THP`.

readings.noteEn: Standard configuration for a durable-state Redis node: combining 1-second AOF fsync with a compact binary RDB preamble for both sub-second RPO and ultra-fast startup.
readings.taskEn: Why is `appendfsync everysec` considered the sweet spot instead of `appendfsync always`?
readings.answerEn: `appendfsync always` forces the OS kernel to physically sync to disk after EVERY single write command before replying to the client, collapsing throughput from tens of thousands of ops/s down to a few hundred disk IOPS. `everysec` offloads `fsync()` to a background thread once per second: write speed remains nearly at pure-RAM levels while maximum data loss exposure (RPO) is just 1 second!

readings.noteEn: Double performance trap when misconfiguring RDB/AOF or accidentally running synchronous `SAVE` in Production.
readings.taskEn: What happens to thousands of connected clients if an admin runs `SAVE` instead of `BGSAVE` on a Redis node holding 12GB of data?
readings.answerEn: `SAVE` sequentially dumps all 12GB of RAM to disk on the single main Event Loop thread! Throughout those tens of seconds of disk I/O, Redis is 100% frozen, failing to answer any `PING`, `GET`, or `SET` — and can even trick Sentinel into thinking the Master is dead and triggering a false Failover!

R13-Q1.qEn: Which Linux kernel mechanism allows `BGSAVE` to dump a 20GB snapshot to disk WITHOUT immediately duplicating 20GB of physical RAM and without blocking the main thread?
choicesEn: Table-level Mutex Locking with multithreading
The `fork()` system call combined with Copy-on-Write (COW), sharing read-only memory pages and duplicating only those 4KB pages actually modified by new writes
Compressing all RAM onto a GPU
Temporarily disconnecting all client TCP sockets while saving
R13-Q1.explainEn: Upon `fork()`, the child process inherits a virtual memory page table pointing to the same physical RAM pages as the parent. Only pages modified by incoming writes during the RDB save are copied separately by the Linux kernel (Copy-on-Write).

R13-Q2.qEn: If you omit all `save` and `appendonly` directives from `redis.conf`, Redis disables all disk persistence by default and runs purely in RAM.
R13-Q2.explainEn: False! By default, Redis ENABLES automatic RDB snapshots (`save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000`). If you want a pure in-memory cache with zero disk writes, you must explicitly specify `save ""` and `appendonly no`.

R13-Q3.qEn: Which standard AOF `appendfsync` mode syncs data to physical disk on a background thread once per second — delivering near-RAM throughput while capping potential data loss on power outage at 1 second?
R13-Q3.explainEn: `appendfsync everysec` is the default and recommended setting for nearly all Production environments with AOF enabled.

R13-Q4.qEn: What core problem does **Hybrid Persistence** (`aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`) solve when operating AOF on large datasets?
choicesEn: It automatically replicates the AOF file directly to a MySQL database

During AOF compaction (`BGREWRITEAOF`), the baseline data is written in ultra-compact binary RDB format followed by trailing incremental AOF commands — making startup reload times many times faster than replaying millions of text commands
It disables RAM completely and serves all GET commands directly from disk
It automatically encrypts user passwords with RSA-4096
R13-Q4.explainEn: Plain-text AOF files containing tens of millions of commands make Redis restart recovery very slow due to sequential replay. RDB Preamble combines RDB's instant binary loading with AOF's 1-second durability tail.

R13-Q5.qEn: On a Linux host with `32GB` RAM where Redis holds `20GB` of data, `BGSAVE` suddenly fails with: `Can't save in background: fork: Cannot allocate memory`. Which Kernel parameter must be enabled on the Host to fix this permanently?
choicesEn: sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
Set Transparent Huge Pages to always
Lower ulimit -n to 64
R13-Q5.explainEn: With the default `vm.overcommit_memory=0`, the Linux kernel pessimistically assumes the forked child might need another full `20GB` (`20+20 > 32GB`) and rejects the allocation. Setting `vm.overcommit_memory=1` lets `fork()` succeed based on actual Copy-on-Write usage.

R13-Q6.qEn: On a Production Linux server running Redis with RDB or AOF Rewrite enabled, administrators should DISABLE Transparent Huge Pages (`echo never > .../transparent_hugepage/enabled`) to prevent latency spikes and RAM bloat during Copy-on-Write.
R13-Q6.explainEn: True! With Huge Pages (`2MB`) enabled, even a single `SET` modifying a few bytes on a page during `BGSAVE` forces Linux to copy the entire `2MB` page instead of a standard `4KB` page (512x heavier).

R13-Q7.qEn: If both `save 900 1` (RDB) and `appendonly yes` (AOF) are enabled on the same Redis node, which source will `redis-server` prioritize when loading data on restart?
choicesEn: Always load from dump.rdb because the file is smaller
Always prioritize loading from AOF (`appendonlydir`) because AOF holds a more complete and up-to-date dataset state than periodic RDB snapshots
Delete both files and start empty to avoid conflicts
Randomly load one of the two files based on even/odd clock seconds
R13-Q7.explainEn: When `appendonly yes` is enabled, Redis always loads from AOF on boot (which already bundles an RDB base + incremental AOF files in Redis 7+/8's Multi-Part AOF architecture) because it guarantees higher data completeness than a standalone RDB snapshot.

R13-FC1.frontEn: Quick comparison of core pros and cons between RDB and AOF?
R13-FC1.backEn:
- **RDB:** Compact binary snapshot, extremely fast boot loading, ideal for remote backups — but loses data written between snapshot intervals (minutes).
- **AOF:** Logs every mutating command, high durability (`RPO <= 1s` with `everysec`) — but produces larger files and requires periodic `BGREWRITEAOF`.

R13-FC2.frontEn: Why is running `SAVE` strictly forbidden in Production, requiring `BGSAVE` instead?
R13-FC2.backEn: `SAVE` writes to disk synchronously on the single-threaded Event Loop, freezing all clients for the entire dump duration. `BGSAVE` calls `fork()` so a child process persists in the background via Copy-on-Write.

R13-FC3.frontEn: How do you completely disable Persistence for a dedicated Pure Cache Redis node?
R13-FC3.backEn:
You must set both directives:
`save ""` (clears all default RDB schedules)
`appendonly no` (disables AOF).

R13-FC4.frontEn: How do the three AOF `appendfsync` modes differ?
R13-FC4.backEn:
- **`always`**: `fsync` after every command (extremely slow, bottlenecked by disk IOPS).
- **`everysec`**: `fsync` every second on a background thread (**Production Standard**, near-RAM speed, at most 1s loss on power outage).
- **`no`**: Lets the OS flush buffers (~every 30s, fastest but high data-loss risk).

R13-FC5.frontEn: What are the 3 components inside `appendonlydir` in Redis 7+/8's Multi-Part AOF architecture?
R13-FC5.backEn:
1) **Base file** (`.base.rdb` — compact binary RDB Preamble baseline).
2) **Incremental files** (`.incr.aof` — newly appended command streams).
3) **Manifest file** (`.manifest` — tracks file versions atomically).

R13-FC6.frontEn: What two Linux kernel settings are mandatory on a Host running Redis with BGSAVE / AOF Rewrite?
R13-FC6.backEn:
1) `sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1` (prevents `fork: Cannot allocate memory` errors).
2) Disable **Transparent Huge Pages (`never`)** (prevents copying massive 2MB pages that spike latency and RAM during COW).

redis-ex-r13-1.titleEn: Completely Disable RDB & AOF for a Pure In-Memory Cache Node
redis-ex-r13-1.promptEn:
This Redis cluster only caches rendered category HTML pages (100% of the source of truth lives in PostgreSQL). Yet its current configuration enables both `save 60 1000` and `appendonly yes`, wasting hundreds of MB/s of disk I/O and causing RAM spikes during `fork()`!

- **Task:** Edit `redis.conf` to turn off all disk persistence:
  1. Replace the RDB schedule lines with **`save ""`** (an empty quoted string to clear all default save points).
  2. Set **`appendonly no`** to disable the AOF log.
hintsEn: Remove both `save 900 1` and `save 60 1000`, replacing them with a single line `save ""`.
Change `appendonly yes` to `appendonly no`.

redis-ex-r13-2.titleEn: Configure Production-Grade Hybrid RDB + AOF Persistence (RPO <= 1s)
redis-ex-r13-2.promptEn:
You are configuring a Redis node storing shopping carts and checkout sessions. The lead architect requires at most **1 second of data loss** during a power outage, automatic AOF compaction when the file doubles in size (starting from at least `64mb`), and **Hybrid RDB Preamble** for ultra-fast restarts.

- **Task:** Update `redis.conf` with all 5 standard directives:
  1. `appendonly yes`
  2. `appendfsync everysec`
  3. `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`
  4. `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100`
  5. `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb`
hintsEn: Update `appendonly yes`, `appendfsync everysec`, and `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` in turn.
Set `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100` (avoid `0`, as `0` disables automatic AOF rewrites!) and `auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb`.

redis-ex-r13-3.promptEn:
Before server upgrade maintenance, the operations team needs a fresh RDB snapshot and a compacted AOF log. An intern's old script uses synchronous **`SAVE`** — which on a 15GB RAM cluster would freeze the entire API for 25 seconds!

- **Task:**
  1. Replace the dangerous `SAVE` command with the non-blocking background snapshot command **`BGSAVE`**.
  2. Trigger background AOF compaction with **`BGREWRITEAOF`**.
  3. Run `INFO persistence` to inspect persistence status.
hintsEn: Delete the `SAVE` line completely, then enter 3 lines in order: `BGSAVE`, `BGREWRITEAOF`, `INFO persistence`.

redis-ex-r13-4.titleEn: Mount a Named Volume at /data to Preserve AOF Data on Docker Compose v2
redis-ex-r13-4.promptEn:
Every time the DevOps team runs `docker compose up -d` to apply a patch to the `redis-state` container, all shopping cart data is wiped even though `--appendonly yes` is enabled — because `compose.yaml` forgot to declare and mount a **Named Volume** at `/data`!

- **Task:** Complete the `compose.yaml` file below:
  1. Change the `--appendonly` flag from `"no"` to **`"yes"`** and add the flag pair `"--appendfsync"`, `"everysec"` in `services.redis-state.command`.
  2. Mount the persistent volume **`redis-state-data:/data`** in `services.redis-state.volumes`.
  3. Declare `redis-state-data: {}` under the top-level `volumes:` key.

R14.titleEn: Replication (PSYNC2), Split-Brain Prevention & Automatic Failover with Sentinel
R14.summaryEn: Master the Replication Backlog mechanism to prevent cascading Full Resyncs, configure min-replicas-to-write to prevent Split-Brain, and understand the SDOWN -> ODOWN -> Failover election workflow of a 3-Sentinel cluster.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> Disk persistence covered in `R13` preserves data across restarts, but **if the physical server loses power completely**, the service remains unavailable (*Downtime*) until a new machine is provisioned. To achieve **High Availability** and recover automatically within seconds, Redis relies on the following mechanisms:
> - **`Master` & `Replica`:** The **Master** node handles all Write commands and asynchronously replicates the command stream to **Replica** nodes (used to offload Reads and serve as standby replacements if the Master fails).
> - **`PSYNC2` & `Replication Backlog`:** When a Replica experiences a brief network drop and reconnects, the Master consults a circular buffer (`repl-backlog-size`) in RAM to send only the missing commands (*Partial Resync*) based on `replicationId` and `offset`, avoiding a full transfer of all data from scratch (*Full Resync*).
> - **`Redis Sentinel`:** A monitoring system consisting of an **odd number `>= 3` of independent processes** that continuously check Master health:
>   - 1 Sentinel receives no response -> marks it locally suspected (**`SDOWN`** — *Subjectively Down*).
>   - **A `Quorum` of Sentinels** (e.g., `2/3`) confirm the Master is unreachable -> transitions to an objective state (**`ODOWN`** — *Objectively Down*), elects a Leader, and ==automatically promotes the most up-to-date Replica to be the new Master==, while updating the new address for applications.
> - **`Split-Brain`:** A network partition where one side of the cluster has already elected a new Master while the isolated old Master continues accepting Write commands from some clients, causing those writes to be lost when the network recovers and the old Master is demoted to a Replica.

```visual

diagram: "redis:r14"

    desc: "Bộ đệm vòng lưu các byte lệnh gần nhất theo replicationId + offset; nếu quá nhỏ (mặc định 1MB) sẽ gây bão Full Resync khi chập chờn mạng."
    tone: cyan
  - num: 2
    label: "SDOWN -> ODOWN -> Raft Failover"
    desc: "1 Sentinel thấy quá hạn là SDOWN; đủ quorum=2 xác nhận là ODOWN; bầu Leader đạt đa số majority (2/3) mới thực thi REPLICAOF NO ONE."
    tone: amber
  - num: 3

    tone: rose
```

steps.headingEn: PSYNC2 Replication Mechanism & Preventing Cascading Full Resyncs
steps.bodyEn:
By default, replication in Redis is **asynchronous (*Async Replication*)**: once the Master writes to RAM, it immediately replies `OK` to the application (`< 0.5ms`), then streams the command asynchronously to Replicas in the background. When a Replica reconnects after a network interruption, there are 2 scenarios:

- [>] **Full Resynchronization (Very resource-intensive):** On initial connection or when fallen too far behind, the Master must call `BGSAVE` to snapshot the entire RAM dataset and send it over the network for the Replica to reload from scratch (on fast internal networks, you can enable `repl-diskless-sync yes` to stream directly over sockets without hitting disk).
- [>] **Partial Resynchronization (`PSYNC2` — Fast catch-up sync):** The Master maintains a circular buffer **`repl-backlog-size`** in RAM. If the Replica's read position (`offset`) is still within this circular buffer, the Master only sends the few MBs of missed commands!
- [!] **Default configuration pitfall:** By default, Redis `repl-backlog-size` is only **`1mb`**! On a system writing `20MB/s`, just a `0.1-second` network blip overflows the `1mb` buffer, forcing every Replica into a Full Resync! In Production, always raise ==`repl-backlog-size` to `64mb – 256mb`==.

steps.bodyEn:

steps.headingEn: Preventing Split-Brain Data Loss & Configuring Application Connections
steps.bodyEn:
> [!WARNING] How do you prevent a network-isolated old Master from still accepting orders and losing data?
> If the network link between two zones is severed: on the other side, `2/3` Sentinels have promoted `Replica-1` to **New Master**, while on this side a few application containers can still reach the **Old Master** and keep writing orders to it — when the network reconnects, the Old Master is demoted to Replica and wipes out those newly accepted orders!
> How to block writes on an isolated Master in `redis.conf`: set ==`min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag 10`== — if the Master does not see at least 1 Replica responding within 10 seconds, it **automatically rejects writes (`NOREPLICAS`)** immediately to protect data integrity!

```conf
# Cấu hình chống Split-Brain & tối ưu Backlog trên Master:
min-replicas-to-write 1
min-replicas-max-lag 10
repl-backlog-size 64mb
```

When writing application code with **Sentinel**, you **do not hardcode the Master's IP**; instead, you pass the list of 3 Sentinel ports (`26379`) so the SDK automatically discovers the current Master:

```python
# Python (redis-py): Tự động tìm Master (để Ghi) và Replica (để chia tải Đọc) qua Sentinel!
from redis.sentinel import Sentinel

sentinel = Sentinel(
    [("10.0.1.11", 26379), ("10.0.1.12", 26379), ("10.0.1.13", 26379)],
    socket_timeout=0.5,
)
master = sentinel.master_for("mymaster", decode_responses=True)
replica = sentinel.slave_for("mymaster", decode_responses=True)

master.set("order:501", "paid", ex=3600)
print(replica.get("order:501"))
```

> [!TIP] In the Cloud: Self-Host Sentinel or Use Managed HA (ElastiCache / Memorystore)?
> - If you self-manage on Linux servers or Kubernetes (**Bitnami Redis / Spotahome Redis Operator**), deeply understanding **Sentinel + StatefulSet** is essential for troubleshooting incidents.
> - If running on public clouds (**AWS ElastiCache for Valkey/Redis Multi-AZ**, **GCP Memorystore**, **Redis Cloud**, **Upstash**), the provider wraps failure detection and automatic DNS/endpoint failover to the standby Replica underneath — but you **still need to understand asynchronous replication and the `WAIT 1 1000` command** to know that failover during a hardware crash can still lag by a few milliseconds of trailing data!

steps.headingEn: Deploying StatefulSet + Headless Service for Redis HA on Kubernetes
steps.bodyEn:
On Kubernetes, stateful database nodes must use a **`StatefulSet`** paired with a **Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`)** so each node keeps a stable internal DNS name (`redis-ha-0`, `redis-ha-1`, `redis-ha-2`) and dedicated persistent volume:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis-ha-headless
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: redis-ha
  ports:
    - name: redis
      port: 6379
      targetPort: 6379
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: redis-ha
spec:
  serviceName: redis-ha-headless
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis-ha
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis-ha
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:8.0-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways from R14
> 1. Increase **`repl-backlog-size` to `64mb–256mb`** and keep **`replica-read-only yes`** on Replicas to ensure smooth **PSYNC2 Partial Resync**.
> 2. Always deploy an ==odd number `>= 3` of Sentinel nodes== across 3 independent servers/zones so majority elections never deadlock in a tie.
> 3. Bound the data-loss window during a network partition (*Split-Brain*) using **`min-replicas-to-write 1`** + **`min-replicas-max-lag 10`**.

readings.noteEn: Standard 3-Sentinel configuration monitoring a Master-Replica cluster: 5-second failure threshold, 2/3 quorum, and sequential sync limit to avoid saturating the new Master's bandwidth.
readings.taskEn: What exactly does the number `2` at the end of `sentinel monitor mymaster 10.0.1.10 6379 2` mean, and how does it differ from the vote count needed to elect the Leader executing Failover?
readings.answerEn: `quorum = 2` is the minimum number of Sentinels that must agree the Master is unresponsive to promote its state from `SDOWN` to `ODOWN` (Objectively Down). However, to actually command a Replica promotion to Master, a Sentinel must win a Leader election with an **absolute majority of all known Sentinels** (`majority = N/2 + 1`, e.g., with 5 Sentinels and `quorum = 2`, it still takes `3/5` votes to trigger Failover!).

readings.noteEn: Complete 1 Master + 2 Replicas + 3 Sentinels setup on Docker Compose v2 ready to test pulling the plug for automatic failover.
readings.taskEn: Why do Sentinel HA architectures always deploy at least **3 Sentinel processes** on 3 separate physical/VM machines instead of placing 2 Sentinels on the Master and Replica machines themselves?
readings.answerEn: If there are only 2 nodes (Master + Sentinel1 on Machine A, Replica + Sentinel2 on Machine B) and Machine A loses power, only 1 Sentinel remains alive on Machine B — it can never reach the `2/2` majority required to elect a Leader and execute Failover! Deploying an odd number of `3` Sentinels on 3 independent nodes guarantees that losing any 1 machine still leaves `2/3` votes to self-heal within seconds.

R14-Q1.qEn: Why does keeping the default `repl-backlog-size 1mb` in a high-write-throughput Production environment risk causing a cascading outage during a few seconds of network instability?
choicesEn: Because a 1MB buffer converts Hash data types into List types

Because the 1MB circular buffer overflows in under 1 second of network hiccup, preventing Replicas from using Partial Resync (PSYNC2) upon reconnection and forcing the Master to fork() a Full Resync that consumes double Copy-on-Write RAM and network bandwidth
Because Redis automatically closes port 6379 when the backlog is full
Because Sentinel refuses to monitor any Master whose backlog is smaller than 10GB
R14-Q1.explainEn: `repl-backlog-size` is the temporary retention window that lets Replicas catch up on missed commands (`PSYNC2`). Setting it to `64mb–256mb` ensures brief network interruptions recover smoothly without resending the entire RDB file.

R14-Q2.qEn: In a 5-Sentinel cluster configured with `sentinel monitor mymaster 10.0.1.10 6379 2`, having only 2 Sentinels alive (with the other 3 shut down) is enough for the cluster to automatically perform Failover.
R14-Q2.explainEn: False! `quorum = 2` is only enough to mark the Master as `ODOWN` (Objectively Down). To actually elect a Sentinel Leader to run the Failover, the consensus algorithm always requires an **absolute majority of total known Sentinels** (`majority = 5/2 + 1 = 3` votes)!

R14-Q3.qEn: What is the standard command since Redis 5+ to detach a Replica from its old Master and promote it to an independent Master?
R14-Q3.explainEn: `REPLICAOF NO ONE` stops the current replication stream and switches the node's role from `replica` to `master`, allowing it to accept new writes.

R14-Q4.qEn: Which dangerous distributed-systems problem does pairing `min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag 10` on the Master mitigate?
choicesEn: Automatically compresses JSON data to reduce size by 50%

Minimizes Split-Brain data loss: if the old Master is network-isolated from all Replicas for over 10 seconds (while Sentinels on the other side promote a new Master), the old Master automatically rejects new writes from Pods stuck on its side
Doubles the speed of the KEYS * command
Allows applications to write directly to every Replica
R14-Q4.explainEn: By locking down writes after 10 seconds without Replica contact, the window during which an isolated Master can mistakenly accept "orphaned" data is tightly bounded to at most ~10 seconds.

R14-Q5.qEn: When the Sentinel Leader picks one Replica among several healthy Replicas to promote to the new Master, what is the first criterion evaluated (after filtering nodes with equal `replica-priority > 0`)?
choicesEn: Pick the node with the highest IP address
Pick the Replica with the highest `replication offset` (meaning it has received the most recent data from the old Master)
Pick the node with the least RAM
Pick randomly by coin flip
R14-Q5.explainEn: Sentinel's selection priority order: 1) Lower non-zero `replica-priority` wins first -> 2) If tied, pick the node with the **highest `replication offset`** (least data loss) -> 3) If still tied, pick the lexicographically smallest `runid`.

R14-Q6.qEn: When the old Master server loses power and later boots back up after Sentinel has already completed Failover to a new Master, Sentinel will automatically reconfigure that old server to become a Replica following the new Master.
R14-Q6.explainEn: True! Sentinel continues monitoring the old Master's address; as soon as it comes back online, Sentinel sends `REPLICAOF <new-master>` to safely demote it into a replica without fighting for Master ownership.

R14-Q7.qEn: What is the standard default TCP port that **Redis Sentinel** listens on to communicate with peers and return Master info to Client SDKs?
R14-Q7.explainEn: Redis Server defaults to port `6379`, while Redis Sentinel defaults to port `26379` (adding `20000`).

R14-FC1.frontEn: What is the difference between Full Resynchronization and Partial Resynchronization (`PSYNC2`)?
R14-FC1.backEn:
- **Full Resync:** The Master runs `BGSAVE` and transfers the entire RDB over the network for the Replica to reload from scratch (very costly in COW RAM & bandwidth).
- **Partial Resync (`PSYNC2`):** After brief disconnects, the Master sends only the missing command bytes from the circular **`repl-backlog-size`** buffer using `(replid, offset)`.

R14-FC2.frontEn: Distinguish between `SDOWN` and `ODOWN` states in Redis Sentinel.
R14-FC2.backEn:
- **`SDOWN` (Subjective Down):** A single Sentinel's local assessment when the Master fails to reply to `PING` for longer than `down-after-milliseconds`.
- **`ODOWN` (Objective Down):** An objective cluster state reached when at least **`quorum`** Sentinels agree the Master is down, unlocking Failover election.

R14-FC3.frontEn: Why should a Sentinel cluster always have at least 3 nodes (an odd number like 3 or 5) on separate machines?
R14-FC3.backEn: To tolerate the complete failure of 1 physical host while still retaining **`2/3` majority votes** to elect a Sentinel Leader and perform automatic Failover without deadlocking.

R14-FC4.backEn: Blocks the current connection until all preceding write commands on this connection are acknowledged as replicated to at least `<numreplicas>` replicas (or `<timeout>` ms elapses) — strengthening synchronous durability for critical transactions.

R14-FC5.frontEn: How do you prevent Split-Brain data loss on a network-isolated Master?
R14-FC5.backEn:
Configure on the Master:
`min-replicas-to-write 1`
`min-replicas-max-lag 10`
If the Master loses contact with all Replicas for more than 10 seconds, it automatically stops accepting new writes.

R14-FC6.frontEn: Why must Redis HA on Kubernetes use `StatefulSet` + Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) instead of `Deployment`?
R14-FC6.backEn: Because each Redis/Sentinel node needs a **stable DNS identity** (`redis-ha-0`, `redis-ha-1`, ...) and dedicated persistent `PVC` storage bound consistently across restarts.

R15.titleEn: Redis Cluster: 16,384 Hash Slots Sharding, Gossip & Solving CROSSSLOT
R15.summaryEn: Break past single-node RAM and CPU ceilings with decentralized sharding: analyze the CRC16(key) mod 16384 formula, Gossip protocol on port +10000, MOVED/ASK routing, eliminating CROSSSLOT errors with {HashTag}, and avoiding the Hot-Slot anti-pattern.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Core Concepts & Real-World Problem
> In `R14`, the **1 Master + 2 Replicas + Sentinel** topology provides high availability, yet remains bounded by the resources of a **single Master node**:
> 1. **RAM Ceiling:** When data grows to `100 GB – 500 GB` on one machine, background snapshots (`BGSAVE`) and restart recovery become very slow.
> 2. **Write CPU Ceiling:** Every write command (`SET`, `HSET`, `ZADD`, `XADD`) still funnels through the **Master's single main thread** (`~100k – 150k ops/s`).
>
> **==Redis Cluster== (*Horizontal Sharding*)** overcomes these limits by partitioning data across multiple Master nodes running in parallel via 3 mechanisms:
> - **`Hash Slots` (`0` to `16383`):** The entire keyspace is divided into a fixed **16,384 Hash Slots**. In a 3-Master cluster (**3 Shards**): Node 1 owns slots `0..5460`, Node 2 owns `5461..10922`, and Node 3 owns `10923..16383`.
> - **Direct hash-based routing:** For each key, the client computes `CRC16(key) % 16384` to determine the exact slot and sends the command directly to the Master owning that slot in **1 network hop (1-hop)** without an intermediary proxy.
> - **`CROSSSLOT` Error & `{HashTag}`:** Multi-key commands (`MGET`, `MULTI/EXEC`, `EVAL` Lua) require all keys to reside in the **same Hash Slot**, or Redis returns a `CROSSSLOT` error. Wrapping a substring in curly braces `{u42}` (e.g., `user:{u42}:profile` and `user:{u42}:cart`) tells Redis to hash only `u42`, guaranteeing all keys for the same entity land in the same slot.

steps.headingEn: Inside the 16,384 Hash Slots Architecture & Smart Routing
steps.bodyEn:
The standard routing formula used by every Redis Cluster client library:

$$\text{HASH\_SLOT}(k) = \text{CRC16}(\text{effective\_key}(k)) \bmod 16384$$

> [!TIP] Why did Redis choose `16,384` (`2^14`) instead of `65,536` (`2^16`)? And when should you adopt Cluster?
> - Cluster nodes continuously exchange heartbeat messages (*Gossip PING/PONG*) carrying a bitmap of owned slots: with `16,384` slots, this bitmap is only **`2 KB`** (instead of `8 KB`), cutting internal bandwidth by 75% while easily scaling up to 1,000 nodes!
> - **Practical architecture advice:** Do not rush into a 6-node Cluster if your dataset is under `16 GB` and under `80,000 ops/s` — a **Sentinel HA** setup (or a vertically multithreaded engine like **DragonflyDB** / **Valkey Multi-AZ**) is far simpler and never suffers from `CROSSSLOT` errors! Only adopt **Redis Cluster / Valkey Cluster** when you genuinely need to exceed single-node RAM or single-node Write throughput.

steps.headingEn: Dual TCP Ports & Routing Redirects: -MOVED vs -ASK
steps.bodyEn:
Every Redis node running in Cluster mode **always requires 2 open TCP ports on the firewall**:
- [>] **Client-facing port (`port`, default `6379`):** Serves Python / Node.js / Go application traffic.
- [>] **Inter-node Cluster Bus port (`port + 10000`, default `16379`):** Where Redis nodes run leader elections to promote a Replica when a Master fails (**no external Sentinel needed!**) and propagate slot maps. Forgetting to open port `16379` between hosts is the #1 configuration mistake that prevents nodes from forming a cluster!

When you add a 4th shard and migrate slots to the new host online (*Live Resharding*), Smart Clients automatically handle two redirect signals:
